review_text: This is a really attractive large park in the town of Kandy, full of wonderful trees, shrubs and plants, many from different parts of the world. Entry is relatively cheap and I would suggest paying a little extra to tour the park with a driver on one of the electric buggies (it is very hot to walk around and explore the whole park - there's a lot to see and the drivers are quite knowledgeable). Most of the trees etc. have descriptive plaques, and you'll notice from the information that many were planted by famous people, some over a hundred years ago. In one area in some fir trees, you'll almost certainly see roosting bats, which was quite a surprise. The Royal Palm avenue is very nice too. Don't miss the Orchid House near the entrance before you leave. Very good.

review_text:
Although my wife and are lovers of all things historical, occasionally we need to refresh the mind and relax. The Gardens were included on our tour itinerary and provided a welcome interlude from the intensity of the UNESCO sites. 
The origins of the Gardens date to 1371 and they were declared a Royal Garden during the reign of King Kirti Sri Rajasinghe between 1747 - 1780. The Gardens on their present site were established in 1821 and cover an area of 60ha. showcasing over 4,000 species. The informative guide map that we received on entry contained a detailed legend and history of the Gardens. We spent approx. three hours strolling the walkways and admiring the beauty of the flora and it's diversity. The Orchid House held a marvelous display and variety of exotic blooms. We enjoyed the Flower garden with many annuals and perennials in bloom. The Palm Avenues are spectacular and include Royal, Cabbage and  Palmyrah, not to be ignored and great for photos, especially the Coco de Mer of Seychelles notoriety. We saw some of the tallest grasses in the world, stands of bamboos on River Drive, including the giant bamboo of Burma. We enjoyed the Fernery, Spice Garden, Cacti and the Arboretum. 
Interesting plaques recognizing world leaders and renowned visitors who planted trees there. Lovely way to spend a morning and then adjourn to the pleasant cafÃ© near the entrance.

review_text:
One of the main attractions in Kandy.  Entrance fees are 2000 Rps per person.

If, like us your time is more limited you can hire a golf buggy for another 2000 Rps (although unfortunately you can't drive it yourself!!).  The guide will point out trees planted by various celebrities and royalty.  Although, I don't think this does the gardens justice and, in retrospect, would have preferred to wander through the pathways and enjoy them at a more sedate pace.

As well as all the interesting trees, plants and orchids you can see monkeys and fruit bats.

Enjoy!

We had the choice of walking the gardens ourselves - or taking a tour on an electric buggy.
We took the buggy - with some 6 other folk, and in a little over an hour saw as much as 3 hours of walking ( in the heat).

The time saving was only one advantage - the buggy driver was an excellent guide that helped appreciate the various plants - and the historic connection of the gardens.

The ride cost us LKR500 each.

review_text:
We easily got a tuk tuk from our hotel to take us to the gardens. Entry fee is about $15 CDN each person. There is a coffee/gift shop at what is the entrance and the exit area. Public washrooms, which are very clean, are at the entrance and throughout the gardens.

review_text:
My wife and myself are currently holidaying in Sri Lanka and this afternoon we visited the lovely Royal Botanical Gardens of Peradeniya in Kandy.

After paying our SLR 1,500 (Â£7 approx) non-resident adult entrance fees, we spent a couple of hours exploring the extensive Gardens which will shortly (2021) be celebrating their 200th Anniversary. When I say extensive, we barely scratched the service but still had time to visit the impressive Orchard House.

I also much enjoyed - particularly, as many of these had involved various members of the British Royal Family - seeing the number of trees planted by VIPs over the years. My personal highlight, however, was not Botanical by nature but seeing the literally thousands of Fruit Bats (Flying Foxes) that were certainly making their presence felt!

All in all, a most enjoyable visit to what - by any standards - are first-rate Botanical Gardens.

There's also an old suspension bridge you can cross, but I wasn't brave enough to attempt it. I spent 2 hours walking around and I don't think I even saw half of it. The gift shop also has really good quality items! If you haven't done your gift shopping and you're at the gardens, do a bit there and save yourself the headache. I found some of the same items from the gift shop at other places and the quality wasn't as good.

review_text: The garden was very large and nice to walk through.  It wasn't as well kept as others I've seen, and not quite as lush, but if you like botanical gardens, you won't want to miss this one.  The plant house and orchid house are small, but have nice varieties.  There is a small suspension bridge towards the back that goes over the river.  It is nice to walk out on it and take a photo.  There are also a couple lanes with palm trees on either side and they make a nice photo opportunity if you can squeeze in between the girls making duck lips and taking Instagram shots.  There is also a large bougainvillea you can sit under and it makes a nice photo too.

review_text:
Well-maintained park, nice flora (plants / trees / flowers) with some cute fauna around. It's pretty and spacious, and nice for a walk on a fine day, but nothing too special, if you compare it with all the other botanical gardens that lots of countries also have.

Or maybe the hoards of flying foxes around are pretty special, if you ask me. They were all flying around in the skies, looking for a spot to rest amongst the tall trees. I'm not sure if that's a seasonal sight, but I saw them when I visited in March.

However for them to be collecting entrance fees for it seems a bit of a money-sucking move. If I were to do away with any humility here, you're welcome to visit my country's botanical gardens. Singapore's Botanic Gardens is bigger, prettier, UNESCO-listed, and free to enter.

Just sayin'.

The gardens are big and nicely laid out, another legacy of the British Colonial era. The air was fresh, nice and cool in the morning and very relaxing.

review_text:
For us this was the highlight of our visit to Kandy.  The gardens are excellent.  Beautifully laid out, well documented and surprisingly peaceful.

They compare very favourably with Kew and those in Madeira.  You do not need to be heavily into gardening or a botanist to enjoy these gardens - just relax and walk.

One word of caution.  It can be very hot, though there is a lot of shade.  Take plenty of water, or, if the heat is problem, use the buggy for a guided tour.

A very peaceful place to visit after the intensity of the surrounding city.

There is also a bus which takes about ten people.

review_text:
We spend a couple of hours here at the end of our day that started in Dambulla and ended in Kandy, and they were a thoroughly enjoyable couple of hours. If we hadn't told our driver to come back in two hours we might have stayed a little longer, but I think we saw most of the highlights.
The orchids are of course fabulous, but to me the most impressive were the tress with plaques showing who had planted them and one. I must say the future Czar Nicholas II did a great job, as did Edward VII while Prince of Wales.
You wouldn't miss a great deal by skipping the suspension bridge
My one regret was that we were too early to see the flying foxes, and I failed to find the trees they were roosting in. You wouldn't think 24,000 of them could hide so well
Lots of rather sweet young local couple walking round holding hands

review_text:
This Royal Botanical garden is really beautiful. We were there for about two hours which was insufficient. Allow as much time as you can as the grounds are vast. If you are short on time, it might be better to take a guide.
The gardens are set in a loop in the Mahawli Ganga (river)  on about 150 acres of land but it feels more spacious.
 Highlights for me: Lovely Orchid house, Royal Palm Avenue, Suspension Bridge, Sri Lankan shaped pond, The Great lawn, the rows of trees planted by visiting dignatories over the years, the fruit bats & the macaque monkeys.

review_text: I will begin by saying that I've been to more than my share of overpriced attractions in Asia. This garden, if you are a fan of gardens that is, is worth the 1500 LKR entrance fee. The place is absolutely huge, rubbish free, and very well maintained. I wandered around for 3 hours and could have spent longer there. I've certainly seen better collections of specific types of plants, but the overall collection on display here, and the overall feel of the place was special. One minor criticism - I would have loved to see an orchid display 10 times the size of what they currently have (think Singapore's garden). You know they grow here, let's show them off! The day I visited there were dozens of students on a school assignment mingling among the foreign visitors, engaging them in conversation as they practiced speaking English. It was refreshing to see their enthusiasm and I was more than happy to take time to chat with them.

review_text:
The park is a haven of peace and serenity against the otherwise manically busy city of Kandy. Ensure that you visit in the morning, its cooler then and with less people. It is exceptionally well kept and the information about the trees and plants  rife. We were further excited to spot, within the arboretum, several clusters of the biggest bat's I have ever seen in my life, so Mrs Johnson was delighted to be able to capture them on camera. A very beautiful park.

Couple of down sides: I had hoped that here I would be able to escape the constant Â£ sign that seems to hang over every tourists head in this country, within the tranquility of the trees. Oh no. Security guards popping over for a quick chat, but swiftly requesting a cigarette to further irradicate their foul, bleeding gums, another chap digging a flower bed bent my ear, all be it politely, about his excellent hobby of collecting foreign currency, very clever, and to top it off, when spotting two brilliantly bright white bovine beats in a clearing, so of course stopping to oggle, their minder pops out from behind a tree and starts jibbering about rupees. Highly annoying.

Further, and my wife thinks I am incorrect in moaning about this, but the incredibly inflated price that a tourist pays as opposed to a local. Yes an average Western tourist is going to have more money, but oh my giddy aunt, the backlash that would ensue if the British charged 22 x local price to wealthy Sri Lankans or indeed any other tourist, to enter into Kew Gardens. We would be called racist, accused of defiling the parks good name and no doubt be obliged to make it a fair price for all. The park management have got this wrong here, leaving a bitter taste.

This especially stands out when the average monthly salary is about $300USD. 

The gardens are beautifully kept up and are very nice a peaceful, especially since it is set in the busy traffic of Kandy.

Go the bridge it is a lot of fun! The orchids are nice although the selection is not impressive.
This is a great place to do a bicycle trip although I don't think that this is possibility. Entrance price is 1500 local currency, no discounts available.

Secondly, you can see a number of colourful birds here. Thirdly, how about the huge red fruit bats that fill the trees in their hundreds! Not to mention the macaques which roam the gardens looking for scraps. There is also a very good cafe which has good value buffet food. review_text:
One of the nicest green spaces i've ever experienced

Just a quick glance at all the trip advisor reviews on here and its obvious the botanical gardens are popular and highly rated.

I can only add weight to that and say that we thoroughly enjoyed spending an afternoon here, though you could spend a full day if you had the time. We were contemplating just having a rest day round the pool at the hotel but decided to make the journey here and we were SO glad we did.

Other places should look to this place as an example of a well thought out, maintained and looked after urban green space.

It contains a bewildering variety of plants and trees, giant fruit bats hanging from and flying between the trees, monkeys you can get right up close to, lakes, and an orchid house with some of the most amazing flowers.

There is a cafe / buffet restaurant in the park, but this would make a lovely place to bring a picnic.

If you appreciate and enjoy nature and green spaces then this is a must visit if staying in or near Kandy. It is approx. 15 mins from Kandy city to here by tuk tuk and the fare should cost about 5 GBP. If you have already been on a tuk tuk with a mad driver then you will understand what an 'experience' this is, and if you haven't then do try to experience this at least once in your travels !

We spent a couple of peaceful hours wandering around these large beautiful gardens. Admittedly there were a lot of people here but it never seemed busy once weÂ’d left the entrance behind. Lots of different garden houses to visit plus a couple of impressive avenues of palm trees, a picturesque lake and plenty of places to sit and watch the world go by. We also saw a whole lot of bats in some strange leaning trees, IÂ’ve no idea why they were leaning so dramatically. If you need refreshments thereÂ’s couple of cafes for a drink. Lovely, peaceful and definitely a good place to wander around if you have some spare time on your hands.

We went on to the 3 temples loop, a nice change to go to sites with only a few other tourists and worth the time.

review_text:
After a morning in the crazy streets of Kandy, it was lovely to get away from it all and visit the gardens. They are quite expansive and if you have a problem walking then there is a golf buggy type vehicle that goes around the gardens. I do not know how often they operate but the trip lasts about an hour. Best ask at ticket office.
There is a cafe overlooking the expansive lawns about 5 minutes after the entrance and this is a good place to plan your route with the map provided as you enter. The soft drinks were reasonably priced 160 for a  Sprite and the cafe has some very clean bathrooms. The gardens are peaceful and whilst there are many more impressive botanical gardens around the world this is a pleasant way to spend couple of hours.

review_text:
One of our favourite stops during our visit to Sri Lanka, these historic gardens are impressive, and beautifully maintained.

Featuring trees, plants and flowers from all over the world, it is a testament to the curiosity of British settlers who first established them (and the to sustained commitment of the Sri Lankan government to preserving the site.

Lovely grounds to stroll, with many spots providing cooling shade to escape the often oppressive heat. 

We spent a few hours roaming, and saw perhaps half of the park. 

The orchid house is s highlight, as are the tree-lined pathways featuring particular species (double coconuts, royal palms, etc).

review_text:
Do not be put off by the word "botanical".  This is a beautiful parkland.  We would recommend hiring a guide and also a buggy which in our case was a necessity but even so our tour lasted over an hour.  The history of british monarchs can be traced here with the planting of trees to mark their visits.  There is so much of interest, trees, flowers, butterflies, birds, insects, amphibians, fish..... and our guide was so informative.  Well worth at least a half day visit. 
The only downside was being ripped off by the tuc tuc drivers.who wait outside.  We were charged 1500 rupees for a journey that should have been 500.  Walk away from the gates and pick up a driver down the road.  The tourist board could help by printing an approximate fare list. Geraldine and Frank

review_text: I used to ride around these gardens when I was a child in the late-1960s and early-1970s. You can't do that now and it's best to hire an electric cart with a guide who can tell you about the plants. Apparently these gardens were first established by a King of Kandy in late-1300 AD. When the British colonised the country they established the Royal Botanical Gardens in 1843. The gardens occupy about 150 acres and are maintained immaculately and meticulously which is great. I spent about an hour because I didn't have time, but I think you need about 3 hours to explore every part of the gardens.

review_text: This is probably the most wonderful botanical garden I have visited. There is a staggering array of trees, bamboos, ferns and colourful flowers from all over the world. Even the huge grassed areas are remarkably attractive. The hundreds of fruit bats in some of the trees are spectacular to see. The orchid house is small but nevertheless very good, although it would help if there were labels identifying the various types. We spent about 2.5 hours here but would have happily spent much longer if time had allowed.

review_text:
Wonderful gardens immaculately maintained with a superb orchid house and plant house.
Set up in 1821, it has been extended and added to ever since.
There are some magnificent trees, both indigenous as well as tropical all set out in extensive grounds. By the river is the extraordinary sight of the flying fox bats with wingspans of over 1mtr.
For those at all interested in flora , this is a must see, and a very enjoyable way to spend a couple of hours.

review_text: We were on a day tour from the Cinnamon Grand to the Elephant Orphanage and Temple of the Tooth and our guide, Nishantha, suggested visiting the gardens. They were stunning. Unlike NZ and the UK there is no need for glasshouses and we saw many beautiful and imposing plants. The age of the trees is impressive as it is an old park (1371AD). The Great Circle was really interesting as dignitaries over the last 150 years have been planting trees. There was a riot of colour in places, awesome avenues and gigantic bamboos. The gardens are huge (147 acres) and  we would recommend paying 250 rupees (2 NZ$) extra and taking the shuttle tour if you only have limited time. You could easily spend a day here and it was a romantic spot for couples.

review_text:
After a long period of non-stop rain, we headed out to the Botanical Gardens in a tuk tuk with our fingers crossed that it wouldn't be a complete washout. The place turned out to be far better than we'd have dared to hope.

The entrance fee of 1500 rupees (about Â£7) for foreigners is not cheap - but nothing in Kandy worth seeing seems to be cheap. I would say though that it was absolutely worth it.

The site is enormous with a spectacular diversity of plants and trees and lots to see and do. The map was a bit rubbish as it didn't really suggest any sensible way to tackle the gardens, so we just blundered about a bit, saving the orchid house until last and focusing first on the outdoor areas just in case the rain came back.

We had lunch at the cafeteria beside the Great Lawn, watching hundreds of children playing tag during their lunch break. The food at the cafeteria was surprisingly good value for such a 'captive audience' kind of place - we had a fish curry set meal including soup and fruit salad plus a lime soda each and it was about 2000 rupees for more food than we could eat.

The fern house was a bit of a health and safety trap with tools and hoses left out all over the place but everything else was in good working order.

We got a bus back to the city for just 20 rupees each after we left. The bus stops are to the left of the entrance. Tuk Tuks were asking 500. Just ask if the bus goes to the clock tower or central market.

Don't miss this.

The Gardens are probably 5km from Kandy, a short Tuk tuk ride. We spent around 3 hours walking around the Gardens. They are beautifully kept and the Trees are spectacular. The clumps of bamboos add to beauty of the Park as do the plants and the river. In one corner of the Gardens 20 plus thousand fruit bats roost which is a spectacular sight.
There are places to take refreshments. 
I would highly recommend a visit.

review_text:
Visited here whilst in Kandy for the day and loved the place. We took a leisurely stroll down the main path to the green, down palm avenue to the suspension bridge, taken in the orchid house on route. Suspension bridge was fun to walk across but not quite sure why there is a gate in the middle with a sign that states stop. We saw some people get to the gate and turn round and then some people got to the gate and opened it and walked all the way across! Then walked along the side of the river and back round to the main entrance. At a leisurely pace this took about an hour.
Nice little cafe by the entrance where I enjoyed a great milkshake.
Great gift shop with some lovely items reasonably priced.

review_text: Our (Sri Lankan) tour guide used these gardens as a lunch stop: unbelievable ignorance. I went hungry and went on a very fast hour's walk around the periphery and wow, was it worth every minute. Their map plus frequent helpful signposts reassured me that I'd find the way back to the entrance, which I did in exactly the hour, most of which time the rest of the party spent waiting for and eating their sandwiches. Around the gardens I met the unbelievable rainbow Eucalyptus tree with its trunk of many colours; cannon ball trees with their scented pink flowers and hard ball fruits; tall fat conifers, Durians, giant bamboos and so on.  Most plants have labels and the whole gardens are curated equal to anything in the UK.

review_text:
Royal Botanic Gardens, Peradeniya are about 5.5 km to the west of the city of Kandy in the Central Province of Sri Lanka. It attracts 2 million visitors annually.The garden includes more than 4000 species of plants, including orchids, spices, medicinal plants and palm trees.Attached to it is the National Herbarium of Sri Lanka. The total area of the botanical garden is 147 acres (0.59 km2), at 460 meters above sea level, and with a 200-day annual rainfall.
One needs at least half a day to trek the whole area. The weather was good. For people, who canÂ’t walk, battery operated car is run for a fee.

review_text: Visited here in Jan/20, likely a couple of months before the park would be seen in its best light. It was not unexpectedly named in 1897 to commemorate the diamond jubilee of Queen Victoria. One of the gardeners gave us a tour for the better part of a half hour, clearly loving to show off the park. The birders are not forgotten nor the ophiophilists. The backside of a cobra was seen, resting among dead leaves! It is a nice spot to chill. There is a kiddies' area. The entry fee for foreigners was 300 rupees.

review_text: My wife and I visited here during our recent Birdwatching Tour of Sri Lanka. This park as well as being beautiful is also International renowned as a must visit Birding location. The park is well laid out with easy to follow paths. Our timing wasnÂ’t perfect as many of the flowers had gone over. However, it was easy to imagine how impressive it would look in its prime. Several of the beds were already being replanted. Around the perimeter of the park there is a very smelly river, this was a magnet for many of the birds including some really sought after species - Kashmir Flycatcher, Pied Thrush, Forest Wagtail, Dusky Warbler and Sri Lanka Bush Warbler. We were so impressed weÂ’re planning a second visit during our stay in Nuwara Eliya. Highly Recommended

For no.monely at all (Â£1.50 or so) you can enjoy the peace and beauty of this lovely calm park. Well maintained plants and beds and an wide range of mature trees and shaded walkways. 
Renovated in 2008, the park is reminiscent of everything English which the Victorians tried to recreate in their colonies. We met one of the garden supervisors who talked to us about the local plants and their properties. Some families were having a picnic on the grass. The garden employs 32 people who take a pride in its maintenance. A relaxed and calm place for an easy meander and reflect on our colonial past perhaps.

I had a couple of hours to spare in Nuwara Eliya so decided to visit Victoria Park. It was a lovely afternoon and I thought I might have a walk round and then sit on a bench to read a book. No problem there except as I entered the park I was accosted by an attendant wanting to see my ticket. I gathered I needed to pay SLR 300 to visit the park.  This is about Â£1.25 so I willingly paid for a ticket but it seems a lot to pay when a tea worker is only paid SLR for a day picking 20 kilos of tea leaves. 
The park is lovely and I believe the charge is only levied on foreigners but I am far from convinced that the money will go to help the plight of the underpaid workers.

review_text:
We went here on a sunny morning in Nuwara Eliya. We were looking for a place to have a walk around after a day of touring in a Tuk Tuk.
It costs 300LKR per adult to enter the park.
First stop was the small museum. It's mostly photos grouped in categories. It's interesting how Nuwara Eliya was essentially developed around the tea industry.
Walking around the park is a pleasant way to spend time. It's a mix of a typical British park with tropical overtones - the locals work hard to keep the park neat and tidy and keep vegetation from taking over. Some parts were clearly a work in progress, other areas trimmed and manicured.
The colonial roots of the park are obvious.
Worth a visit

review_text:
Victoria Park, Nuwara Eliya

First thing to note, although this is common, foreigners (you) get charged 300 rupees to enter. Locals are free. 

We paid our fee to the lady behind the counter. As I turned around a male guard asked to check my ticket. HeÂ’d just seen me buy it but never mind. 
We saw signs stating no plastic bottles or bags were allowed as they become litter. 

The place was filthy with litter of all types but mostly plastic bottles. In one of the free flowing water areas there were several old tyres which had clearly been there for ages.  It was obvious the bottles were not all from the day before due to the condition or grubbiness  of them. We picked some up and gave them to one of the many guards and staff but there was too much for us to manage. 
No one appeared to be proactively litter picking when our perception was that a person could have been tasked with this.  

There was clearly ongoing work judging by the piles of garden debris but again our perception, this appeared to an effort to tidy the place up when it had been neglected over time. 

We noticed some of the plants were covered in graffiti scratched into their leaves. Some people eh! But then we saw what appeared to be locals rather than foreigners doing exactly that. Despite the wealth of staff and uniformed guards this behaviour was unchallenged so we did, loudly.
These plants surrounded a water feature which was not in operation. There was a wooden jetty into the feature which looked 20 years past its prime, basically derelict and in need of removal. 

I know this is not main season so the gardens would not be at their best but the overall impression was of poor and overdue management. 

Overall we were disappointed and would not recommend this unless you have nothing else to do. 

So we left and walked up to the nearby lake which was even worse! Again we were asked to buy a ticket, from where we were we could see rubbish floating everywhere.  DonÂ’t bother unless you want to see a few horses tethered. 

Nuwara Eliya is grossly overrated and was a shame to waste two booked nights there.

review_text:
We visited Victoria Park twice during our time in Nuwara Eliya. The first time to just explore and the second time for a nature walk organised through the hotel.

There is an entrace fee for the park, which would be fine if the park was actually maintained with the fee. We were incredibly dismayed by the sheer amount of litter in the park. Surely someone or a community group could organise some clean ups (if I had had a spare bag and gloves during our visit I would have happily removed some of the plastic waste myself).

Rubbish aside, the park is a pleasant place to spend some time. There were plenty of flowers out when we visited (albeit the same as the ones we frequently see in the UK) and different areas to explore. Many local children come to play games as well as couples and larger families just enjoying the surrounds.

From a nature perspective there were a few bird species and squirrels but not the rich levels elsewhere in Sri Lanka.

It is only Rs. 300 to get in.

review_text:
This is a lovely open space in the middle of the town. We visited for the birdlife that can be seen there. Early morning is the best time before there is too much disturbance from human visitors. As well as the obvious egrets in the open areas there are different birds all along the stream and vegetation on the opposite side of the park. This is a site for wintering Pied Thrush

At the time of one of our visits see saw two wedding parties having photographs taken.

There are small kiosks for buying drinks and snacks.

Odd quirk - mens and womens toilets are at opposite sides of the park.

The charge to enter is 300 rupes for tourist and much less for locals.

review_text: Visited this park just before a rainy shower - beautiful variety of shrubs, flowers and trees, well maintained and thoughtfully designed. Heavy rainfall led to us taking shelter in the park's central shelter where we found many families enjoying their day out; we ended up making lots of new friends, young and old. There is a reasonably priced restaurant at the entrance with an adequate, if very limited menu, as well as a cafe inside the park serving drinks and snacks. Staff are friendly and helpful and the park was a welcome change from the frantic pace of the surrounding area. review_text:
Any place should be evaluated based on what it offers, not for what we hope to find there. Victoria Park was not meant to be a tourist attraction. It's a local public park with some interesting history.

We visited in February and it seemed some of the beauty had faded away in the winter months and some planting and gardening works were going on. I bet it looks much more beautiful in Spring and Summer. We still found it to be a lovely park for a pleasant stroll while also exploring some of its historic areas and trees. The playground had lots of fun rides and our daughter enjoyed them a lot. Like most places we visited in Sri Lanka, mornings and evenings seem to be the best times to visit the park.

Ticket prices are very reasonable and should be appreciated because the money goes into the maintenance and upkeep of the park. I recommend it for tourists who appreciate leisurely walks in relaxing settings.

review_text:
I was deeply shocked to be asked for 300 rupees to enter this park. Whether this is the official foreigner rate or a scam I don't know. In England parks are free. I have no objection, as an overseas visitor, to making a reasonable contribution to Sri Lankan parks such as this but excessive demands will result in NO revenue. I just walked away.

If an individual was trying to make a dishonest charge, he should be sacked. If not the authorities need to review their charges. It would be sensible if charges were advertised at the entrance. A tax rate of 0% or 100% will yield nothing. An excessive park charge will yield nothing.

I love Sri Lanka and especially the people but beware of greed. Foreigners are not silly and news of bad experiences travels fast.

review_text:
We visited the park with our two children, aged 9 & 10. You have to buy tickets to enter the park. There seems to be a scam going at the ticket office, where the posted price does not match the ticket price. The price for foreign adults is R300 each, but the children's admission price is not indicated. We gave R1200 and got four tickets and no change. Off we went to visit the park, however a short while later, on examining the tickets, we noticed that the children are charged at half price, i.e. R150! We went back to the ticket office to inquire and immediately the R300 change appeared, as if by magic...

As for the park, it's quite pleasant but definitely overrated.

review_text:
It was a Festival Day in Nuwara Eliya and the park was full of local families out in the sunshine enjoying themselves.
We were lucky to get chatting with the head gardener who had a wealth of knowledge of all the trees and flowers in the park. He showed us many beautiful smelling flowers. He explained that now is the season for them to be planting and tending new seedlings. Many were covered to protect from frost. He said in another couple of months the park will be full of flowers and look very pretty.
It was lovely to walk around anyway. There is a very large playground for younger children.

The down side, you have to pay an entrance fee.

review_text: The gardens were very nice and spacious but at this time we were there they had building materials lying around as they must have been doing renovations or something. Also, there was not many flowers blooming and a lot of stray dogs all around the park. However, the kiddies park, which is hidden through some trees, is absolutely great. There is plenty of awesome playground equipment for the kids to play on and there is some cheap rides (Ferris wheel, bouncy castle, train, pony). I think, at the moment, it's only really worth it to go there if you have young children because the rest of the park is a bit underwhelming.

It is a lovely place to stay within the Fort so you can soak in the experience.

review_text:
The fort is an amazing place to walk around. 
It has signs here and there with information about the fort, which was built and added to by different countries.
 While it's not all there anymore, what is left is quite impressive. Look for the coral in the wall and ground of one part, and the view over the ocean is very pretty, so I'm sure it's a good sunset place.
There are a lot of markets and restaurants around, so while we didn't, it would be easy to fill in most of a day around here.

review_text:
Had a lovely few hours at Galle Fort,  a World Heritage site.

You can walk all they around on the fort walls,  lots of information on the Portuguese, Dutch and British history.

Lovely streets to meaner in and some excellent cafes.

Loved the green space (think called ramparts green) and all the local school children running around. Seems to be a place for young, courting couples and its stunning watching the sun gone down. Great view of the Galle cricket ground from the north side of the fort.

Thanks to painstaking efforts of some people you can see this Dutch fort in its original manner. Though the fortress was not damaged All other equipment such as lighting was changed. But now all fittings are in the original shape. Even the buildings are now reinstated to original glory. One of the photos shared show a restaurant. This was a government Office around 40- 50 years ago. 
Most interesting places would be the dungeon near to the light house. There are ample restaurants serving all types of food. You can even taste Gellato in Galle Fort. I am sure you would love that as Sri Lanka is a tropical country. 
Galle is also a favourite destination for many Yachts. Windsor's are the best Yacht agents. They are really helpful people.

review_text:
We very much enjoyed touring Galle Fort, appreciating the old fortifications, the mix of architectural styles, and opportunities to learn more about the history.

Lots of great shops and restaurants within.

Our driver made the brilliant suggestion of going later in the day to avoid the heat, and take in a stunning sunset. Highly encouraged to do the same.

review_text:
An old fort with a clock tower and an old prison at the bottom of the fort. 

I found the prison quite interesting as it has no roof. With one access door, the prison is exposed to rain or shine. 

From the top it has a great view of Galle and also the cricket ground. 

Highly recommended.

review_text: One of eight World Heritage Sites in the country, the fort area allows you to explore influences from Portuguese, Dutch and English perspectives. The fort area is largely on a grid pattern. Many old buildings have been put to modern uses [shops and restaurants] while others are in a state of decay. You can walk the ramparts around more than half of the fort. Sites to see include churches and several museums. There are many cafes to have a cool drink to escape [somewhat] the heat of the day. review_text:
A wonderful, compact historical fort city located along the sea. What we liked:

- compact, can be explored at your own pace and can spend a couple hour or all day if desired
- accessible. Very easy to get to. Bus, taxi, tuktuk, Uber
- beautiful location. Magnificent views of the sea and waves crashing. 

ItÂ’s easy to navigate so easy to with small children. Bring a hat and sunscreen. There is almost always wind so itÂ’s quite cool but the sun can be very strong so burns can happen quickly.

The cafes and restaurants are priced higher than outside the fort. There are hits and misses so scout for locations before sitting down. You can look at prices from outside in most places. Many places are quite expensive.

Highly recommend.

Galle Fort is about 10 minutes walk from the Galle rain station.  

Fort it self is built and conquered by the Portuguese later on Dutch invaded the fort and the city it self and used it as their main trading port, end of the 18th century the British invaded Sri Lanka took control of the fort. 

ThereÂ’s lot of mixed colonial architectural buildings to see around the galle fort area, 
busy narrow streets with loads of small boutique coffee shops and hotels. We spend few hours exploring on the fort walls, beautiful sea views. Magical little city so please do visit enjoy.

review_text:
Galle Fort area is really charming and historical for the area.  The Dutch influence is still prevalent today.  Buildings and cobble-stone streets still maintain the Dutch look and feel. Many streets in the area are far to narrow for cars, only motorbikes and pedistrians.  I believe this is what elevated the charm of this area.  It's clean, quaint and deliberate in it's design. The Fort area is avery large land mass (not indoors) and could potentially take all day to see, if you are walking at a leisurely pace.  I recommend seeing it more than one day in order to spend time relaxing and taking in all of the majestic, panoramic views.  An added bonus is the Galle Cricket Club is directly across the street and you get these amazing views of cricket practice and games....at no additional cost. Tuk Tuks are plentiful in this area and their prices are extremely reasonable.  Lots of great variety in cuisine at reasonable/low prices.  I even stopped to have the most delicious scope of pineapple gelato on my walk around.  There is an ATM in the area at the centrally located round-about (it's bit harder to find an ATM for Union Pay, but if you leave the Fort area and head less the 600 meters across the street, you will find banks that take Union Pay).
All in all, a great place to hang out.

review_text:
You don't have to pay any entrance fee to enjoy Galle Fort :)
It's a nice walk along the wall, and it's all connected. You can walk from one end all the way to the beach and viewpoint area. 

It's amazing how the fort is standing for so long through history.
There's an area where there is a huge drop, sadly there are a lot of rubbish thrown down there. It's a pity how people can fail to help maintain things.

There's a small beach but crowded with people. Walk further up and you will see sort of like a Viewpoint, also crowded with people. Before the viewpoint there is an area not too big almost nobody (think it's opposite the white mosque). We sat there with our legs hanging over the cliff while waiting for the sunset. It's a very high fall but doesn't seem like it in the picture I attached. 

It was amazing, peaceful and windy. Our enjoyment was short-lived as people began flocking to the spot we were at and started taking pictures. 
Do make sure u check out the fort at least once, I think it's worth taking the time.

review_text: It is interesting to see the fortification and explore the fort area built by the Dutch on this beautiful rugged coastline. We walked round the walls, saw the lighthouse, walked through a parade of high end shops in an old restored Dutch building, passed the High Court building and watched groups of young boys playing cricket in the square. review_text:

Early morning activities recommended. 
Can never forget this place.

review_text: The impressive old Dutch fort/ rampart is in great condition. review_text:
Galle Fort is a UNESCO site first built by Portuguese and then expanded by the Dutch to protect the natural deep water harbour of Galle.  Much of the walled ramparts that encircle the inner city remain and are able to be walked upon, offering views across the harbour or back into the inner city. 

We were taken around by a Sri Lankan local and expected to learn more about the fort's purpose, operations and maybe visiting one of the museums. Rather despite it being quite hot and humid, we basically walked the ramparts. 
It is such a significant feature in Galle so it's worthy visiting.

review_text:
Galle fort was extremely interesting to visit and I enjoyed my day there.One scam to watch for is people selling old coins purported to come from ship wrecks.It is against the law in Sri Lanka to remove artifacts from wrecks that are 100 years or more old. This alone should make you wary.
The coins are nicely corroded to look like they are from the sea but in the days when anyone can look up the value of coins on the internet why would anyone sell a 1641 Dutch silver dallaar worth over $300US for $20-$27.
The coins are fake so don't get caught.

review_text:
The fort area of Galle very historic and definitely worth a trip.
The whole area oozes charm, with lots of historic things to see and do.
There are plenty of beautiful shops, galleries and restaurants to help you wind your way through the small pretty streets.
It does however all seem to close quite early and most places close by about 9pm and lots of the restaurant are full by 7pm to factor that I when looking for something to eat.   A lot of restaurant do not serve alcohol either, so be sure to check that out before you choose a table.

review_text:
We spent the last 3 nights of our Sri Lanka tour at Galle, with time to wander round the old area near the lighthouse. Despite it being busy with tourists it's well worth a visit.
There are many old buildings such as the lighthouse, police station, magistrates court, Dutch Reformed Church, Great Warehouse and the Dutch Hospital to name but a few.
The local fish market and fishing boats are also worth seeing as well as the street market. Find a courtyard for a cool drink in the shade.

review_text:
We were staying at the Amari Galle, which is a 10min tuk tuk ride away from the fort. It cost us 500Sr each way (Â£2). Our first driver offered to wait for us but there really is no need. ThereÂ’s loads of tuk tuks around and it was easy getting back to our hotel. We had a leisurely walk around the walls which took about 40 mins at a slow pace. Along the way there was a very picturesque lighthouse and for cricket fans; a cracking view of the Galle Stadium. We also wandered the streets inside the walls, which had a very chilled out vibe and bags of colonial Dutch charm. Loads of restaurants around if you fancy a refreshment break. This was definitely worth seeing and would recommend. 

Iain, London

review_text: We visited Galle Fort for a few hours.  It is a complete walled town dating back to the Dutch origins with interesting and intact buildings from that time.  The walls are grassy park areas where games and general relaxation takes place.  Within the walls there are a lot of touristy shops in addition to thriving business.  For greatest enjoyment at this time of year, head there early in the day or later as it is very hot.

review_text: This is a really nice fortress complex on the sea front at Galle. Entry is via an arched opening in the walls, and once inside the peaceful ambience is quite different from the hustle bustle of the main town. You'll find little lanes lined with shops, restaurants, bars, and the occasional museum. There are also small guest houses, hotels and lanes with attractive private residential properties. Walk up to the lighthouse and you'll get good views out to sea. Also make sure to find the clock tower. This was a real town back in the 17th century and still retains that feel. Really nice.

review_text: Galle Fort is a wonderful example of 17th Century fortifications. The Fort was improved over the years by both the Dutch & lastly the English.  The Fort in its heyday was a bastion of the Dutch East Indies Company and is still in remarkable good condition. The old town is mostly a mixture today of shops & accommodation with private residences as well. Stroll the ramparts & look out to sea to repel all invaders like days of old !

review_text:
Short trip from hotel by tuk tuk. Great views out to sea from the fortress walls with a cooling breeze. Excellent photo opportunity.
Like a small town built within the fort, lots of little boutique shops (particularly jewellers) to browse around. Very little traffic so able to walk round without danger. It was nice to be able to stroll without the craziness of the tuk tuks on the main street.

Bought some relatively inexpensive clothes in a couple of the stores and some more expensive earrings in a jewellers but I was glad to put some money into the economy of the hard working and patient shop holders.

There is a bar there where we enjoyed cooling drinks (twice) and they provide you with a token which allows you to use nice clean toilets across the square.

We both enjoyed our time at the fort and would recommend this trip.

Following Shanjei through little backstreets and corridors of the inner sanctuary of the Fort was very interesting. He had some wonderful tales of history and cheeky gossip that was both amusing and educational. 
We finished our tour by offering him a beverage and he found a beautiful place with a rooftop bar for us to finish on. 
After our time together we felt very confident walking around the Fort and we stayed and had a lovely massage at one of the spa salons in the old town. We had lunch at another of ShenjeiÂ’s recommendations,  a rooftop restaurant with amazing views.
We highly recommend this wonderful experience because Shanjei has a way of bringing the old fort to life.
Shanjei also offered for us to contact him any time during our stay in Sri Lanka should we require advice or suggestions... local knowledge is invaluable.

review_text:
The beginning of the fortÂ’s history, which was built by the Portuguese, along with a Franciscan chapel (now mostly in ruins) inside the fort started  in 1541. 100 years later the Dutch, with a force of some 2,500 men under Koster, captured the fort from the Portuguese in 1640. They started building the fort as seen in its present form in the Dutch architectural style. Fortifications were added up to the early 18th century. The British took over the fort on 23 February 1796, one week after Colombo was captured. Sri Lanka remained a British colony formally from 1815 till it became an independent island nation in 1948. The importance of Galle also declined after the British developed Colombo as their capital and main port in the mid nineteenth century. 
Today the Sri Lankan government and many Dutch people who still own some of the properties inside the fort are looking at making this one of the modern wonders of the world!  This work is going on still very slowly, I guess there is not enough money yet to build up the Fort to this modern wonder. Maybe the next generation!?

review_text:
The horrendous rain simply would not stop all morning. The moment it became a drizzle, we grabbed our guide and off we went for our planned Fort tour. 

The drizzle then became a small storm. We were not dressed properly to take in the relentless wind and poodle of water, with our umbrellas threatening to fly away during our walk around the walls for defensive purposes.

It was the most speculator sea ever. Gazing out, I could imagine how the four metres high waves swept over the train station and bus station located right next to the Fort, and those inhabitants in houses on that Boxing Day. 

Our Tuk Tuk driver told us his then fiancÃ© had an urgent need to pray at the temple really early that morning.  Everything and everyone in her family was gone upon her return. He then took her in and gave her a home. IÂ’d told him to treasure her - what immense luck to be the sole survivor.

We entered the Fort from the old main gate. The walls were erected by the Portuguese in the 1500s and later added on by the Dutch and the English. During the walk, the guide pointed out the Fort Lighthouse and the many Bastions. The UNESCO Fort was truly a fusion of fantastic European architecture with Asian influence. 

The 300 year-old Dutch Reform Church was a humble establishment. No one was in there during our visit. The stained glass panels were worth looking at. We ended our tour at our hotel. 

I so named the City of Galle as the City of Gale right after our eventful walk that day.

review_text: Galle fort is very accessible by foot, you can walk through most of the inner streets within an hour or so. By walking up on to the ramparts you get a great view of both the interior and the bay and surroundings outside. There is also a good view of the International Cricket ground from the rampart adjacent to the main gate. Within the fort there are many cafes and boutiques, some of which are quite expensive but if you wander you will find pretty much a place to suit your tastes or your budget. There are lots of gelato stores and tuk tuk son every corner, also banks and ATMs, absolutely worth a visit and there are also high end hotels and restaurants within the fort

When the British arrived at the end of the 18th century, they applied their own touch too, with the odd lighthouse.

As a consequence, today, the Galle Fort area is unlike any other place in Sri Lanka: a European/colonial feeling in the deliciously salty tropics.

The old beautiful buildings of Galle Fort today house chic boutiques, trendy shops, cafes  restaurants and design hotels.

Unmissable destination on every Sri Lankan itinerary.

Would definitely recommend going before 11am or after 3pm as we went in the middle of the day and it was sweltering heat with very little shade around the outer wall itself. Also there are a lot of people trying to sell you Gem's, wooden elephants and the usual Sri Lankan gifts which at times is a little bit annoying.

review_text:
Loved Galle Fort, Loved learning the history behind this place, from the ancient spice merchants to learning how the Fort was constructed.
The cobblestone streets with their interesting names housing many sophisticated cafes, restaurants and beautiful boutique hotels, spice shops to the original little hole in the wall shops.
I hope in the future it still retains some of its original old charm. We totally loved Galle Fort, was one of our highlights, especially early morning walking the streets in relatively cooler conditions in search of caffeine!! Was peaceful and lovely to see the fort slowly waking with early tuk tuk bread deliveries, cats still asleep front of house, locals going about their early mornings, and the call to prayer breaking early morning silence.

review_text:
Like Paris, no high rise buildings. Utterly cute peninsula, completely surrounded by ramparts. Great walking. Tiny streets and 5 star low rise hotels with beautifully plated and elegant meals. There are also tiny eateries, look for the A rating for cleanliness.  The Jewellers LAKSANA, is a very reliable dealer; always bargain for a 20% discount..I often get more. Before getting into a tuktuk get the charge for the ride.
Antique shops, elegant interiors in hotels and inns are worth looking into; staff are always friendly and English speaking.
I stayed at Villa Aurora; I have lived in the US for nearly 50 years and speak all the SL languages. Look for small gems run by, usually European couples, who have fallen in love with the island and are above the political fray. Great locations to visit outside the Fort.

Galle Fort is a must see for anyone travelling in southern provinces. Full of history- Portuguese, Dutch and English.

review_text:
I liked the tour through the historical sights of Pollonaruwa a lot. The places are visited by tourists, but also by locals, since the temples are still active. 
This is definitely a whole day trip as the places are far away from each other. You will need to get tuk tuk or taxi to manage everything. I recommend to have 1 driver that will go with you through all the sights, as the locals know the town and an arranged tuk tuk/car makes it very convenient and comfortable to move around. 
The tickets need to be purchased at the ticket office of Archeological museum in Polonnaruwa, where you will also start your tour and get the most basic information about the place.

review_text:
The ancient ruins of hatadage of vijayabahu empire are still in excellent condition.
The moonstone depicting various phases of life are beautiful work of art.
The royal palace quadrangle with more than thousand years old ruins give a glimpse of the flourishing art and culture of the bygone era.
The bathing ghat, the round Buddha vihara with the statues of Lord Buddha in various postures facing the cardinal directions glimmer even today.
The place is still a pilgrimage place for Buddhists.
There are a number of stalls selling refreshing tender coconut for the thirsty tourists.

Worth visiting.

review_text:
Another UNESCO World Heritage Site that worth a visit especially for history buff. An interesting history where the kingdom was built during Chola Dynasty since invasion from South India to the capital city of Anuradhapura, then Polonnaruwa since 10th century. It is said to be a systematic destruction of Buddhism civilisation from the north in Anuradhapura and built Shiva Temple with Hinduism influence. Polonnaruwa was then established with various significant architecture including more superior water irrigation system that flourished agriculture and trade. Both metropolises were then destroyed and burnt after the war and invasion by Kalinga Magha  (founder of Jaffna Kingdom) in 13th century. There are many remnants of the ruins with intriguing stone carvings. Some of the checklist for places to visit at this site include the below: 

a. Thivanka Image House**
b. Polonnaruwa Nelum Pokuna - Lotus**
c. Gal Vihara (Rock Temple)**
Kiri Vihara - 91**
Lankatilaha Viraya - 90**
d. Alahana Pirivena - 73**
Rankot Vihara**
Pabalu Vehera - 52**
Sheva Devale - 2-54**
e. Hetadage
f. Nissankalata Mandapa - 43**
g. Vatadage - 39**
h. Dalada Maluva - Polonnaruwa**
i. Hindu Temple God Shiva Devalaya**
j. Palace of King Nishshanka Malla**
k. Deepa Uyana
l. Palace of King Parakramabahu**
j. Council of Chamber**
k. Pothgul Viharaya

Well worth the steep entrance fee of USD25 and take your time to enjoy the site at your own pace with half to full day tour. Hiring a driver is essential when visiting this site. We used Â“BLUE HAVEN TOURSÂ” with an excellent driver Mr Sugath. Drinking water  is essential too.

review_text:
Lots to see in this ancient and well preserved city which is rightly a UNESCO world heritage site. Shamefully, we spent less than two hours here when at least three would've given us the opportunity to see even more. 

The Buddhas at Gal Vihara are an magnificent site and we were lucky enough to witness a Religious ceremony during our visit.

The Rankot Vihara dagoba was extremely impressive and is still used by pilgrims to leave offerings, most of which were snaffled up by the ubiquitous and fast moving monkeys!

Thoroughly recommended.

review_text: I visited Polonnaruwa on the way from Negombo to Sigriya. It requires atleast 2-3 hours and is worth the visit. Entrance fee for SAARC citizens (includes India) is USD 12.5 and  you need to produce the passport at the counter. At the museam office they handout a one page guide / map with major attractions, you can go from one place to another in car and visit as many as interest you. Reading the reviews of the key places to visit and keeping a note of them before arriving there is helpful, so as not to waste time there figuring out what to see. There are quite a few to choose from. review_text: Polonnawura richly deserves its status as a World Heritage Site. It can be visited over the course of a day. While a ruin, there are enough tantalizing remains to interest any traveler. The area ruled Sri Lanka from the 11th through 13th centuries. Several buildings here likely held the Tooth Relic. There are other unique structures like the circular Vatadage and the oddly shaped Satmahal Prasada, the purpose of the latter unclear. Places like the Lankatilaka Vihara, stretching to the heavens, will catch any photographer's eye. The sublime sculptures at Gal Vihara represent the best of Sinhalese craftsmanship, the artistry of the Kumara Pokuna, the royal baths, not far behind. It is a more impressive site overall than Anuradhapura.

Everything is labelled in English too, so you can get some background information at each individual site.  It took us a good 3 hours to go round the whole site on bikes - there are various vendors around the site selling snacks, drinks and souvenirs.  The whole experience was very pleasant and a relatively easy ride with only a few slight inclines.  It was interesting to find out more about the ancient civilisations and learn about the culture. A good trip

review_text:
It is not a large area and the ruins arenÂ’t as intact as in Angkor Wat, if a comparison needs to be made. But it is a good introduction to the history of Sri Lanka. 

The second most ancient of Sri Lanka's kingdoms, Polonnaruwa was first established by the Chola dynasty after their successful invasion of the country's then capital, Anuradhapura, in the 10th century. The Ancient City of Polonnaruwa has been declared a World Heritage Site. 

Polonnaruwa is the second largest city in North Central Province, but it is known as one of the cleanest and more beautiful cities in the country.

Polonnaruwa was ruled by the Kings Vijayabahu I, Parakramabahu the Great and Nissanka Malla Â– all 3 of these rulers devoted themselves to fostering agriculture, religion and social development and the kingdom prospered under their reign during this era.

review_text:
From the museum to the many sites throughout the ancient city, Polonnaruwa was probably our favourite stop in the Cultural Triangle. 

Not as old as Anuradhapura, or as well preserved, it is better organized and you can more easily develop an understanding of the different eras and constructions. 

YouÂ’ll need a few hours to see it all, but youÂ’ll want to spend time checking out the different sections and appreciate the artistry evident in many of the ruins.

The only drawback are the numerous, persistent vendors at nearly every stop (something that isnÂ’t condoned at Anuradhapura), but be firm, polite and keep moving and they will leave you be (eventually).

review_text:
The ruins and artefacts of Polonnaruwa, the centre of Sri Lanka's second most ancient kingdom established by the Chola dynasty in the 10th Century, are widespread and impressive.
Given the time we had, our tour took in the most significant of the ancient ruins, but you could spend several days covering the entire World Heritage area of around 100 sq km.
The royal palace and citadel area is a good place to start, as the centre of this ancient kingdom, then fan out to nearby attractions. Water was gravity fed to the royal bath, captured on the slightly higher ground of the palace itself. 
You must ensure your tour includes Gal Vihara, to see what are considered the best rock sculptures in Sri Lanka.

review_text:
My wife and myself are currently holidaying in Sri Lanka and earlier today we visited the old Capital of Polonnaruwa.

We began our visit at the Archeological Museum (see separate Review) which gave a sense of what lay in store but the scale and size of the main site has to be seen to be believed. It is also hard to believe that barely 5% of the site has so far been excavated so you can imagine what treasures will be unearthed in years to come!

As such, to get the most out of oneÂ’s day visitors are strongly advised to plan their visit well in advance. We all have our own preferences but my selection would include the Royal Palace Grouping, Quadrangle, Northern Group (particularly the Rankot Vihara & especially the Buddha Seema Prasada & Lankatilaka) and - even though I wasnÂ’t personally over impressed - Gal Vihara.

Believe me, to see everything would take the best part of a week but plan ahead and you should have a most enjoyable day out!

review_text:
This site is used to take money from tourists. It is that simple. 4500Rs for an adult "foreigner" to enter.

On arrival at the museum to buy your ticket you will be surrounded by local tour guides trying to be employed. They do not take no for an answer. Ignore them; walk the site yourself. They will tell you it is too big to be walked, trust me, it does not require a tuk-tuk. Walk.

The museum was worth one trip round, but better to get to the ruins themselves. Once there, they are lovely to see. Amazing history. All of which can be walked around. The Temple to the north was really special and well kept.

It is the local tack sellers and temple "life guards" blowing their whistles which ruined the day for me. They walk around in shoes whilst barking at tourists to remove theirs - it's ridiculous - especially given how hot the sand is in the sun.

review_text:
We visited Polonnaruwa on a typically hot, humid day, which would've been no big deal except for the fact that we did a tour of their "museum" too.

I mean, knowing it's hot and humid, I can accept that it will be tiring under the sun while viewing the ancient ruins. 
But I really, really thought it was downright pathetic of them to call their museum a "museum", because that's indoors, and it was a literal oven cooking everyone inside alive.

We visited the museum prior to actually viewing the ruins, and there, the ventilation is not poor, it's NON-EXISTENT. It's so damn stuffy you have difficulties breathing, and while there are these industrial air-conditioners fixed from the wall, they are not in use at all. Instead, they put fans and those coolers around, expecting these little machines to provide the ventilation and cool air the place actually needs.

It was an epic fail. Unless you stood right in front of a cooler, you'd feel like you're burning from inside out, all the time. The moment you step way from a fan or a cooler, the heat literally engulfs you. 

The museum content is actually quite interesting. The ruins themselves were also impressive. But the ventilation and air-conditioning of the museum is worse than crap. If I could I would just visit the ruins and skip the oven they call their museum.

review_text:
Spent half a day exploring the ruins of Polonnaruwa and very much enjoyed this UNESCO World Heritage site.

It was a hot day and we'd thought about cycling around, but ended up having our taxi driver take us around. The sites are quite spread out, so its definitely worth having transport to get around.

Bring a pair of socks for the sites that require shoes to be removed (e.g. at the vatadage). Must sees within the compound, if you are short on time, are the Gal Vahara (for buddha statues) and vatadage. Personally found the Lankatilaka Viharaya of most interest - its a large site and there was hardly anyone there - it was a very atmospheric as a result.

Polonnaruwa is a fascinating site which can't be missed if in the area. Try come early before it gets too hot and the big tour groups. Food and snacks are readily available around the site.

We have to be honest we did not know much about this ancient site before our visit, as we were with a large tour group and just tagged along.

This was once the capital of Sril Lanka (or Ceylon in those days).  ItÂ’s now a UNESCO World Heritage site.  Certainly interesting and sometimes referred to as the Angkor Wat of Sri Lanka. We wouldnÂ’t go quite that far, but the day was dragging on a bit and we didnÂ’t visit all the possible sites within. We did a down a dirty visit for about 3 hours, being shuttled to each site/sight, it was a really hoy day and the ground was cooking, (the shoes off rule when visiting scared sites was a challenge), so we weren't keen to hang around.

Eight hundred years ago this was the place to be, now just ruins are left of its former glory, we hit the high points as directed by our guide.

The Quadrangle - a concentration of important monuments ie, temple of the tooth of Buddha.

Rankoth Vehara dagoba - a  massive stupor, at 54 metres high 

And Gal Vihara - beautiful rock carvings, Buddha, and some others

As we were with a group the tickets were just part of the package, however, the  entrance fee for Foreigners is 4500 LKR (or 25 USD), seems a bit much, as independent travellers we might have thought twice.

All in all worth a visit.

review_text:
The former medieval capital city of Polonnaruwa covers a very large area and you need to allow several hours to walk around the many temple ruins and statues. It is arguably the most important archaeological site in Sri Lanka that is still being discovered today. It is no wonder it's a UNESCO site. At times you will need to remove your shoes to enter some off the temples. Beware that their are plenty of mischievous monkeys here that may charge at you if you get too close and please do not feed them. You will also experience many locals trying to sell you postcard, wood or other souvenirs.
I thoroughly recommend this site to visit and it sits comfortably as a major attraction with nearby Sigiriya Rock Fortress (Lion's Rock).

review_text:
This is a fascinating place to wander around for a few hours. But these ancient ruins are spread over a vast area, so youÂ’ll need a car to get around. We were told it takes around 3 days to see it all (not that you need to) but our Trailfinders guide showed us the highlights in a morning. A lot of it is quite similar and can easily be skipped. Sections of it are impressive to say the least and some of it less so. My girlfriend thought parts of it reminded her of Angkor Watt. 

This is a religious site so make sure you cover shoulders and knees, this isnÂ’t just a suggestion. We saw one lady having a right tantrum when they refused to let her in one of the temples, because she wasnÂ’t dressed appropriately. Even when another member of the public offered to lend her a scarf she carried on screaming at the guards, which had no effect whatsoever. 

Also make sure you donÂ’t pose for photos with your back to Budda, itÂ’s a big no no. There are monkeys everywhere, so avoid carrying food or drink and theyÂ’ll totally ignore you. We saw what happens if you have food and itÂ’s not pleasant. Pollonaruwa Ruins are impressive, intriguing and well worth seeing. It was definitely one of my highlights of our Sri Lanka trip. 

Iain, London

review_text: As per my own schedule, this visit was done on a rainy day. I had a private driver and upon arrival at the building where one is supposed to buy a ticket, the entrance is crowded with people trying to seek shelter from the rain. The parking area has no proper pathment so prepare to dirty your shoes since it's wet and sandy. Got myself an official guide which cost 3000lkr for 2 hours and I deeply regretted it.   Not only the guide has bad breath and I find that my movement were very retricted as he wanted to move fast and was quite impatient to wait for me or help me to take photo. The Audience Hall was ponding with water. I also did not go into the The Vatadage, Rankot Vihara and Gal Vihara as these places requires removing of shoes to walk in the wet sandy ground. And in the end, I gave 5000lkr to the guide expecting him to give me the change of 2000lkr but he just keep the money and feigned ignorance. I had to demand from him to give me back 2000lkr in change which he did upon my insistence. He also trying to sold me some private spa and dining contact places he had which I refused.  Overall I like the sites but due to the various factors, I did not really enjoy my experience there.  My advice, read up on the various locations, go on a sunny day and go around casually at your own timing without the annoying guide.

review_text:
This is one of the ancient capitals of Sri Lanka, centuries old and with a number of sites contained therein. Entry is USD 25 for foreigners and USD 12.5 for children (half rate for nationals of SAARC countries). Payment can be made in USD or LKR, but change is returned in LKR only. Paying in USD is every so slightly cheaper when you do the reverse forex rate calculations. 
Upon paying the entry fee, you can enter the area and see all the various attractions. There is not a lot of information available on-site, so hiring a guide can be worthwhile. There is a museum in the building where you buy tickets, entry to which is complimentary with the Polonnaruwa tickets. However if running short of time, can skip this (which is what we did).
Since there are around 26 sites within the premises (all spread apart), it can easily take upwards of 1 whole day to see the place in its entirety and enjoy its beauty. If running short of time, you need to plan in advance and shortlist the places you want to see and first finish those (and then, time permitting see as much of the rest as possible). The Golden Quadrangle, Palace Complex and Gul Vihara are some of the places that i would recommend as must-see.
Suggest carrying a lot of water, wearing hats and covering knees.
As with most historic ruins, children and people without a sense of history will find this dull, so i would suggest they opt out (instead of paying 25 USD and then realising that they didnt appreciate the beauty of the ruins).

review_text:
We were pleased we hired bikes - from Polo at the Cafeteria in the museum car park - to explore this interesting site. A relatively quick trip around the museum allowed us to orientate ourselves as well as get an idea how the site originally looked before we set off  along the main road before taking the turn into the site itself. 

We immediately headed north and enjoyed the less crowded Gal Vihara - awe inspiring- and Monastery area before joining the crowds at the Quadrangle and Royal Palace group. The latter was rather disappointing- we had previously strolled around the (free entry) Island Park group of ruins near the museum and found them to be more informative and certainly more comfortable. 

Allow 3-4 hours - on bikes - to explore the main site and be prepared to observe standard temple visit practices - remove shoes, hats and cover shoulders and knees - at multiple stages of the visit. Water very welcome although there are multiple vendors en route. 

We visited in August - Sri Lankan school holidays and ahead of the apparently imminent rainy season - so many parts of the site were crowded. An early start might be wise.

review_text: The world heritage ruins at Polonnaruwa appear to be on the list of every tour that passes through Sri Lanka's cultural triangle.  We were staying locally so could get a head start on most of the tours before they poured in.  Most people seem to cycle around the ruins and I could see why this would be attractive - it's cheap, easy and safe, and you can move between the different sites fairly quickly.  However, we were advised by a local to head to the top of the site by tuktuk then walk back to town, and I'd highly recommend this approach too - you'll get to see a lot more wildlife when you're walking, and trust me there's a lot to see if you keep your eyes open!  Saying that, you'll probably be fairly tired by the end, and make sure you take plenty of water.  The ruins comprise of a number of main sites interspersed by smaller, less-visited sites.  Be prepared for crowds at the main sites, with far fewer tourists at the smaller ones.  All are worth a visit though.  OK, this is not Angkor or Bagan, so don't expect it to be - I've been to both those and still reckon this is worth a visit if you're up in the cultural triangle.  However, I wouldn't bother staying in Polonnaruwa, I'd probably stay somewhere else - such as Dambulla - and get a tuktuk across for the day.

review_text:
Once an ancient capital of Sri Lanka, Polonnaruwa is a must-see on any visit to this beautiful island.  The site itself is vast, with lots of ruins of ancient stupas, temples, water gardens, monk's lodgings, moats, etc  dotted around. it must have looked somewhat like Angkor Wat in its heyday. It is also hauntingly beautiful now, and although one of the more popular tourist sites, never seems crowded because of its vast size.  Towards the end of the site are exceptional and magnificent representations of the Buddha carved in stone - standing, seated and laying down. Definitely not to be missed!... 
For me however, the most intriguing building of all at this ancient site is a very odd and out- of- place (i.e.not buddhist nor hindu ) temple that has puzzled even eminent archaeologists which bears remarkable similarity to the architecture of the pyramids of the ancient Maya.  How can that be possible?......  A real mystery!

review_text:
Terrific for a day, only an enthusiast would need longer. 

I had pre-arranged a scooty rental with the same company doing cycle near the entrance. It was delivered to the hotel and for LKR 1,500 thought it was worth not having to pedal in heat and humidity. 

The area is well spread out and fairly busy the day I went. The strategy I used, which worked well, was to do the north then head south towards the main entrance. It seemed to beat the worst of the crowd - most buy the ticket at the musuem, use the nearby entrance and head north.

The museum was excellent and set the scene well for our leisurely tour around the ruins.  Everything is so well kept and well organised - we bought an English guide book and our driver helped fill in the important historical background. review_text:
The Archaeological Ruins date back to the time when the Capital of Sri Lankan kingdom was located there in Polonnaruwa, few centuries ago. The ruins are mostly of Buddhist and some of Hindu structures. The ruins are scattered within a area of few square Kms and are difficult to cover on foot. Tuk Tuks are available for moving between the ruins and cycles are available for hire. Entrance fee has to be paid to enter the area of the ruins. Though the structures are in ruined state, they are still impressive and indicate their glorious past. The area of the ruins are well maintained with proper passages and greenery all around.
We had hired a Tuk Tuk on the Main Road, from where the side road leads to the Ticket counter and driver, Mahinda, acted as our guide. He was quiet informative and entertaining.

review_text:
Keep in mind that the ticket office and the entrance are not in the same place! The tickets are a bit pricey, 4000 rupees per person (aprox 25 US$ per person). Where the ticket office is, is also the small museum where you can read about the site. Dont forget to take a map from the ticket office (it is free)! No way of getting around otherwise.
It is a huge place, and my advice is to hire a tuk tuk to drive you around from one ruin to another. I think it is the best way to explore this amazing ancient site! We hired a tuktuk from Sigiriya to take us to Polonnaruwa and around Polonnaruwa. It took us 1:45 minutes to get there from Sigiriya, and we spent another 2-3 hours exploring the ruins of the site (with a tuktuk, walking would take us the whole day). That half a day trip with a tuktuk cost us 5000 rupees. (Use your bargaining skills)
I saw you can hire a bike to explore around the ruins, but considering the sun above us, not the best option (if you want this option, take some hats and sun protection)
Most places there you will have to take you shoes off, so if your feet cannot handle heat, bring socks with you! The sand and the stone can get really hot. Also, like all buddhist holy places, keep you shoulders covered and wear longer pants.
There are a lot of vendors there where you can buy cold drinks, but a bit exspensive.
I think it is a nice trip for families, couples, friends - everyone.
You can buy nice suvenirs there like wooden elephants and Buddhas. But remember, always bargain! We bought a small wooden carved elephant- the original price was 4500 rupees, and we bought it for 1000 rupees. (Walking away after not agreeing on the price is the best method)

review_text:
We thoroughly enjoyed our visit here, and the ruins are amazing. Our favourites were the Image House next to the freshly painted white stupa, and the temple with four huge carved Buddhas (including the reclining one).
Some tips to make your visit more enjoyable are:-
If you have a driver, use them to take you around the site. There is a lot of walking at each of the sites anyway, but it is so spread out that it is not possible to see everything, and even with the bicycles available for hire it would be exhausting just getting between the various ruins.
Make a priority list of what you want to see as you canÂ’t do it all.
There is very little information available at each of the ruins, so take a guidebook or print out information from the internet before you go.
Make sure to wear clothes that cover the shoulders and knees or you wonÂ’t be allowed to enter some parts.
Wear shoes that are easy to get on and off as you will need to do that continuously.
Take old socks to wear as the rocks can be very hot.
Use plenty of sunscreen and take a hat and water as it can be very hot indeed.
Enjoy - an amazing place.

Polonnaruwa is an amazing place and the obvious attraction is it's stunning archaeological site with the kings palace, library, baths, council house etc. The site is dominated by the Sacred Quadrangle with the stone book, Vatadage and Hatadage as well as numerous temples.
The site is busy in places but delightfully quiet in others and thoygh absolutely huge if you  do it all on foot, especially in the heat we experienced, it's still small enough to do in a day if you hire a bike or a guide with a car as we did. A guide is vital as you just won't get the same level of knowledge of the place  from books or display boards and you get the personal touch and knowledge of an expert.
One of the best days out I've had in many a long year. Loved the place.
