review_text:
I dont realky know where to start in trying to even sum up how fantastic and amazing this archaeological and historical gem is.
We had the most wonderful day exploring as much of the site as we could. A guide is vital as you just won't get the same level of knowledge of the place from books or display boards and the personal touch makes all the difference.
The Sacred Quadrangle is the highlight with the stunning Vatadage where the Buddha Tooth was kept, the Hatadage, the stone book and other temples.
The Royal Palace and Baths are beautiful too and we particularly loved the Royal Library and the Kings Council chamber.
The Gal Vihara statuary complex is just jaw dropping with the reclining and standing Buddha's carved into the granite rock.
As I said, the place is an absolute wonder and it's been a long, long time since alive had a more enjoyable day on holiday. 
Utterly amazing, captivating and unmissable.

review_text:
Go straight to the museum and pay for the entrance fee on the archeological site + USD20 for the tour guide (look for Sunil). 

You start at the beginning by visiting the museum where all the statues are kept and you will have a chance to understand the whole picture of the site you are about to visit. 

We saw people riding bicycles (in hot weather!) however we went by car so if you are doing this by bike it will take longer. 

Make sure you use a Saron to cover up to your knees and ideally flip flops as in some temples you are requested to remove your shoes. Ladies may be requested to bring an scarf to cover their shoulders. 

The place is full of history and the guide takes you into that journey as he walks you through the different locations. He reminds you of some of the important learning you take from the museum visit. 

That helps to get the whole picture of it and its significance for the Sri Lanka nation in the XII century (just about the end of our Middle Age).

review_text:
The ruins are really impressive and only really need a day. The most impressive are "Gal Vihara" or rock monastery and "Lankatilaka". We went in the afternoon/early evening and so this meant it was much cooler and probably slightly more enjoyable.

We decided to go by tuk-tuk and our driver tried to make us go with his "special price". This entailed not buying the official ticket and paying him the cash instead which he could use to "bribe" the guards. Overall he tried to convince us this would save us approximately Rs 2000. We felt really uneasy about this and declined, deciding to buy an official ticket. He then got really angry and then refused to drive us to the north site. 

We spoke to a local about this and apparently it is a really common scam and those that have gone with the "bribery" option haven't been able to get in to see some sites, particularly Gal Vihara. Our advice would be to be very clear before getting in the tuk-tuk about what is going to happen.

review_text: Came here for the day with my partner and our three youngest.  Our guide drove us between each site but there was still a lot of walking and it was very hot - so make sure you take plenty of water and a parasol/umberella for children to shade themselves (whilst we were there we saw 2 local children faint due to the heat).  There is plenty to see and the ruins and architecture provide plenty of photo opportunities - although there was some confusion as to what you could include in your photos - we knew from visiting other areas that you must not take selfies or pictures that show you or your party with your backs to any buddas, however our guide (who was a local Sri Lankan) told us that if you stood next to a budda - ie at its side and not with your back to it  then that was fine.  However when we did this we were told off and made to delete the photos - our guide did not understand this and spoke to the man who made us delete the photos at some length and told us that this had never been an issue before - however, best advice is do not have any people in your photos wherever they are standing!! In addition, please dress respectfully. Also, there are parts where you must remove your shoes so we always carried a little pair of socks with us when visiting any of these type of places so we could pop them on as the ground was not only stony but extremely hot!  We saw a lot of people who simply had to miss out some of the areas as they could not walk on the ground in bare feet due to the heat.

review_text: The Polonnaruwa site is as magnificent as the reviews say it is and it is a must do on your Sri Lanka trip. Don't just do the big name buildings, Royal Palace, Quadrangle and Gal Vihara though. Take the time to stroll through the huge monastery ruins between the Quadrangle and Gal Vihara and make sure you check out Lankathilaka. Make a detour too to see the only frescoes remaining on the whole site at the Tivanka Image House in the far north. The only small downside of our day was right at the beginning when we went to the museum to buy our tickets. The tickets were LKR 7950 for two. We paid with 2 x LKR 5000 notes. The tickets were handed over with an LKR 1000 note and a LKR 50 note. I waited. The ticket lady put her hand in the drawer and pulled out a stack of LKR 100 bills and started talking to me. As the conversation continued, she put her hand and the notes back in the drawer. Chat over, there was a pause."You have to give me more money," I said. She pulled her hand out of the drawer, counted out some LKR 100 bills and pushed them over. I picked them up. There were nine. "One more please", I said. She peeled one more off and laid it down. Not a word. I counted everything out again, said thank you and walked away, making a mental note to include this in my review to warn future travellers. That's it. It's still a terrific place to visit, just watch out for the short-changers at the ticket office.

review_text:
We stayed at Sigiri and travelled out each day to Polonnurawa and Anuradhaphura. 
Polonnurawa is certainly worth a visit. There is really a lot of history here. We came with a tour guide so we got the low down on the history.  
Again expect to pay for the admission which is around 3500 LKR ( pls check before going ) each.  This is about the same price as for Anuradhaphura . The majority of the  entrance fees go towards maintaining the site and further excavations, so you are funding a good cause.  After paying for the admission do go round the museum which is where you get the admission tickets.   The visit to the museum is worthwhile especially if you donÂ’t have a guide. It explains each monument and the history behind it.  And also the history as to why the Kings moved from   Anuradhaphura to Polonnurawa to start a second kingdom.
All the places are concentrated in one small area so walking from one to another is quite straightforward.
Polonnurawa  started in the 10th Century as the capital city  and ended around the 12th Century . 
Apparently it had lain undiscovered until British archeologists began probing in the late 19th century when the whole area was covered in forests.  When you look at the buildings do look at the surrounding trees. Their bases are about 1.5 m to 2 m above the ground of the excavations. It will have taken some serious excavations to get to the monuments.
Some places are just spectacular.  The Royal palace for one, the second is the lake or a Â‘tankÂ’ as they call it.  This huge lake of 25 sq km was manually excavated in the 12th century by people and elephants.  It really is quite an awesome task. 
There are some temples which are in ruins and previously held the Scared Relic of the Tooth ( now housed in Kandy).  Just do note that the dress code applies to temple ruins as to living temples. No shorts, or crop tops and no slippers on the temple grounds ( even abandoned ones).  A few visitors were caught out and not allowed in. 
Having visited both Polonnurawa and Anuradhaphura I think if you donÂ’t have enough time then Polonnurawa is the better choice.  But if you have the time and inclination then do visit both places .

review_text: The ruins are part of the middle ages period, and in a not too terrible state of conservation, but there is just too much visitor pressure and the heat and the religious requirements -walking without shoes and not wearing hats- make it a very unpleasant experience. I happened to visit coinciding with a large tour sponsored by an insurance company (6 or 7 buses), which didn't help but this seems to be more the rule than the exception as there is no control on the number of visitors. What would have been a pleasant visit in very early morning or late in the afternoon was a pain in the late morning. 1 Entrence ticket area having museum also

4 Quadrangle area adjacent to citadel having Atadage,Vatadage, Hatadage, Stone book, Shiva temple,Vishnu temple, Satmahal Prasada, Lankathilaka image house etc
5 Another area having Gal Vihara, Lotus pond.
Tickets- For SAARC nationals $ 12.5 or LKR 1937.5
              For other tourists $ 25 or LKR 3850.
Qualified guide is must to visit these ruins ,Charges approx LKR 1500 to 2000
Bargaining possible.
Must visit place

Polonnaruwa was royal ancient city of Kingdom of Polonnaruwa in north central province of Sri Lanka. It was first declared capital city by King Vijayabahu 1 in 1070 AD. Nissankamalla was another great king who established matrimonial relations with south India kings leading to Hindu influence on archaeological ruins. One can experience grandeur of that period after seeing its ruins.

We then dropped our guide back and gave him lots of donations that I had collected from my local community at The Gap for his young family.  

You could even ride a bike through these ruins.  Especially on a hot day I wouldnÂ’t recommend walking the big area. Either local driver or bicycle.

review_text: I was a bit sceptical to start with visiting Polonnuruwa ruins after previously been to Siem Reap (Angkor Wat) 2 yrs ago. I didnt really know what to expect probably due to my own ignorance but upon visiting with my wife & 2 young kids (8&10), I was very impressed. There are plenty of well retained ruins steeped in history. Its a really interesting bit of history. The ruins are over a large area, you can cycle around or get a guide & transport or if you have a driver use your vehicle. It would be hard to walk around due to the heat. My two daughters struggled a bit with the heat but in their defence they climbed Lion Rock earlier in the morning. I highly recommend visiting the museum to gain a little knowledge before browsing the ruins. Highly recommend visiting this site whilst in the Cultural Triangle.

review_text:
We visited this site in early February on a fairly warm day i.e. temperature about 23 degrees. We had guide with us. The advantage of a guide is that they can help you make the most of your visit by selecting out what to see and more importantly they have the knowledge of what is inter-connected and in close proximity too. 
This is massive heritage site and you cannot explore all of it in one day so selecting out points of interest and finding them is a challenge. Best to read up about it before you arrive as that may help you select out what you think suits you best. Alternatively just meander and explore. 
There is an option to hire cycles and that could be a good way to explore the site. Whether walking or cycling or with a driver guide you will almost certainly come across structures which will amaze you. The architecture is a delight if you have not previously seen buddhist or hindu heritage sites before. One of the joys was seeing carved granite carvings in the structures which convey stories. Hindu architecture is very different from Buddhist architecture. One revers the Buddha without much reference to the animal kingdom and the other is prolific in carving animals, 'grotesque' masks and moonstones with story telling symbolisms threaded throughout the buildings and statues. One is also relatively simplistic in design while the  other is over complicated, yet they are in harmony too.
So this a site where you can marvel at the size and shapes of early structures, whether they be structures like a giant wedding cake or stupa's which are round and dome like. Another joy of visiting this place is the sense of freedom you have to explore it. However there is an obligation that visitors show extra respect for those sites with a special religious significance. This presents no problems if your address is appropriate i.e. no knees (men and women) showing and the female head is covered. However this applies only to certain special places here not all of them. This is also a site that has grass and avenues of trees to contrast with the massive  brick structures. 
Until I visited this place I never realised that bricks were being made in the 12 century and were being used to build multi storey buildings and places of worship. 
If you are not keen on heritage ruins and history you will probable not rate these sites very much. For me it was interesting, enjoyable, varied and wonderful because of it heritage. I have not previously seen a nothing quite like it on this scale despite travelling to over 20 countries.

review_text:
This is a must do on any trip up into the cultural quarter of Sri Lanka.  This is a UNESO World Heritage site which in its hey day was in the 11th/12th century and was one of the most important cities in Sri Lanka.Overall it is not bad shape! There is so much to see that you should plan on spending 1/2 a day here. You can walk it but it could be quite exhausting and extremely hot and there are no shops for water etc. Hire a bike or better still an A/C car. You should hire a guide as they have a wealth of knowledge  and it will avoid you missing out on stuff. 
I suggest that you start in the museum (next to where you pay), the head  south to Potugal Hihara, then do the Royal Palace Complex, then the Quadrangle and then work you way up the site to Gal Vihara (the star of the whole show) then head a tad further north to the "Lotus Pond" and finally the Tivanka-Patamaghara ( a hidden gem).
Doing the Complex properly makes a great day!

review_text: This is a truly impressive site with many buildings which have been rebuilt as far as possible.  When found the site was covered in jungle and over many years has been reconstructed.  Certain artefacts are in the museum, where there are scale models of the original buildings.  Visit this either before or after you visit the site to get a true perspective on what the site was like originally.  A guide is recommended to avoid missing the most important buildings and temples.  Socks are recommended on hot days, if you want to visit the temples!

review_text:
We would highly recommend Polonnarawu (people staying at our guest house who visited both Polonnarawu and Anaradhapura found the latter disappointing in comparison).  Entry is not cheap -  25$ per person Â– but it is an impressive site, with well-preserved monuments and good landscaping.  It is a generally peaceful site, with a prevailing air of calm and respect.  The one exception was the completely inappropriate loud music blaring from the refreshments area half way round.  We spent around four hours there which enabled us to visit all the temples and monuments.  We spent a further 30 mins in the museum adjoining the ticket office.
Practicalities:
Polonnarawu covers a large area, so walking the whole site, which covers a large area, might be a challenge - particularly in the 30 degrees heat.  We had hired a driver for the day so he came with us into the site (entry is free for locals) and dropped us off at each of the main areas to wander around at leisure Â– the car a/c in between stops was very welcome!  Another option is to hire a bike outside the site, which a number of people did ( depending on where you hire bikes from the downside is that you may have to cycle for a stretch on the main road Â– contending with all the usual crazy Sri Lankan traffic- either at the start of the tour or end).   Socks are recommended when entering the temples as it can be very hot underfoot.  About half way round there are toilets Â– those for foreigners were clean & in a reasonably good condition.  There were also the aforementioned refreshment stalls.   There are similar facilities (albeit less clean toilets) just before the exit.

It was interesting to start the visit from the museum, where we could understand some info about the history and see pieces of stones, statues we would recall diring the visit in the outside area.
Weather wasn't good despite the dry season.

Go and enjoy on this amazing place!

review_text:
We visited the site today independently. To enter you must first purchase your ticket through the museum $50 US which also entitles you entry to the museum. The entry to the site is about a kilometre away, you can traverse the site by a number of options - walk, bicycle or tuk-tuk. You can hire a guide to explain all of the different areas for a price if you like. Because of the distances around the site we chose to use a tuk-tuk we negotiated a price with the driver (donÂ’t pay over 2000 LKR) as we wanted him for over 4 hours. You will be overwhelmed by the history dating from the 10th century I believe. Most of the structures are in a state of disrepair but it looks as if the government is taking steps to rectify this. You may wear hats and footwear and take photographs in all places except religious shrines and monuments but this is signed to make you aware. Be aware this site can get extremely hot but there are plenty of stalls selling cold drinks as well as the usual trinkets, souvenirs,post cards etc.

There is a place just past the museum behind the Ekho Lake House called Island Park which is free to the public and contains some sites.

This World Heritage Site should not be missed.

review_text:
I hired a Tuk tuk for 5000R for a return journey from Sigiriya including waiting time. The ancient ruins which were abandoned over 700 years ago cover around 4km north to south, and there are about 6 or 7 main sites spread short distances apart from each other, but too far to walk in the baking heat, so having the Tuk Tuk was ideal. I did however see some people who had hired cycles, but it was too hot for me! It was 4525R entrance fee with the ticket office next to the museum, but there wasnÂ’t much to see and the information and presentation was quite dated. Fortunately my driver ordered the sites so I started with the smaller less impressive sites first, followed by the more impressive ones late on, including the 55 metre high red brick Rankot Vihara Dagoba and the quadrangle of Dalada Maluwa which at one point housed the Buddha tooth relic. Remember many of the sites are holy so you need to remove shoes when entering, so bring socks as walking bare foot on the stones gets hot! Also a real Â“no noÂ” is taking pictures posing with your back to any Buddhas. 
If youÂ’ve been to some of the major Buddhist archaeological sites like Ankor Wat, Bagan, Borobudur etc. you wonÂ’t be blown away, but still this was very enjoyable, and you can easily spend a day seeing the full city. This was one of my favourite attractions in Sri Lanka.

review_text:
We stayed in Pol in order to see the Archaeological ruins. On our arrival day we walked round the small site  directly beside Ekho Lake side hotel where we are staying, this appears to be free of charge and was a useful introduction. The next day we bought a ticket from the main ticket centre/Museum and hired a guide. Hiring a Guide 'on-the-street' as it were is always a gamble, the first person who latched on to me appeared to speak OK English, but after asking him a few questions it was apparent that his English was not really much good. The second person who approached me claimed to have been an english language teacher and was much better - but far from perfect. I'm not sure that a guide  you pick up on the street is really worth the hassle. Ours was quite useful in the Museum, but his interest waned during the next few hours and having made enough money from me  was keen to get back to his family for the rest of Poya Day. I thought we had agreed a price, his reccollection was slightly different ( take a piece of paper, write down the agreed price and each kepe a copy!) and when it came to tips, it was OK, then he suggested I also give him something for his lunch, then he spotted that my wife had Â£'s in her purse and so suggested  Â£10 towards his air fares fund! So altogether cost about double what I thought we  had agreed - but at the end of the day wasnt really much in European Terms. You would probably be better off with a good guide book and research printed off before you went. 
The sites are fairly spread out and the entrance is about 2-3Km's from the ticket office. So you need transport (we already had a van and driver for this part of our trip), I guess that visiting all the central sites and then back to the Museum was about 5-10kms, so it's not surprising that the further you travel the less busy the sites become - and actually they are the best parts, Tivanka Image House in particular. Some hire cycles to go round the sites - I would not reccomend it in 30+ degrees unless you are very fit.
I would like to have spent more time there but  3-4 hours seemed to be the expectation of the guide and our driver. If I had wanted to visit for even 30 minutes the next day it would have cost another $50 for two of us. 
Having been to the Angkor Wat archaeological sites the previous year, there is no comparison, Angkor is much larger, much busier, much more interesting but also more expensive, but you can buy 3-day non consecutive tickets.

review_text:
Unlike Anuradhapura where the ancient sites are dotted around the town, Polonnaruwa is contained in a fenced area several kilometres long. Weirdly the ticket office, not far from the clock tower, is tucked away in a commercial area one kilometre from the entrance gate. Why, who knows?. The site itself is too much to walk. Rent a bicycle or a tuktuk driver for the duration, about 2000rupees for 3 hours. Or for self drivers just go into the area in your car. At each of the four groupings of monuments there is a car park so its well set up for using a car. Lots of people are there with tour company drivers in cars and tuktuks, for obvious reasons to utilise tour companies, they don't publish advice that you can use your own car.

review_text:
Polonnaruwa is a well maintained and well enough run ancient city/archaeological site in the cultural triangle. Its very easy to get around via tuk tuk (and fairly inexpensive too) or you can go the bike route if you don't mind the heat. There are a number of sites to see but it can all be done in about three hours if you have a tuk tuk.

Visitors should be prepared for crowds of people, many of whom will ignore well placed and easy to read signs about taking off shoes and not climbing on crumbling walls. There will be people in all of your pictures as well.

Ultimately I have two different recommendations re: whether to visit:

(1) If you have never seen a similar site I would recommend going - you will be interested the whole way through. 

(2) If you have been to  multiple other sites as I have, including in Cambodia, throughout Thailand and Burma this is ok to skip. I grew bored pretty quickly and didn't see anything new/different that made it worth a special trip. If you are in the area with an afternoon to kill (as I was) there are way worse ways to spend your time but be prepared to be underwhelmed.

We generally enjoyed what we saw here but we found that the support provided fo tourists is very poor. We were only provided a very basic map and were then largely left to the mercy of all the local touts, tuk tuk drivers, etc.

After several 'bum steers' we eventually worked out what to do and where to go and saw some quite interesting ruins. Information provided at the ruins is generally very limited - our LP travel guide helped us to plug a few information gaps.

Overall we felt that the site management is not really well tuned into the needs of tourists and is missing out on optimising the site's tourism potential.

review_text:
We had this visit booked by our tour company and they had arranged a UNESCO guide.  Our guide was very knowledgeable and we started at the small museum before progressing to other sites.  The whole site is vast and we travelled by car between the various areas of ruins.  There are areas where you have to remove your shoes as they are religious parts but this is very much the normal at all religious sites in Sri Lanka.  I would firmly recommend having a UNESCO guide otherwise you'll miss bits and it certainly enhanced our experience here.  The ruins are very well cared for with ornate and elaborate carving of rock showing fantastic craftmanshp.

This is a a must do when visiting Sri Lanka as it helps you gain a perspective and understanding of the ancient history of a beautiful country.

review_text:
We had a 3 hour guided tour of this ancient city provided by Walkers Tours who are the largest suppliers of Tours in SL.  Our guide and driver was extremely knowledgeable and understandable. 

The city is spread over a vast site. We saw some people using push bikes to travel between the various areas which looked hard work. An air conditioned car was much preferable!

The history here is amazing if not a little repetitive.  The highlight without doubt is the Gal Vihara - a group of 4 massive Buddha rock carvings in fantastic condition. Our favourite was the reclining Buddy although the 7m standing one was also great.

The rock carvings throughout the site are mind blowing considering the period when they were made.

WeÂ’re not particularly keen on museums but the one here is worth a visit. Although you canÂ’t take photos, you can touch many of the ancient exhibits which somehow makes you feel closer to the history than our sanitised western museums!

Well worth itÂ’s status as a UNESCO world heritage site

review_text:
As I was staying in Dambulla, I had to take a bus to visit PolonnaruwaÂ’s sights. From the main street of Dambulla, there are regular buses heading towards Kaduruwela Â– which is an adjacent part of Polonnaruwa where the train and bus stations are located. Hopping onto any bus that is heading to Kaduruwela will get you into Polonnaruwa. 

However, it is best to tell the bus conductor to drop you off in the Â“Old TownÂ”, which is (I think) the first main drop-off as you enter Polonnaruwa (from the direction of Dambulla). The bus journey took about 90 Â– 100 minutes, and cost 100 rupees.

After getting off the bus in the Old Town, ask around to get to the Museum -- just short walk away along a canal -- where you can buy a combined ticket for the museum and the archaeological sights. It cost 3975 rupees but is valid only for one day.

The museum gives a so-so introduction to the history of the Sri Lankan kingdoms, putting the ruins of Polonnaruwa into a larger context. Curation has room for improvement. Moreover, the airconditioning was weak and it was warm and humid inside the place.

The ticket comes with a pretty useless map. The staff know that the map is useless. So the lady advised me to take a photo of the wall-mounted map which gives clearer directions of where the ruins are situated. What's so difficult about designing and printing a new map? The fact that no one has yet done so gives you a clue about shoddy management standards.

From the museumÂ’s exit, walk northwest through a small garden to the group of ruins on the shore of the lake known as Parakramabahu Samudera. Then walk east and cross the main road, to the entrance to the other section of the ruins. Your ticket will be checked again.

The ruins are in three main clusters: the lakeshore cluster (also known as the Â‘islandÂ’ group), the royal palace cluster and the quadrangle cluster, each about 500m from each other. But there are plenty more sites scattered a few kilometres around. Some ruins are in bad shape; the ones in the sacred quadrangle are perhaps in the best condition.

It wasnÂ’t possible to cover much more than the three main clusters in the time (a daytrip) that I had. Based on my experience, IÂ’d say that if you want to examine most of the ruins, I think you will need a much earlier start, which means staying in Polonnaruwa the night before and the night after.

I am rating his site as merely "average". Even allowing for the fact that ruins that are 800 - 1100 years old can't possibly be in good condition, when I compare it with other archaeological sites of similar vintage around the world, Polonnaruwa is not outstanding. The stone construction does not look to have been built to a high standard; the sculpture works were relatively few and not particularly good aesthetically. The fundamental reason, I suppose, is that the kingdom over which Polonnaruwa controlled was probably a smallish one (by world standards) and it might never have had the resources to build a truly great capital city. As a second-class city, today we have second-class ruins. Add to that sub-par management, lack of cafes and toilets in the sites despite the heat and great distances... and my feeling at the end of the day was a degree of dissatisfaction.

review_text:
We spent an enjoyable few hours exploring this ancient site.  We were on a bit of a tight time deadline and were torn between Polonnaruwa or Anuradhapuda, am glad we chose the former as it's a fairly compact, self contained site, with good access to all the ruins.  Yes it's not as glamorous as other countries' ancient sites, but it is of great historical and cultural significance in Sri Lanka and several of the buildings are well preserved to say they were buried beneath jungle for centuries!

There is ample parking and good visitor facilities (toilets, wash facilities, food and drink)
We travelled around by car, which was straightforward enough.  There are several services hiring out push bikes, which seemed a pleasant way of getting around.

We had a very informative guide book, which we used to navigate and inform our route round.  There are some information boards dotted around, but they don't give particularly detailed descriptions.  As with any historic site visit, there are several 'guides' hanging around offering their services, if you are without a guidebook and find a good guide I would recommend it as you will miss out on a lot of information and even miss some of the well hidden sites altogether!

You do need to remove headwear and footwear to enter a large number of the sites, so come prepared and maybe bring something to dust the gravel off your feet after.

I would highly recommend a visit here during a tour of Sri Lanka's 'cultural triangle'.

review_text: Polonnaruwa used to be the capital of Sri Lanka, for long enough that a major series of temples, palaces and other buildings were built there.  There's a decent museum summarising the history, and then you tour the site.  It's all spread over rather a large area, so you either want to do it by car, or possibly bike if you're feeling energetic.  There's a lot to see; it takes several hours to do all the main bits even quickly, and could take longer if you wanted. We climbed without a guide Â– the route is clear, and we were happier by ourselves. The climb took us about 35 minutes, and was at times quite steep, but there are plenty of places to rest.

The view at the top is spectacular Â– make sure you leave plenty of time to explore Royal Gardens at the bottom, Boulder Gardens at the end, and the archaeological remains at the top. We had a wonderful time.

review_text:
Definitely a must-visit if you are in center-north Sri Lanka. The views from the bottom/garden are already great, but from the top it looks amazing.
Not recommended for people with vertigo (due to the last round of steps) or impaired mobility.
Climbing is easy even for elder people as long as you make a few stops on the way up (I went with my father 65+ Yo, that has some problems doing long walks / climbing, but stopping a few times worked out very well for him. Managed to go up and down in a total time of 57 minutes).

The history of this place is also very interesting. You can get leaflets at entrance. Expect lots of locals trying to guide you up (I think its totally unnecessary to hire one specially considering the very poor English skills..but it's up to you. They will try hard).

The only bad thing is families that don't respect the wasp warning signs resulting in incidents. Wasps can be triggered by sound - as advertised everywhere. Unfortunately we saw families with kids screaming, loud music and others crying out loud precisely in the designated "Wasp attack zone". Avoid going with kids to keep this place safe for everyone or at least take them to non-attack zones.

In fact, although it is 1200 steps up and the same down, taking a steady pace, it wasn't too bad.  If you don't like heights - just keep going and don't look down.  The metal walkway takes you up the last few metres and it's worth it when you get up for the view (and sense of achievement).  Don't miss the side walk across the front of the rock and the spiral staircase to visit the caves.

review_text:
Offers lovely views of the region.

There are about 600 steps to climb, the first few are steps in rock and later on steel steps bolted on rocks. The climb is steep but doable. Contrary to earlier reviews, all the steps now are in perfect condition and it is safe to climb. There are railings throughout so you have something for support. There is a lush green garden before you begin the climb and a small musuem.

While on top, you can see the remains of the foundation of the erstwhile palace, and the pond (/swimming pool). 

There are only about a few trees so make sure you carry sun protection and plenty water and some snacks. There are no shops / shacks en route or on top. 

On the way down, you can climb up a few stairs again for paintings in the cave.

PS: if you're from SAARC countries, do NOT forget your passport. The ticket prices are significantly lower for SAARC citizens but you'll get that rate only if you're carrying the passport, soft copy is not accepted.

review_text:
Loved our trip here, we went in the morning arriving by 9am and it wasn't too busy at all. 
The museum part at the start is a bit rubbish of the old photos but it was nice to see the jewellery and things uncovered from the site. 
The walk along the flat to the rock just brings home the scale of the place its just incredible. 
The climb up is all even steps and in different sections, the first part is steady wide stone steps with places to stop on the way. Once at the top of that you can see the stone lions feet as the entrance of the fortress itself. There are some dogs/ monkeys about so be careful of having food and drink out here but they were very calm and I never saw them trying to get anything from people. 
From here its tight metal steps and no places to stop but not as bad as it looks from the bottom. 
Once at the top of the fortress there is beautiful views over Sri Lanka. Easy to spend and hour or so wandering around and some places to sit and enjoy the views too. 
Definitely worth the money. Not sure how anyone can moan about the difference for tourists and locals - is their country of course they should enjoy it cheaper and tourists who can afford to travel should pay more to upkeep this beautiful place.

review_text:
What can I say, this is one of the highlights of my 13 day trip to sri lanka!
There are govt approved guides at base if you want to have a little history lesson and guide all the way to the top. I declined because I wanted to experience without alot of talk. Obviously  I went when  tourism was down in sri lanka so there were only about maybe 25 people or so I got to enjoy to myself. I took over a 100 photos and had all developed. There is photo opportunities at every step. The hike up and down took me about 3 hrs but I took my time, its steep but I'm used to hiking uphill. I can say it's safe but I would recommend being fit. The cost as I saw some complaining is NOT expensive of what you get to see. This is on the same scale as Machu picchu or chichennitza in cancun. So ignore those posts. $30is nothing to someone who comes from the west and travels that far!!. 

On a historical note this fortress dates 500 yrs before Christ. There's only one place at the top which you cannot take photos and a man sits there so you don't and thats ancient Buddhist frescos which very colorful. 

Once again, this fortress is an incredible place

review_text:
I and my boyfriend are a living proof that this place is manageable even on a rainy day. Actually, the experience is amazing! There were almost no people, shorter or none queues. Just bring a raincoat or an umbrella, and open sandals, and you will be fine. 
The complex consists from the rock that you will climb using the famous stairs. In the second half of this journey, there is something called Mirror Wall and then frescoes, which is a small cave with very old pictures with still vivid colors. 
The place is full of self-employed tour guides - locals that will follow you around, saying that they are tour guides and that you definitely need one. Then they will walk with you, talk with you, and expect money at the end. We were warned that there is no need for a tour guide and that the place is mostly about walking the stairs and the view afterwards. 
Lion's Paws is the stairway where are normally those long lines of people that are trying to get to the top of the rock. At t the base of the stairs, there are statues in a form of lion's paws, so hence the name. This place is what you want to experience when someone talks about Sigiriya Rock. And form my experience, it's the biggest fun!
The Mirror Wall itself is not that wow, I would say. It's not shiny anymore, you can't touch it, it's just therein its not shiny form. 
Frescoes that are waiting for you at the end of the line are much more interesting, since it's something to look at. The line leading to the frescoes is heading among the Mirror Wall. It's not possible to take pictures of frescoes, thought, there is a lot of staff watching everyone so nobody does it. 
I didn't see any toilets on the way, just those at the ticket office. So count with that, if you want to spend few hours of wondering at the place, or if the queues on the particular day are too long.

review_text:
Sigiriya Rock, also known as Lion Rock, is an impressive landmark located just 30 minutes away from Dambulla village in Sri Lanka. The rock can be reached by tuk-tuk or bus and is a must-see destination for any traveler to the country.

It's recommended to arrive early to avoid the crowds and make the most of your visit. The entrance fee is $30, but it's worth it for the breathtaking views from the top. The climb is of moderate difficulty, so make sure to wear comfortable sneakers and bring a bottle of water to stay hydrated along the way.

As you make your way to the top, you'll pass by ancient ruins and intricate frescoes, all while taking in the stunning scenery around you. Once you reach the summit, you'll be rewarded with a panoramic view of the surrounding jungle and countryside. Don't miss out on the opportunity to experience this incredible piece of Sri Lankan history and culture.

One of our party dithered about taking part in the climb because of a fear of heights. The steps are uneven up until the Paws, where, if you don't have a head for heights you can wait whilst others ascend the slightly rickety staircase to the top. I wore Merrell sandals with grip soles and they were great. If you are nervous about following the route, or needing a little help, you can hire a guide.

The views at the top are stunning and it is worth the climb, popping on the way back down, up to see some lusty murals. Again the cage, circular staircase, isn't for everyone.

At the top the world and his wife seem to have assembled, but it is worth it.

" Mapagala Fortress, Galkanda Temple, Kaludiya Pokuna, Ritigala, and jungle safari ". If you want, you can help Chandu get a guide to study history or the past in depth. There is a lot to write but I will stop here. Chandu's service is excellent and I highly recommend him to you.

The climb up Sigiriya is well worth it! Take your time and you will get there :)
It's best to start the climb early if possible around 6.30-7.00am. It is also worth getting a guide as they can explain the history of the  rock as you go. If you go early there  are far less people and it is much cooler for climbing. It can get very hot from about 9.30am on, and those 1,200 steps can become challenging. It will take about 2-3 hours to climb up and back down, but the view from the top is well worth the effort.

review_text:
My vertigo has got worse with age. It was put to the test getting up the stairs to the top of the rock, but thankfully one of the local guides put his hands on my waist and guided me up. It gave me a little bit of security that I needed to finish the trek.
The fact there was one of Sri Lanka's many cute stray dogs at the top of the rock just rubbed salt into the wound and made me realise I should have been a little more robust.

Sigiriya is one of Sri Lanka's best-known sites to see and it easy to understand. It is an incredible archaeological site, and the mind boggles when you reach the top passing the ancient steps people clambered up, and you realise a whole civilisation lived here. The views from the top are truly breathtaking and well worth the wobbly legs on the way up. Monkeys and butterflies and fortunately no hornets were enough distraction from the rocky drop below. 

The walk-up is a workout, and I was dripping with sweat when I reached the top but having said that it was over 30 degrees, so dripping with sweat was just the norm. 

If you go to Sigiriya and don't think you will make it to the top, then I would recommend not going. Getting to the top is what this excursion is about, and once there, the sense of achievement is tremendous but more significant is the experience of what you see all around. 

There are plenty off guides around if you want one. I would have got one personally, but my partner is a little more frugal and not as free-tipping as I. But when a man is willing to hold the waist of another grown man with wobbly legs to get him to the top - he deserves a tip.

Sigiriya is the kind of place that now lives in my dreams, and for that, I am grateful.

We were lucky that because of the coronavirus outbreak, there were very few people there, so we were able to rest at frequent intervals on the the climb: there are plateaus on the way up. Take lots of water and sensible shoes, and arrange a reputable guide before you get there (there is a lot of history to be explained) - there are lots of men at the entrance who offer to take you up but expect a lot of money.

My trip to Sri Lanka had only one item which was to get to the top of Sigiriya and I succeeded.

The site is very well maintained with it very well set up to show the site and its history. Getting to the top was hard due to the temperature but the crowds are the only problem.
The site is very important to Buddhists who wanted to see the painting but I didn't and there was no easy way to bypass it.
It was well worth the climb

review_text:
I am in my early sixties, with a lung condition. Was very hesitant to climb the zillion or so steps, so climbing this was , for me, a trial of resolve. I managed it, but took my time. Sri Lanka, right now, is sparsely touristed-but not at Sigiriya. I would dread to think what it is like when the overseas visitors arrive back en masse, once the memory of the 2019 bombings and Coronavirus are ancient history. This place gets crowded and people taking it slow like me tend to get in the way of the more fit individuals. Mind you, I was not the slowest by far. Unfortunately, however, being slow attracts the attention of Â‘helperÂ’sÂ’. Fit young Sri LankanÂ’s standing like hungry carrion, scanning for prey and constantly picking at the perceived weak ones and Â“assistingÂ” up each flight of stairs, whether that attention was requested , required or not. Their keen eye for a sucker is uncanny and they latch onto a potential monetary catch like seagulls on a chip, regardless of whether you are struggling or not. If you are not quick with a kind hearted rebuke, then they claim their prize and the hassling for large tips starts. They have a hide like an elephant and nothing short of an angry expletive will shake them off.  Be aware. These guys get aggressive and persistent  if you donÂ’t make it absolutely clear that you do not wish their assistance. However, you are not out of the woods, as a couple more of these vultures wanting an easy kill will be at the next flight and the process starts again. I hated that and my patience and initial good natured banter was retired in short order. This spoiled things for me, but that is just my personality. Being honest, Sri Lankans are a good natured and, largely, well mannered bunch, but I set my standards for other peopleÂ’s behaviours at, possibly, unrealistic levels. This is a dirt poor country trying to provide for itsÂ’ peoples and the population have grown to act in a certain way to feed their families. Their behaviours are borne from a need to earn money and, as a result, they can be a bit pushy bordering on exasperation at times.
Did I enjoy the Sigiriya experience? Well, besides the huffing , puffing and wanting to turn back at every step, I guess I did. Was that enjoyment because I was using the      climb as a yardstick for my failing fitness and a small mental personal victory was my just reward? Probably. Would I do it again? - Not a chance!

review_text: We arrived at Sigiriya at around 7:15am and there were already people ahead of us. Buy your ticket in the museum near the car park. Because this is not a sacred area, you do not need to cover your shoulders or knees. I recommend sneakers and dressing for a hot sweaty walk up many stairs. It took us approximately 35 minutes to walk up with very little in the way of crowds. We looked at the murals and mirror wall quickly on the way up and then went straight to the top and explored for about an hour. On the way back down, we went more slowly and looked at the lion paws, octagonal pool, caves, and gardens. This is an incredible place and is famous and a major tourist destination for a reason. Highly recommend going and getting there as early as possible to avoid heat and lines. I would say youÂ’d want to be in reasonably good shape to make it up without too much suffering. Bring water and a hat too!

review_text: This was our second time of climbing the rock having done it two years ago. Amazing place and every step is worth the effort. This attraction is vastly improved from our last visit however there was a few things that could of been clearer. Guides now are registered and have to be engaged before you enter the ticket site. They should cost no more than 2000 rupees but some folks where charged 5000. The car parks are different than before and you are dropped off outside the ticket office however your car or Tuk Tuk then collects you after your climb in the foreigner car park in a different area. No issues as such but this means you must do the museum before you climb. Some guides just want you to commence your climb and donÂ’t give you this choice. Also it is not clear when you buy your ticket. The friends of Sigiriya are still at the bottom to assist you up if you require and this can cost 2000 rupees or more. The ticket price is $30 each and when you now exit there is a little market selling what you would expect at variously different prices depending on which one you would chose. The toilets in the Foreigner Car Park are extremely good. This attraction is worth a 5 star review but the lack of information regarding the museum and the car parking arrangements just made it a four.

review_text:
An amazing place that you must visit, if you're in Sri Lanka. Most package or guided tours will take you here (or get a taxi/tuk-tuk), and if they have any sense, you'll arrive early in the morning, That way you not only miss the queues at the entrance, but you can be up, down, and gone before the hot sun makes it even more difficult! There are a lot of steps (1200), and some of them are steep/high, and some of them are a little bit scary - especially if you have a poor head for heights. There are no facilities for wheelchairs. In fact, you probably need be pretty able bodied to do this one.
We had a guide who took us slowly from the top to the bottom, stopping to show us the small details we might otherwise have missed, and also to give us a breather! There are plenty of things to see before you reach the upper staircase. But once you are at the top, it provides a spectacular view (though early morning mist can limit this), and there are some extensive ruins. You'll be scratching your head trying to figure out how they got all the bricks up there. Get there early to beat the queues (the stairs are very narrow), or get there later for a clear view. 
Take your pick. Definitely one of the highlights of my trip to Sri Lanka. There's nowhere else like it.
Tips - wear sensible shoes, carry water, and although a hat is useful, it can get pretty windy up the top, so hang on to it.

review_text: Quick review to say that this site is not to be missed. But I found no reviews on how vertiginous the climb up might be.  Clearly it wld be steep climb but for those    who have a slight fear of heights the issue is whether you felt Â‘safeÂ’ making the climb. We asked a few of our fellow hotel guests the night before and had a mixed response.  So we gave it a try. However I only got one third of the way up via means of a broad staircase which reached a platform with some terrific views over the countryside. But then onwards it became more challenging as I saw a steel caged spiral staircase built into the rock face. I knew straight away I wld freeze half way up and not be able to come down!  So I agreed that my partner would carry on up and I would meet him an hour later down in the visitorsÂ’ car park. I had an enjoyable hour watching everyone come and go for an hour and the wonderful vistas knowing I had made the right decision. This was confirmed by my partner when he got back to say it only got worse going up and he witnessed a number of people being vertiginously challenged on the way down. Phew! But it sounds worth the challenge if you know you can get back down. I was happy with my own 1/3 way up kind of achievement! Later found out that the steel spiral walkway (to see some cave paintings)is not obligatory and can be bypassed as you make your way further up. But you still faced further open and steep staircases built into the rock face.  But not me!

This enabled us to enjoy the area mainly to the 20 in our tour group and meant we could meander at leisure and also take our time climbing to the top without being pressured to move on, or be held up. 

The climb itself is very steep in parts and with over 1200 steps to climb, you would need a moderate level of fitness to make to the top. There are plenty of places to rest on the way though if needed. 

If they want any improvement, it would be a zip-line to get back to the start! We could see our bus waiting for us below and what fun it would be to have a buzz on the way down!

Entry fees were included in our tour, so not sure how much they charge. From reading other comments, I feel it was well worth it and money goes to preserving this historical site.

review_text: Well worth a visit.  Recommend that you take one of the numerous guides who are at the entrance waiting for tourists to roll up.  They all wear a uniform polo shirt so you know that they are offical guides, however as like anywhere you need to be prepared to negotiate a price.  We paid $20 US for a guide for 3 hours, our guide was excellent giving you a lot of background to the fortress which you would not get from reading the information pamphlet you get given with your ticket.  There are toilets located just by the ticket office, very clean but no toilet paper so make sure you take tissues.  There is also a water station before you enter with purified drinking water where you can fill up your water bottle.  Be prepared to climb up narrow stairs to get to the top, the view is amazing and worth the climb.  When we went in Feb there were no hornets which we had read about however we were told that it was the wrong season.  Beware of monkeys everywhere which is all part of the Sri Lankan experience.  When you exit the fortress there are numerous toilet blocks which were all clean and well maintained, again take your tissues.  Make sure you wear comfortable walking clothes, shoes, hat and take water, there is nowhere to purchase water along the way until the exit.  We arrived about 9.30ish which we found to be fine, the heat was bearable, the timing of your visit will all be dependent on the time of year you go.

review_text:
My Husband and I were here 4 weeks ago and decided to go early in the morning at 7am as the heat and humidity was just horrid anyway and thought it would be less then, but it really wasn't. Anyway we went shortly after opening time which is at 7am. Now, we are both nearly 60 years old and totally unfit fatties and both of us have bad hearts, bad knees and ankles, plus me with an already sprained ankle from a collapsing bridge a week earlier, but hey, I wasn't going to come all this way from Australia and not climb this Sigiriya Rock right?. Anyway we climbed to the very top in 50 minutes from the very start to the very top, including a few stops in between to catch our breath and trying to stop out hearts from exploding, but just quietly were were so very proud of ourselves, so kudos to us. Now just a word of warning, for those of you who have really bad knees or ankles this climb is not for you, and if you have even the slightest fear of heights, this climb is definitely not for you. I'd say go as far as the Lions feet and that's it as it is really frightening after that especially if people are trying to get past you and your clinging to the edge of the rock for grim death while letting them pass. For those of you who are not scared of heights then go on up to the very top, the 360 degree view you will love and you get to see all the ruins also. I must say watch out for the scammers too who will approach you along the way up at different points, they will make conversation with you and try and help you get up rocks etc and they will start to tell you all about the rock and the history and then they will become your guide without you even knowing about it and it will cost you money, but if you want to use them then go ahead, these locals are desperate for money. Also when you get there, there is no signage, well in English anyway, to where you buy the entry tickets from, we found it a bit confusing where to go to get the tickets, and that's a walk in itself too. There are plenty of Tuk Tuks at the bottom when you come back down that will take you back to your Hotels at a reasonable price. Just be aware that where the Tuk Tuks will drop you off at the start where you buy your tickets from is not the same place where you finish up when you come back down from the rock, you seem to get rail roaded out a different exit to an other side of the rock so you end up having to go past all the souvenir stalls. review_text: Nothing prepared me for this and I was glad I was wearing sturdy trainers.  The climb is quite steep for the uninitiated!  It's a combination of stone steps, some rickety and on occasions nothing to hold onto and metal open stairs, with railings.  You really have to look where you're going!  There are various stopping points on the way so you don't have to do it in one go. A good tip - our guide took us up early, as it opened - about 7.30 I think.  We were at the top by 9.  It's quite a steep climb in parts and not for the fainthearted, but I didn't see anyone turning back.  When you get to the top it's a stunning 360 degree vista and well worth the climb.  How they ever built a palace up there several hundred years ago, I can't imagine.  There are various interesting features on the way up and down, one being the wall paintings, hundreds of years old.  You have to climb up a metal spiral staircase on the side of the rock, but you are caged in.  As with many things in Sri Lanka, its very ad hoc!  What an amazing morning!

review_text:
We decided to venture to Sigiriya Rock, to climb to the top in order to see its famous views.  

On the way to the Rock itself, we were surrounded by beautiful manicured grounds, gardens, and pools.

As I have a fear of heights, I wasnÂ’t sure what to expect.  I will say that I struggled on the the way up and going down, as my anxiety took over.  My other half had no issues, but I found the narrow and very open stairs difficult to traverse.  Having to stop a few times, not due to the physical activity, but for me to be able to control my vertigo.

The trek, and shaky legs, were worth it as the views were worth it.  From the top, you can view a 360 degree view that Sri Lanka has to offer.  One view was reminiscent of a Jurassic period of a beautiful lake leading to a distant mountain.  You will also see remnants of a fortress, as well as some wildlife (mind the cheeky monkeys, as they will steal what they can).

I would highly recommend it, as the adrenaline rush is great.  Those with a paralysing fear of heights... donÂ’t go.  

Note:  Go early, bring water and sunscreen, as there is very little shade on the top.  Also, go to the bathroom before heading up, as there are no facilities on the the way up and on top (a poor gentleman learned the hard way ??).

Took me by surpise how magnific it is. I can hardly imagine what a wonder it was when everything worked and people lived in it.
The rock itself is a very special, add to that the ingenuity how they used it. 

1200 steps, worth every one of them. Sound frighteningly high but you will manage. There are sections where you are almost alone, but you are gonna cue especially on the iron steps and there you can catch your breath.

It is good to have a guide. There are several licensed ones and I suggest that you take one of them ( you can hardly avoid). They show you detailes you could very easily miss.

The view upstairs is stunning as you can expect.

review_text:
Took me some time to decide scaling Sigiriya due to one bad knee but am glad I attempted it upon hearing the story behind it and reached the top after much huffing and puffing.  Having done it, I must say the stairs are manageable if you pace yourself and keep hydrated as the temperatures can go up as the day progresses. There are also many locals who would offer to help for a fee, but I found that saying no thanks decisively holds them at bay. 

After reaching the Lion's Staircase, the climb u the metal stairs are a little more steep with less resting platforms but once you reach the top, one can appreciate the ruins of this architectural monument. Hard to imagine how one can build a palace on the rock until you see the remnants of ancient urban planning for yourself.

review_text: This is one of the impressive UNESCO World Heritage Sites we have visited. Steep entrance fee LKR5,460 per person, but it is well worth it! Since 5th century, this place was built by the King Kashyapa who killed his father, King Dhatusena, usurping the throne of his father. He eventually fled to Sigiriya from Anuradhapura to avoid the retaliation of his half-brother, Moggallana who was the rightful heir of the throne. Kashyapa ordered to build fortress and palace on top of Sigiriya Rock. Eventually, Moggallana came to Sigiriya for revenge and war was declared between the brothers. Kashyapa lost the battle and committed suicide, and Moggallana returned to Anuradhapura after winning the battle, and Sigiriya Rock was converted to a monastery. Four parts to appreciate this site: First, the fortress at the foot of the rock with viewing site of Sirigiya Rock from far after passing by the main entrance surrounded by moat. Some of the highlights are the Summer Palace, Cobra Hood Cave, etc. Second, the decoration of the authentic fresco half way up to the rock, reachable by spiral staircase. Third, the small plateau half way up the rock with massive gateway of Lion Rock with gigantic rock carvings of Lion Paw as entrance to the palace to the top of the rock. Fourth, where is the last part at top of rock where the ruins of the palace is located. The idea of building a Palace on top of a massive rock is already very incredible! 360 degree panoramic views from the top is amazing with sunset view in the evening. In summary, this heritage consists of intriguing historical background, plus the incredible architecture back then in 5th century. It is one of the highlights of our Sri Lanka trip!

This staircase is optional. Then up a few more stone steps to a rest point, were you can top up your water bottles for no charge. 
Then the slightly scary metal steps. There are around 7 flights of 25ish steps. You donÂ’t need to go straight up them all in 1 go. 
Then the impact of the view hits you. 
There is shade at the top which is very welcome. 
Ps there are monkeys everywhere including up all the staircases.

review_text:
Awesome 5th Century palace split into 2 sections. One palace is at the bottom of the rock and the other at the top. Many many many steps, even on the lower section and they can be uneven and worn in places. A lot of the steps still have their original white marble coverings and when the are wet are extremely slippy. Get a Guide, the whole history of the place is brought alive. The guides don't have a set cost, you just tip them what you think their service was worth. The frescoes are incredible. I would say that getting here (halfway up) is a must, even if you can't make it to the top. The rock formations and the construction techniques used to build the place are quite awe inspiring. The views from the top are simply stunning, but it rained the day that we were there and was somewhat misty. You may want think about if the climb is worth it on a rainy day. Slight downer was that you had to run the gauntlet of the looky looky men on the way out and the attendants in the Free public toilets practically hold you to ransom for toilet paper and a tip. 
Very long journey by private car to get there (about 4.5 hrs) from the Bentota area south of Colombo.

If you have the time to wander both below and above, so much the better.

review_text:
Trip advisor Sigiriya 

I am writing this mainly for people who, like me, have a fear of heights. 

Most reviews focus on the effort of getting up the rock. I am moderately fit and found it hardly taxing at all. My Apple Watch said I had climbed 48 flights of stairs but it did not feel anywhere near that much. 

More of a challenge for me was the height and especially the two separate  flights of iron stairs. 

I had debated whether to do the climb at all and was pretty apprehensive. Having done it, my advice would be to do it if you have a mild fear of heights or a moderate fear that is under control ie not subject to serious panic attacks. It also helps to have a supportive companion. I would suggest not doing it if your fear is more severe. 

Most stairs are stone with balustrades but there are two iron sections:-
One that leads up from the mirror wall via a caged-in iron spiral staircase to the cave paintings. (You go up to the paintings but then have to come down again to continue.) The steps are solid so one cannot see the drop below but of course you can look out as you go round. I managed this by focussing on the central post of the staircase and talking encouragingly to myself! if you are anxious about this you can probably bypass the cave paintings and head straight for the Lions Claw platform, although the paintings are interesting. 

Another section leads up from the Lions Claws level to the top. This has iron sections crossing the rock, again with solid steps, but is more exposed. Going up was easier as one faces the rock. I was more anxious about coming down but my husband went in front of me so I could hold on to his back with one hand and the railing with the other. The walkway gets quite crowded which slows the descent but means you are surrounded by people. This made me feel less exposed. I was nervous but it was very manageable. I have found other places more challenging like going up a tower in San Giminiano and inside the dome of St PaulÂ’s. 

I would make two other points:-
There are guides along the way who look out for people who look anxious and are quite insistent about holding your hand. Kind but probably better declined. 
The remains at the top and the views are very impressive - well worth the effort - and if you get there with your fear of heights, a real achievement. 

I hope this is helpful - it would have helped me if I had been able to read this before I went.

review_text:
Firstly, this point should be covered either early morning or later afternoon unless the weather is good. 
If it is hot, then you might not enjoy this place that much.

Coming to the place now. Entry Fee is 15 USD for SAARC nations and 30 USD for others. I paid 2760 LKR per person. 

You have to walk for about 10 minutes to reach the point from where the climb begins. 
However, the place is extremely well managed and surpassed my expectations. 

It is a world heritage site and known as the eighth wonder. 

There are gardens and mini water bodies on both the sides. 
There is a very small bridge with water on both the sides just after the ticket checkpoint and one can have nice clicks standing on that.

Please DO NOT THROW away your tickets after this point since it is again checked midway into the ascent.

Coming to the climb, there are about 1200 steps. The difficulty is moderate. It surely tests your stamina.

But if the weather is good, it is all worth it.

As you keep on climbing, the view of entire surrounding just keeps on getting better. I doubt if you can get better views from any other place.

It took us about 30-40 minutes to complete the climb. Do not recollect noticing any restrooms on the way so be mindful of that.

Once you reach the top, you truly appreciate the work that has been done at such a height. It is a refreshing feeling at the top.

You can easily spend an hour at the top, just sitting and roaming around.

While climbing down, check with someone the way to Tourist Car Parking area since that is different from the original place where your driver might have dropped you.

It is must visit place. If the weather is on your side, then you will have an Unforgettable time.

This was the best sightseeing point for us on our entire Sri Lanka trip.

SigiriyaÂ is one of the eightÂ WorldÂ Heritage Sites of Sri Lanka. It is one of the best preserved examples of ancient urban planning worldwide. There are remains of an extensive network of gardens and reservoirs. Some structures like fountains are still intact today.
The monolithic rock itself is a lava plug left over from an ancient long extinct volcano. It rises 200 m from the green scrub jungle surrounding it. Today on top the visitor finds the ruins of what was once a kingÂ´s fortress in the sky. Â 
While climbing up the steps there was a lady before us who got in the middle of a fight between a monkey and a dog. She got bitten by the dog and needed to go down to get treated by the red cross at the lionÂ’s gate. This is nothing that you would like to happen to you. So be aware of stray dogs and over-curious monkeys. If they approach you too boldly you might want to try out a self defense technique Marcell has discovered to be effective. He has successfully kept monkeys distant by using insect repellent.

review_text:
For me it was an achievement as I had had surgery a couple of weeks prior and was nervous about the climb especially as our driver mentioned that we would be 4 hours or so. It was a challenge but doable and a great feeling when you reach the top. 
We only took one bottle of water each (contrary to others advise, which Im glad I didn't take) and only had a drink when we got to the top (or it will weigh you down). Also visit the washroom before you start. We arrived at 830 after breakfast and had a very comfortable climb without to many people, however on our way down, there were heaps of people crawling single file up the stairs.... you can go for sunrise if you choose and its quiet but dark.
Spectacular views 360 degrees

review_text:
A visit to this UN World Heritage Site is a must. It's an exhilarating climb and amazing remnants of the ancient civilization that built this fortress city centuries ago.  We recommend staying at one of the great hotels just walking distance from the site, so you can get an early start before the crowds and the heat increase.
We were fortunate to have a break in the rain for the morning, and were treated to fantastic views from the top. It's a steep climb but all stairs with handrails, so even those with aversion to heights should be able to stomach this.

It will well worth the journey up to the very top if you can.  The views from up there see unforgettable.  You can see everything.  It is tough to imagine from the bottom how many buildings could have been up there during it time, however,  when you reach the summit, you can see how vast an area it really is.  If would have been a truly magnificent site when all the buildings are temples were standing!

The walk is quite tough, especially on a hot day.  There are lots of different heights steps so.e of which are steep.  You must also take a metal staircase up to the top via the side of the rock, which could be scary fot those afraid of heights.

On the way up, the frecos on the ceilings are worth looking at. Remember no pictures, but it is amazing to see how vivid and detailed the paintings are still, and unbelievable to think the whole area would have been covered in such figures.

The gardens at the bottom are equally majestic.  They are vast and very well preserved. you could easily walk around these and not do anything else.  There is also an ebony tree in the gardens which is worth looking out for.

A must if staying in Sigiriya.  It is a once in a lifetime experience

My first time climbing a rock fortress. I have climbed many mountains, visited dozens of temples and ancient sites to. However this one is awe inspiring and majestic both in its simplicity and 'remote' location. Located a few hundred kilometers (and miles) from Colombo, you can book several tours that will get you there in a few hours from any part of Sri Lanka. It is an island after all. 

We spent a few hours here after going to Dambulla and I'm glad we did, as this was scenic yet serene. A tour guide is not necessary as the place speaks for itself and large group tours can be rushed to get from A to B. We were in a small group and allowed to take our time. Even though we did this, I could easily have spent more time exploring the place and taking in the setting. Its not an arduous climb, although the spiral metal staircase about halfway to the top can leave one feeling a bit dizzy. However, if you have vertigo you would not be climbing this rock. One of my favorite places in Sri Lanka, which is a beautiful country. Definitely would recommend a visit if in Sri Lanka.

We made the journey, and we didnÂ’t regret it. It was a good experience, it essentially rained the entire climb which meant just taking it easy to avoid slipping. It is over priced like everyone else has mentioned (but so is stone henge, and that was far more disappointing!). When it isnÂ’t wet, itÂ’s very quickly very hot (so bring water!). 

On reflection I would consider not climbing the rock when it is wet. It becomes seriously slippery, the stairs become the run off for water and you are exposed to the elements when at height. If something was to go wrong, youÂ’d be in a bit of strife. 

We went on a Monday at approx 10:30am and it wasnÂ’t busy and we were back in our car by 12:30pm.

A guide could be handy next time to give you context on the history (we overheard one guide for a couple and he was very informative). But make sure they are wearing a white guise top

review_text:
At  USD 25 per person, not a cheap day out for a family  But that is true of most sights in Sri Lanka.

There are over 2000 steps, but its not as bad as it sounds as they are quite well spaced out into various sections (2 main ones).  And the view at the top is definitely worth the effort.  

If you are a little wary of heights watch out for the official looking guides (in matching T shirts) who will rush to help you (or may help even if you don't need it).  In particular they can be found on the last steep section (as you go through the lion paws). Once you are at the top they will demand money for their services!  And not small amounts at 1000 Rps.

Luckily we had our own real guide for our tour of Sri Lanka.  And there are a lot of details that he relayed that made our visit all the more interesting.  For example, how did they get water to the top of the rock?  And pointing out  the fountains fed from pools at the top of the rock.

If you are lucky you may spot a crocodile in the pools at the base.

I highly recommend getting there in the morning before the sun rises over the rock and beats down onto the steps.  We arrived around 0930 and were back down within a couple of hours and were in the shade whilst climbing.

review_text:
This ancient attraction is just as impressive and awe-inspiring as websites and other reviewers have said. The site is a massive one and other than the rock fortress (for which there is an entry fee), there are other places which visitors can roam for free. As you get down, you will be approached by numerous guides who will try to dissuade you from buying tickets to the rock fortress by mentioning the arduous 1200 step climb and instead offer you a tuk-tuk ride covering the places which are free. They arent aggressive but can be pushy, so you need to firmly tell them off.
Foreigners need to but tickets from the museum (entry to which is USD 5 if brought separately and complimentary if you purchase the rock fortress tickets). The museum is a good place to start off your visit.
The tickets to the rock fortress are USD 30 for adults and USD 15 for children. SAARC country nationals are entitled to a 50% discount on the adult price but no further discounts for children (so USD 15 for both adults and children). Payment can be made in USD or LKR but change, if any, is returned in LKR.
The climb itself is actually quite difficult, especially if you go in the afternoon. The place is also crowded on weekends because of lots of locals coming for a picnic.
My suggestion would be to go early morning to beat the heat and the crowds. Carry lots of water and snacks as well, as there werent any outlets selling food or water.
The way up is different from the way down, so take pictures as you go up, because you wont get the same view on the way down.
A lot of people have suggested the recommended length as being 3-4 hours but from my experience, it takes a lot longer, especially if you have young children and also explore the whole place. So in my opinion, take your time and enjoy the whole place in all its splendour and beauty. Dont try to rush things through and combine this with another attraction (like Dambulla, Anuradhapura etc) because those places too require more than 3-4 hours and it would be better to comprehensively cover both places rather than do a bit of both.

It's hard to beleive that this was man made so many years ago on top of this rock without modern technology and tools. It's a tough climb up the stairs but if you start early in the morning just when the park is opening it will be easier. We also went in October where the weather was not so hot and cooled down by the rain showers.
Sigiriya refuses to reveal its secrets easily, and you'll have to climb a series of very narrow steps. The staircases attached to sheer walls to reach the top. On the way you'll pass a series of quite remarkable frescoes and a pair of colossal lion's paws carved into the bedrock. The surrounding landscape Â– lily-pad-covered moats, water gardens and cave shrines Â– only add to Sigiriya's rock-star appeal.

review_text:
This ancient attraction is just as impressive and awe-inspiring as websites and other reviewers have said. The site is a massive one and other than the rock fortress (for which there is an entry fee), there are other places which visitors can roam for free. As you get down, you will be approached by numerous guides who will try to dissuade you from buying tickets to the rock fortress by mentioning the arduous 1200 step climb and instead offer you a tuk-tuk ride covering the places which are free. They arent aggressive but can be pushy, so you need to firmly tell them off.
Foreigners need to but tickets from the museum (entry to which is USD 5 if brought separately and complimentary if you purchase the rock fortress tickets). The museum is a good place to start off your visit.
The tickets to the rock fortress are USD 30 for adults and USD 15 for children. SAARC country nationals are entitled to a 50% discount on the adult price but no further discounts for children (so USD 15 for both adults and children). Payment can be made in USD or LKR but change, if any, is returned in LKR.
The climb itself is actually quite difficult, especially if you go in the afternoon. The place is also crowded on weekends because of lots of locals coming for a picnic.
My suggestion would be to go early morning to beat the heat and the crowds. Carry lots of water and snacks as well, as there werent any outlets selling food or water.
The way up is different from the way down, so take pictures as you go up, because you wont get the same view on the way down.
A lot of people have suggested the recommended length as being 3-4 hours but from my experience, it takes a lot longer, especially if you have young children and also explore the whole place. So in my opinion, take your time and enjoy the whole place in all its splendour and beauty. Dont try to rush things through and combine this with another attraction (like Dambulla, Anuradhapura etc) because those places too require more than 3-4 hours and it would be better to comprehensively cover both places rather than do a bit of both.

I've seen elderly women in their late 60's or even 70's, with walking canes, that climbed it all the way to the top (very slowly, though). So I guess that any healthy person can do it!
The view was spectacular and the frescoes are beautiful and intriguing. definitely worth the effort. 
DON'T FORGET TO TAKE A LOT OF WATER AND A SNACK! You don't want to find yourself with no water on the top of the stares.
