review_text: It is a must do "tourist thing" in Sri Lanka although it isn't that 'impressive' in real. It is USD30 for the tourist to get in. A very well maintain site, clean, easy to walk around and climb up. It is not that tough to climb the stairs, just need to be careful as it is quite steep at some point. If you don't have knee/leg problems, you don't need to worry about it. It is a ruined ancient city up there back in thousands of years ago. Therefore, it is pretty empty on top of the rock. But the view is great. It is literally 360' degree of view for you to see what's surrounding the rock. The wind was strong when I was there but I rather it was windy than hot, there will be no shelter on top of the rock. So, it is good to go in the morning than mid day.

Definitely explore the surrounding gardens, as there are lots of hidden treasures. We enjoyed looking at the caves, which were carefully created to protect from the rain, as well as the surrounding pools. Also, visiting the museum before entering the grounds definitely gave us a lot more insight into what we were about to see.

There are limited information boards with a few snippets, so a local guide would be of benefit - but check their ability to explain before hiring them.

review_text:
My third climb this time with a 9 year old in tow.

Left the hotel a bit behind schedule which meant were were at the car park around 9am.

While driving I spotted a board mentioning local car park. So I drove towards that. Car park to entrance ticket counter is about 01 +KM walk. I didn't measure, alternatively you can take a tuk for a few hundred rupees.

Due to the pandemic the crowds were less and it was nice to have space and less crowd to e joy the climb up. It was a lot g climb. Walk past the garden to the base and then comes the first set of steps to reach the lions paw area.

Onwards are the rest of the steps via a iron staircase and a narrow one to the top. The last bit of stairs and you are at the top. Exhausted!

Amazing views all around and my son enjoyed exploring the area while I caught my breath!

It took as about two hours from car park to the summit. With plenty of breaks in between. Coming back down was a far more pleasant experience, we didn't walk up to see the frescoes as my son had enough and wanted to get back to the hotel. It took about 45 mins coming down. 

Like another reviewer has suggested I do recommend purchasing drinks or other items from the vendors below on your way down as they are most impacted by the decline of tourism in that area.

entrance tickets for locals are 100 rupees.

review_text: The rock is very impressive, standing quite alone in the middle of the forest. At the beginning, you will cross the former gardens with some water basins; one of them is in form of octagon. Then you begin to climb the stair, about 1.600 steps! However, you will find several terraces and belvedere where you can stop and take advantage of the view. I stopped at the platform where the ruins of the Lion Gate are because I had crutches for walking and it was impossible for me to go ahead. Pay attention you must not have vertigos to climb the last part, the stairs are actually in the void! More or less at mi-walk you will find wonderful paintings, unfortunately, there is not a lot of place and you cannot stay long time. Pictures are strictly forbidden. It is suggested to visit the rock in the morning or in the late afternoon, you will find less tourists and less humidity. Take some water with you there are no kiosks inside the site.

review_text:
While I was on a trip of Sri Lanka with G Adventures, I hired a driver to take me out to see the Sigiriya Rock as it is #191 on the Lonely Planet's ultimate travelist.

Since the entrance fee into the area of the rock is $30 USD, I did not climb the rock as it has 1200 steps to get to the top.  There are also many tuk tuk drivers that try to get you to pay $30 USD to take a tuk tuk around the base of the rock.  I did not take them up on their offer as you can walk around the base of the rock and see the moats without their services, and you do not need to pay anything to do this.   

I think that $30 USD is way overpriced as the locals pay only a fraction of this cost. Sri Lanka is not the only country that charges too much for foreigners.  I found that this was true in India and Nepal as well.

Set off at 4pm, a short drive from my villa. When reaching there, we had a site guide. He explained as we move along towards the Lion Rock. The excavation, moats, lower compounds, caves, even the steps has its reason why it was coated. 1200 stairs up. 1/2 of the journey to the frescoes and wall mirror (no photos & videos allowed). 3/4 to the base of the lion 's paw entrance to the Palace up on top of the rock. By now, my legs almost gave way. I stayed at the lion's paws. But my hubby & site guide went all the way up to the top. He explained that the highest is not 1200 stairs but 1202. There are 2 steps of stone right in the centre of the Palace!
Worth participating in this UNESCO site. Entrance fee USD30 each. They accept USD.

review_text: WOW! If you're visiting Sri Lanka you really should consider putting this on your itinerary.... It's like nothing I've ever experienced or seen and is such a unique 'rock' and ancient kingdom. There are approximately 2000 stairs which wind their way up the face of the rock, arriving at the summit which is where the ancient kingdom was. It requires a moderate level of fitness, although you can take your time and do it at your own pace. Be sure to go earlier if possible as it does get quite warm.... also wear shorts or loose fitting light clothing (particularly for the ladies) as you do work up quite a sweat. Also make sure you explore the entire area at the top as there are some resident guides who will show you some interesting aspects.... and don't worry, they are not your typical money hungry types.... a donation once you're finished will suffice. Incredible experience and one for the bucket list!

review_text: One of the historic places to visit in Sri Lanka. Also known as the lion rock, sigriya is at a distance of around 3 hours from Kandy. We had not stayed in sigriya and hence we started early from Kandy and reached the rock around 10.30 am.  The climb takes around 1 hour and you can expect too much rush. It is advisable to stay here previous night as start climbing early since the rock opens at 6.30 am. There is a huge entry fee of 30 dollars which seemed a bit in reasonable. You also have an option to take an tuk tuk and visit the nearby places from where you get good views of both the rocks and a few farm too however you don't get to climb the rock in that case. Overall a nice place to visit barring the high ticket cost.

review_text:
The ancient city of Sigiriya is an archaeological site whose ruins point to the opulence and architectural wonders of this ancient city. The Rock dominates the area with the ruined fortress on top, a 1247 step climb for the energetic. We wished that we had visited years ago as old legs were unable to obey the spirit. 11 of our group of 34 made it to the top, the remainder were in awe at the photographs that captured snapshots of the ruins and views of the surrounding district. 
Those of us left at ground level enjoyed the hours viewing the ruins, ramparts, moats, miniature water gardens, fountain garden, octagonal pond and so much more of the area surrounding the base of the Rock before heading to the interesting museum.

review_text: Reading the reviews had me worried and nervous for this climb. But actually it was totally fine. I would advise getting there early to avoid the crowds. I got there at 8am and left as the tour buses and queues were building up. The rock entrance opens at 7am and closes at 5.30pm but get there early to avoid the afternoon heat. The climb itself only took 45 mins up - and I took my time. I got to the top and walked around for 30 mins before coming back down. I would say the whole experience took under 3 hours. There are a lot of steps but it's totally manageable if you just take your time and wear sensible shoes. I had my hiking sandals on. Some locals wore flip flops which I personally wouldn't recommend.

review_text:
This World Heritage site shows the ancient Sri Lankans' ingenuity in construction, architecture, design and engineering.

It took us several thousand steps to get to the top. This place is full of interesting stories of the past ancient king. 

If not for the history, come for the view. You might think many times if you're afraid of heights but the view from the top is gorgeous and definitely worth it.

Bring sun protection because there's very little shade. Wear comfortable clothes and footwear. Bring a cold bottle of water and some trail food if you get hungry easily.

review_text:
We visited as part of a tour. There are a lot of steps and if you need help, there are some men who will drag you up the steps and give you some info about the site. The negative is that I repeatedly told one of these men I did not need his help and he just kept grabbing my arm, then had the cheek to tell me I must pay 20 dollars for the help, which he said he had negotiated with our tour guide! We did not pay it, so he got in a real strop.
The views are pretty amazing, and what remains of the ancient city after so many centuries is intersting.
I would recommend a visit, but leave plenty of time as there is a lot to see. I know the helpers have to make a living, but either make it clear what you will pay from the start or send them away. Take a hat and water. There are some facilities about half way up. The climb is about 200 meters of steps.

review_text: If you suffer from vertigo, then you will need to take a very deep breath before embarking on the climb to the top of Sigiriya, which rises 200 metres straight up out of the surrounding countryside.  The steps up the mountain are universally steep and often hang from the side of the mountain out over the space below and to see the magnificent painted Sigiriya Damsels it is necessary to scale and then descend two winding spiral staircases attached to there rock and with nothing but air below.  While all the steps are quite secure, you sometimes feel as if you are suspended in space! The climb is quite a hard slog and there is little shelter so it is best to go early in the morning.  The remnants of the water gardens and other construction at the base of the mountains, the painted ladies, the extensive remains at the top of the mountain and the spectacular views are well worth the effort.  It seems absolutely amazing that such a construction could have been built with minimal equipment in such difficult terrain 1500 years ago and that the King responsible for the works then rashly decided to leave his impregnable fortress and fight his enemy at ground level only to be defeated and commit suicide.  Such incredible folly!

review_text:
We were counting on the climb to the Sigiriya ancient rock fortress to be one of the highlights of our trip to Sri Lanka.  And it certainly was!  The best piece of advice we can give you is to go early.  This will help with the heat and with the crowds.  The rock opens at 6:30 am, which is when we arrived.  However, it appears that the ticket office opens earlier, so I suggest arriving around 6:15 and being among the first to go through the gate.

Be warned that the price is hefty: around $30.  At the gate, a guard will take any label off your water bottle, so you can save time by doing this in advance.  Then, you will proceed on a straight path for about 10 minutes just to reach the beginning of the stairs to climb.  We were pleasantly surprised that the climb, while strenuous and very sweaty, was not as difficult as we expected.  We were not hurrying, and made it to the top in about 20 minutes.  I do feel this is primarily because there was no one else in our way on the stairs.  I can see how this would easily become a bottleneck and slow down your progress.

Once at the top, you will be rewarded with beautiful views of the surrounding area.  The ruins are peaceful to explore when crowds are light.  On our way down at 7:30 am, the crowds were now rolling in, so even 8 am is too late to embark.

Do go early, do take water, and enjoy the experience!

review_text:
Sigiriya is ancient rock citadel located in Sri LankaÂ’s cultural triangle. The enormous rock towers above the surrounding jungle offering extensive views. I will suggest to stay nearby and start the hike as early as 06:30AM as the temperatures rises to 100 degrees Fahrenheit and humidity around 80%. You have to climb about 1200 steep steps with elevation gain of about 650 feet. My advice is to start early, drink water regularly, wear hat, use sunscreen and go slow. If you are from SAARC countries then carry your passport to get 50% discount on admission ticket. 
Sigiriya is a world heritage site declared by UNESCO in 1982. It is a unique combination of 5th century urban planning, architecture, engineering, hydraulics, garden design, painting and poetry. 
The city is designed in a square module 2750 meter east to west and 925 north to south. 
1. Royal Gardens- This is massive water gardens. 
2. Three water gardens. 
3. Boulder Garden- It begins at slope of hill at base of the rock. 
4. Cistern Rock- Huge stone that has been split. 
5. Audience Hall Rock
6. Preaching Rock
7. Painted maidens- These frescos  are preserved in a cave pocket about 40 feet above walkway. 
8. Mirror Wall- Highly polished surface is original stucco. Most poetic verses had been written in praise of maidens on cliff face. 
9. Lion Terrace. 
10. Palace- It is located on summit but none of superstructure remains.

review_text:
An absolute must do for anyone who is able to make the ascent, Sigiriya Rock is stunning! 

Seen from below, the massive granite outcrop looks daunting. ItÂ’s a  challenge to climb, but mainly because of the heat and crowds. (Go early enough and you can mostly avoid both.)

We made it to the top in 30 minutes, with two young kids, and two adults with bad knees! We arrived around 800 and were glad we had because it was incredibly crowded as we descended. 

The water gardens viewable on the approach are impressive. Incredible feats of ancient ingenuity and engineering prowess. 

The climb is well organized and with the $30 US for adults (kids 6-12 are half price). Most of the way you go up metal stairs the are secured to the rock face. These are narrow, and a bit unnerving when the wind gusts, but we saw people of all ages and fitness levels work their way up.

It is worth the sweat and sore legs when you reach the top!

The palace ruins are incredible, but it is the 360 degree vistas that are the real payoff. We spent close to an hour roaming around and snapping breathtaking pics.

The descent retraces the final section of the climb, at first, before reaching a much easier exit pathway. Again, it took roughly half an hour.

One of the coolest, and most singular, experiences IÂ’ve ever had!

review_text: Climbing the Rock Fortress is not for the feint of heart or weak limbs. I was daunted looking at the fortress from afar. But what gave me strength was the sight of families, grandparents, parents, and children--barefooted, in flipflops, sandals--climbing to the top. With digestive cookies and water and rest stops, I was able to climb to the very top in around 2 hours! People were waited patiently for the slower climbers. And what a view! 360 degree view of the sunset! We waded in the ancient swimming pool and enjoyed the cool breeze. I was immensely glad I had the courage and strength to complete the climb. A midafternoon climb after the Dumballa caves culminated my day.

review_text:
It is a major tourist attraction in this area.  The place is very crowded with 95% locals.  They pay only R50 but the foreigners pay R5000.  

You have to walk through a huge garden and walk up many steps to see the Lion Rock and to climb up to the top to see the view.  You need good shoes as the stairs are not even.

The day we visited the place, it was very crowded.  We could only move a couple of steps at a time and waited for the next step.  We had to walk through some walkways which were built on the side of the rock.  The narrow walkways were made of metal and with metal support welded into the rock.  It has to support a lot of people at anytime.  I was a little concerned about the safety at that time. 

It took us a long time to go to the top of the rock because there were a lot of people.  It was extremely unpleasant under such hot weather to be stuck with hundreds of people.

The top of the rock is not really big but the view is stunning.  Unfortunately, there is no sign and no brochure about anything of the rock.  We spent about 15 mins there taking pictures.  Going downhill was easier but it was also very crowded.  

Before we walked to the foreigner parking lot, we walked through a few stores and bought a couple souvenirs.  I am not sure if there is any washroom at all.

review_text:
We visited sigirya during our trip to Sri Lanka. I was already knackered from waking up at 7 am to get there early (trust me - don't do this later than 10 am)

Having said that climbing Sigirya is 100% the most fun activity my wife and I did during our trip to Sri Lanka. It costs $20 or $30 to enter (expensive compared to the $2 entrance fee at Pidurangala).

It's a steep climb easier than Pidurangala and there are stairs for most of the way up but everyone can do it. I saw people with babies doing it with one hand and old people with sticks getting pushed up the hill. 

Apart from the fun way up you get 360 views of Pidurangala, Dambulla and the nearby parks. 

I left with major aches in my legs but I can't stop thinking about that day . I would do it again on a heartbeat.

If someone asks to help just refuse politely. I was scammed again and some "helpful" employee extracted 3000 rupees from me for grabbing my wife's hand to "help her up" . He wouldn't let go. For this behavior alone I am not willing to give 5/5

review_text:
We started our hike through Horton Plains early in the morning to catch a sunrise over the misty hills and terrains. What can I say, it was definitely worth waking up so early. We saw plenty of deers eating fresh grass even before we entered the main gate of the park, and then had an enjoyable walk along the route towards Baker's Falls. 

There are two options: you can start with the Falls and finish by the Little World's End or vice versa. We chose the first option and did not regret it. After we saw the sunrise, the sun quickly disappeared behind the clouds and we did not see it much until we reached the falls and the skies became blue. We took wonderful photos and had our packed breakfast right there on a bench, which was so romantic and enjoyable.

When we continued our route towards the World's End, we realized how right we were in taking that path - we almost always hiked down rather than climbing up and it made our trekking way more comfortable and less tiring. The day before we hiked the Adam's Peak, so we could not feel our legs and feet after that and this path we chose turned out to be helpful :) 

Unfortunately, when we reached the World's End, a big cloud hung on top and covered all the view. We waited for 30 minutes and the situation remained the same. We still were pleased with the hike and the World's End because there was a certain mystery in this endless mist over the edge. You can literally feel you are on the edge of nowhere.

P.S. In my opinion, you won't need a guide to hike Horton Plains. It is super easy and it is impossible to get lost on the way. There is literally only one path and it is a round journey, so whatever way you choose - you will end up in the same place. Only if a lady is solo and scared of being attacked or something??? But generally, for me it seemed peaceful and safe. And if a leopard comes out from a bush, I don't think that having a guide will be helpful right??)))

Also the time you will spend there will be at least 4-5 hrs if you do not want to run along the whole route and wish to take nice pictures and just enjoy the nature around you. So don't listen to people who tell it is like a 3-hour hike. Maybe, if you don't complete the whole circle..)

review_text: Lovely hike with amazing views. Took us about 4 hours total while carrying our 9 month old baby in a sling. We saw fluffy purple bear monkeys, reptiles, deer and even signs of leopards. It was chilly so bring layers! Make sure you hire a proper guide with a 4 wheel drive or a van to take you up - we saw some hair raising scenes of small cars struggling to drive up the mountain. I would highly recommend hiring a guide for the hike - you don't need one but you will learn so much more about the local wildlife and see so much that would otherwise miss! Can highly recommend!

review_text:
This is a lovely trekking place with fresh air and beautiful scenery along the trekking paths. Some beautiful stops worth to check out are: 
1. Little WorldÂ’s End view point 
2. Great WorldÂ’s End view point 
3. BakerÂ’s Waterfalls 
We were so lucky to be able to see a wild Sambar Deer right in front of us up close before the starting point of the trek. Entrance fee is quite steep at LKR3,850 per person. Suggest to go early in the morning as we departed from our hotel at Nuwara Eliya at 5am. On the way up to Horton Plains, before reaching the ticket booth, we stopped at the roadside to watch the sunrise above the sea clouds. Horton Plains is a UNESCO World Heritage Site where is protected areas for its nature beauty. It is a plateau at 2100-2300 meters above sea level. Hence, be prepared for the warm clothing since it can be very chilly early in the morning. A complete route of hiking require at least half day time (4-5 hours depends on individual fitness level) and the trekking path is relatively easy for all age, but good walking shoes are necessary, plus adequate drinking water. Packing breakfast is advisable for people who do morning trek. Tight security check of the bag/ haversack at the entrance of trekking and no plastics allowed at the park. We were so glad that we did morning trek as the weather was cool and pleasant and completed our trek slightly before noon. Hence, most people do morning trek and be there early as there will be long queue for security check. An afternoon trekking would be warm and sweaty due to warmer weather in the day. We simply love this place and the beauty of Mother Nature!!!

It's a real photo opportunity while hiking, so we really enjoyed it, despite the hard slog we had to put in!

review_text:
My friend and I visited in January 2023. Overall, I would recommend choosing antoher of the many attractions in the hill country over Horton Plains.

Why go: it's a pretty and clean walk through a high-altitute plateau to a wide outlook down to the plains. We saw some deer in the open fields and interesting descriptions of the cloud forest. The walk is comparable in enjoyment to many temperate walks elsewhere. Easy to hire a return car trip from Nuwara Eliya (10,000 LKR). You can easily do the circular walk in 2-3hrw. Take sturdy shoes and a warm top layer. Start early: be at the park centre for 6:30am to get the best chance of the views before the clouds come in. If money is no question, then you will enjoy the park.

Why skip: regretfully the park management seem to have taken to an extortion racket. A single person ticket for a foreigner will cost you around USD40 with the ticket price and the 'service charge', and even more if you actually want to pay in dollars (the clerk at the entrance will happily exchange to rupees for a hefty fee). That's probably about 40 times the price for locals. That is absurdly expensive for Sri Lankan standards and it's very expensive for what you get by Western standards, as it is just an unguided walk through the nature.

review_text:
Get ready for a walk, walk and walk for approximately 9.4 kms !! (Pheww)

Undoubtedly this hike will give you a beautiful experience of walking in sweat, clouds, mist, rain and breeze ! One can experience all of them in the total hike !
To consider for people who are not so adventurous and who prefer less walking. The plains may mislead you about the difficulty level !
There are levels of walking and they are easy, difficult and more difficult!!
And there are definitely the same the way they are listed. In the rains the rocks, the waking passage can be slippery making your hike really challenging. Till you reach bakers fall you will get an insight of your journey anyways !! One should be with very good quality hiking shoes with good grip which will be helpful while waking. Rain Coats, cap and some food stuffs are very important along with you. Remember to carry them in a paper bag as no plastics are allowed inside. They will remove the plastic covering of the water bottle too ( a good initiative though)
Do try to start your journey maximum by 7:30 am to see a clear view near the world end ( if you fortunate). Else the clouds will cover you well and give another experience for photography only ??
You will enjoy the named places called and mini worlds end and worlds end. They are the places where you can have a breathtaking views if there are no clouds.
Be very careful of the steep elevation of the worlds end while doing some photography.
This may take a minimum of 3 to 4 hours depending on the walking speed and time.
Apart from this: undoubtedly this will give an amazing feeling once you finally see the finish gate ??
# leaving your foot prints behind ??
# mythological: In the story, Hanuman set fire to Horton plains and that fire lasted for a long time. The original name, Maha Eliya Thenna carries the meaning, 'The hugely lighten ground'. Even now the upper layer of soil can be seem in a blackish grey colour. There had been some soil tests done by local universities, and it revealed that upper layer contains a high amount of Calcium Carbonate and Potash.

review_text: This is a beautiful hike --- it would be worthwhile to secure a guide who will know where to stop to view what will be the most AMAZING sunrise you will ever see.  It simply took my breath away -- I compared the experience to Haleakula and this wins.  After the sunrise we then proceeded into the park.  We elected the clockwise path which is a bit shorter distance to the World's End which improves your chances of getting the view before the fogs set in.  Although it did seem that even when there was fog, it was like weather at home:  just wait a few minutes and it changes.  The last 1/3 of the trail TO the World's End was so dense with shrubbery that without our guide I'm not sure we would have thought we were on the right path.  For the number of people that take this experience, we thought it would have been more trodden, but it seems Mother Nature tries to keep it fairly dense.  After viewing W/E, the remainder of the trail is a really nice nature walk.  Keep your eyes out for green lizards that sit on top of the trees, little brown frogs that are fun to watch puff up with their croaking, and the variety of birds that inhabit the area.  Unless you're familiar with how to spot these critters, this would be another benefit to befriending a guide.

review_text:
Read so much about World End at Horton Plain. We like to visit. I am also expecting the long walk, but never did I realise that the 9.5km walk is really not simple, at least for me.
The path initially was easy, as it is flat, but once entered the grassland, the path was rough with obstacles along the way. Ups & downs, under shade of the trees. Open space grassland path is easier to walk but under hot sun. We did not see any animals at all. 
However when reaching the mini world and hike another 1 km to the World End and further 2km Baker's Fall is really a reward. Another few km to the exit, for unfit people like me must reconsider. The path is a loop. 
I would say it is good for those who like hiking.
Entrance fee is not cheap too. LKR7, 670 for 2 foreigners, 1 local, parking, tax.

review_text: Interesting part of the tour of our trip.  We were advised to go very early having left our hotel at 5am, we were lucky that our hotel catered giving us a awesome breakfast pack.   We were greeted with other tours lining up in the morning to get tickets, one word of advice is also to dress warm as in the morning it was VERY cold.  The national park also restricts bringing in any food and you are checked at the entry point, it was strange however to see other tourists eating at the peak, i wasn't sure why our drink was confiscated.  The hike was amazing, one of the best experiences ever, in the morning the hike was sublime, the pure calm and beautiful scenery was amazing, the best part was that luckily we had a good guide and was able to take a different route where we didn't see anyone. review_text:
It is worth walking the distance just to witness the famous worlds end.  The walk is about 3 miles, which is not yoo far and there is plenty to stop and see along the way.

There are birds of different kinds everywhere, as well as plenty of animals, including the deer.  We were lucky enough that one got  very close on our way back to the car park!

There is a very nice waterfall in Horton plains too, which is worth taking a small detour for.  It was brilliant to be able to get so close to it.  We could feel the water spraying on to us which was good in the heat of the day.

Wobrlds end was spectacular.  It really does look like what the words mean! The views were breathtaking.  You could easily stay here and look out over everything for some time.

There is also mini worlds end here which is very much the same but on a lower level.  You go past this to get to, or return from worlds end.  It to is worth admiring for a fair while.

Definitely worth going to while here

You will come to the point where the path splits, we went right as had read this way is much quieter and it's TRUE - it's like you have the whole place to yourself, we didn't really pass anyone until over half way as those that went left passed us! The paths are narrow and congestion slows you down
The difference to turning right is you go to bakers fall first, the other way you do little  worlds end first, so another advantage to going right is that you see the vista from works end before the little one so you get the majesty first not the glimpse which I think could take the edge of worlds end if you saw that first
The ground is quite uneven and if been damp or raining the clay soil is sloppy
Some of the walk requires some mild climbing - we had read it was a non challenging easy walk and I would debate that for those with poor knees etc - its misleading to say that. It's not rock climbing but there are definitely areas that require effort and thought 
The views are incredible 
Out of this world worth every step
We are fairly fit and active and took us just under three hours 
There are about 3 loo stops on the loop which I was really impressed with

review_text:
My lovely wife and I took the morning hike through Horton Plains National Park to World's End. It's a hugely popular hike but in truth is rather unremarkable. 
The trail meanders through rather mundane scenery to the lookout point which offers pretty impressive views. Having said that, I wasn't entirely blown away by them. There are, for example, plenty of vistas in Scotland that are equally if not more impressive.
The high numbers of visitors mean there isn't a great deal of wildlife to be seen. There were sambar deer hanging around near the car park, which I believe there often are, and we were lucky enough to spot a purple-faced leaf monkey while driving back to Nuwara Eliya. But don't expect too much. Leopard sightings around here are almost unheard of.

All in all it was actually a pleasant enough hike. But the trouble is that it costs way too much for what it is. Entry fees for the two of us came to around 8,000 rupees (Â£35, $44, Â€40) which is just crazy. You'll also have to pay transport costs on top of that - for example we paid 3,000 rupees (Â£13, $17, Â€15) for a tuk tuk from Nuwara Eliya. And it simply isn't worth the money for what it is.

review_text:
This national park is the source for four of Sri Lanka's major rivers, so it's not unusual to experience a bit of rain. Fortunately, the heavy rain dropped the night before our 9.5 km trek through the park, which took in the spectacular World's End. It made some uneven parts of the trail a bit slippery, so solid hiking shoes or, at minimum runners, are essential.

Only a moderate level of fitness is required to navigate the main trail, which takes in World's End and Bakers Falls. However, anyone with some walking or climbing disability should take note that there are those uneven areas to negotiate. 

World's End is so called because of its 900 metre vertical cliff face that drops into the forest of the valley wall. It's hard to capture its scale in photographs. There are two viewing decks at World's End. Beware, particularly for children, that there are few barriers to prevent falls over the cliffs, both on the decks and on the short trail between decks. My impression was that the coiled razor wire would merely lacerate you during the fall rather than prevent it. The higher deck gives a much better view of the main cliff face. The steps down to Bakers Falls are also quite steep.

Hortons Plains features a wide variety of landscape and an explosion of different colours from the many plant species that adorn the plain. The area is also a good place to see Sambar Deer, one of Sri Lanka's larger deer species.

review_text:
I was traveling alone and staying in a guest house in Nuwara Eliya so my transportation was arranged for by my wonderful hosts, but my tour guide/driver picked me up at 5am to take me out to Horton Plains. We got there early a) to beat the crowds, and b) because I had an afternoon train to Ella to catch, but we actually got there so early that the ticket office hadn't opened yet. 

The hike isn't too difficult, it's about 8 miles with a few portions of steeper climbing, but getting there in the morning allows you to see some GORGEOUS views. My driver gave me the tip of sitting and waiting at World's End because a lot can change in the scenery in a matter of minutes, and it was the best advice. I ate snacks I packed (remember to do this) and took a 40 minute rest up there and watched in awe as clouds and fog came in and out (at one point completely blocking the view and then clearing up to reveal a gorgeous drop and the plains beyond). 

I wanted to take pictures every time I turned the corner because I was treated to new views every mile or so - the diversity in ecosystems and flora/fauna is INSANE. 

If you're in Nuwara Eliya, make sure you make time for this hike! I actually stopped in Nuwara Eliya JUST so I could get out here! Definitely get an early start (apparently sometimes in the morning you can see deer and elephants if it's early enough!) so you're hiking when it's cooler and to beat the crowds.

review_text:
We had a very unfortunate experience when buying tickets to enter Horton Plains National Park. We visited on the morning of Friday 12th July. Apologies for the long and less than positive review, I am also posting this hoping someone may be able to point me towards a way to lodge a complaint with the Park itself as I havenÂ’t been able to find this online. 

Ticket prices are not advertised as prices tend to fluctuate so there is no price list at the ticket booth. We asked for Â“3 tickets, one person is localÂ”, however this was interpreted as 3 tickets plus one local. A foreigner ticket at the time was ~2,650 rupees. With no price list, visitors the transaction is based purely on verbal communication with no calculator or screen to show how prices are calculated (there are three taxes on top of the ticket price). Understandably this is also a quick, rushed process during busy times such as when we visited.

Unfortunately, we were unable to realise we were overcharged until we had driven 10 minutes from the ticket office to the park entrance. At the park entrance we spoke with a number of staff and based on what they advised we decided to enter the park rather than drive back and seek a refund (lucky we did this because as we found out, we would not have been refunded anyway and it would have ruined our visit). 

On our way out we approached the ticket booth and fortunately the same cashier was working (a middle aged man, moustache, larger, has worked at the park for over 15 years). We were very careful to politely inform that we were accidentally overcharged (e.g. we avoided saying Â“you overcharged usÂ”, instead saying Â“we were accidentally overchargedÂ”) however he immediately went on the defensive, became very rude and irrational and refused to help us. He accused us of being irresponsible and not communicating with him properly. He also said there is no possibility of a refund once a sale has been made and its the customers responsibility to know what they are being charged and that he does not make mistakes so it must be our fault.  

When we tried to explain that we were not trying to pass blame and a simple misunderstanding had occurred, he became argumentative and started insulting our tour guide/driver in Sinhalese and saying he was not looking after us properly. He refused to call the park manager (he said there was no phone reception, although all three of us had reception) and said nobody would help us because it was our fault. There was lots of back and forth about ticket prices not being advertised, no way of knowing what we have been charged for until transaction has been finalised etc. until we finally decided that nothing we did or said would help us obtain a refund. Overall, this left a very sour taste in our mouths and our tour guide/driver felt ashamed that a park ranger would behave in this way. Unfortunately, the cashier did not have an ounce of empathy and his behaviour screamed dishonesty and not a care on the world for doing what is right. Had he at least even tried to help us in the slightest, our experience with him would have been completely difference. 

Lesson: when buying tickets and you have a local guide to accompany you, be very clear to say X foreigner tickets and Y local ticket. Avoid assuming any statements like Â“3 people, one is localÂ” as this will be interpreted as 3 foreigners, one localÂ”.

As for the park itself, it is beautiful and the views are amazing. It was lovely walking through such stunning scenery. However, the price is quite high especially in comparison to similar yet free experiences we have had in Sri Lanka as well as other national parks we have visited around the world.

review_text: The price is quite steep, when paying for a family of 5, but it was totally worth it.  Prices - Adults just under 3000 LKR and half the price for young children. That roughly equates to Â£12 per adult. You can see the breakdown in the photo. The hike was a gentle walk for half of the way. The last part, to get to WorldÂ’s End and BakerÂ’s Fall was trickier but still manageable. The whole hike was breathtaking. It took us 2 1/2 hrs for the whole hike (some say between 3-4 hrs). ItÂ’s is clearly signed and there really is no need to have a guide. At one point you can choose to go left or right. Going left means that you will visit WorldÂ’s end first and right will take you to BakerÂ’s Fall first. ItÂ’s a loop so it doesnÂ’t matter which way you choose. Many people have shared that you are not allowed to take any plastic with you, however the rangers do help you with this. We went there with water bottles, as we had nothing else to carry the water, and some snacks. When we got there they removed the plastic labels off the water bottles and then provided paper bags for our snacks. We were very impressed with the care and attention towards the conservation of flora and fauna and they should be applauded for it. We didnÂ’t see a piece of rubbish and it was completely unspoiled. A must if your are in Nuwara Eliya.

The park itself is beautiful with well graded paths leading to 'worlds end' viewing point.  Well worth the walk.  9 km round trip (felt like more!!)  but completed within three hours with a well timed breakfast break at worlds end.  Ask your hotel for takeaway sandwiches and water.

Lovely waterfall not far off main path and leopards roam the area.  We saw leopard scat!!!!

review_text:
We hired a guide/driver from Nuwara Eliya to travel to Horton Plains to ensure that we both appreciated the views as well as the wildlife. 

Unfortunately our hotel delayed us significantly as they forgot our packed breakfast which meant we ended up missing out on the views. Had we got there 10 mins earlier we would have seen what we headed to Nuwara Eliya for.

While we missed the views, the hiking was still pleasant with nice scenery around and the waterfall made for a diverting stop. The round trip from the car park to the view point and then the waterfall is just shy of 10km. We found it an easy walk and most people should be able to do it easily.  There is a fair bit of wildlife to appreciate: birds, lizards and frogs. We came across an organised birding group so I imagine its a good place to see birds.

In order to have the best chance of seeing the views and the end of Sri Lanka try to get to the viewpoint before 8am as it clouds over really quickly. There definitely seems to be no point doing the walk mid/late morning or the afternoon as the whole place will be covered in cloud.

review_text:
We were taken here as a part of a tour of Sri Lanka. The circular route is 11Kms long and very tough with many steep ups and downs.
The route surface is also not smooth, and you have to clamber over rocks, boulders and tree routes. This is made tougher as it frequently rains here and the rocks and mud become slippery.

Not a walk for all ages or abilities. Wear sensible shoes and take water and food.

The views are spectacular from Worlds End and the waterfall is worth a visit.

review_text:
- We did the full loop and really enjoyed it. The landscape was very similar to Kosciusko in NSW Australia especially the low bushes. It did not have that many flowers nor birds to look at except rhododendrons.

- The walk was not too arduous but if you do have walking poles would suggest to use at least one to provide support & security as certain parts of the track were steep and narrow. We (over 60 & 70 yo respectively) managed to do it under 3.5 hours without walking poles.

- Arrived at 8am as per the guide's recommendation and the car park was full. When arrived it was a bit cool but certainly not cold (for Kiwis & Aussies) and getting warmer later on.

- Make sure the seal and label on plastic water bottles and any plastic wraps etc. removed before the walk as it would be inspected and removed  by park rangers at the park entrance.

- Barkers' fall was nothing special but the views from the World's End & Little World's End were spectacular.

Its worth doing!

Staying in Nuwara Eliya I hired a tuk tuk for a return trip for 3000R. Leaving at 5 a.m. we got there just after 6 a.m. and there were already lots of people queuing for tickets. It was 4777R for one person plus driver which I thought was very expensive. The general advise is to get there early morning as the views at worlds end clouds over after 10 a.m. ItÂ’s a 9 km walk in a circular route, where you have the choice to go left or right at the first junction. Going left you reach worlds end first, as opposed Bakers fall by going right. I took the left to get to worlds end early and was rewarded by only having a few people there. The views are good with a vertical drop of over 800 metres. After 20 mins lots more tourists arrived so I moved on. Luckily when reaching Bakers falls later again there were very few people. The rest of the walk is nice but nothing spectacular and took around 2 hours in total. I didnÂ’t see much in terms of wildlife but there are deer and even Leopards supposedly. 
In summary, this is a nice walk, but rather expensive if you compare it to walking in other national parks.

If you have the energy, take the steps down to Bakers Falls as it is spectacular.
Good footwear is essential for hiking in Horton Plains.
No plastics are allowed in the park &  any thing in plastic packaging will be confiscated at the gates.

review_text:
It's not the greatest walk I've been on, but it was different and enjoyable.  I wouldn't want to do it in the middle of the day as I thought it was quite hot when we walked - from about 7.20 to 10.30.

There is a cloud forest in this area so you'd have to get there very early or be very lucky to strike the World's End without a lot of cloud.  But they said, I didn't mind standing near the edge and watching the cloud roll in and up and over the cliff face.  Sit long enough and the cloud lightens enough for you to see the valley below and some of the tea fields.  

If you follow the track on the left it is the shortest to the viewing platforms but it makes the walk back via the falls a steeper climb, so I personally preferred walking anti-clockwise and getting to the platform after the crowds and then having an easier walk back along the less steep ridge.

Frogs, forest pigeon and a Sri Lankan giant squirrel were our rewards for walking this trail.  The squirrel looked like an Australian tree kangaroo in the face but had a large bushy tail.  You can hear the bear monkeys in the jungle here as well and we're so lucky in that on the very bumpy drive back down the plateau a bear monkey was posing for us on a tree Top. So keep a look out.

As walks go it was moderate - some steep slippery sections, and the landscape it crosses was quite interesting - undulating hills, interspersed with grasslands and forests.

I don't know what the park fees were as we did it as part of a package so in some respects it's better not to know and as I think the most expensive fees, it was nice to see the Rangers being very vigilant with hikers as far as long plastics go and to search each bag and advise to bring everything back out. So surprisingly I saw very little plastic litter - the off pieces carelessly dropped but good to see they are trying to keep the area litter free - except the toilet area - unfortunately full of rubbish.

review_text:
Staying in Nuwara Eliya we took a tuk tuk to Horton Plains leaving our hotel at 6.00am. We met a line of traffic entering the park but once tickets had been obtained we were on our way in. It is quite an expensive place to visit, although the same as many other national parks in Sri Lanka  - $15USD per person, $8USD service charge, plus the vehicle and driver entrance 185Rs plus 15% tax on top of all of that! The tuk tuk ride from Nuwara Eliya was 3500Rs.

There was a long line for the toilets at the entrance but there are more toilets inside the park where the walk starts from. ItÂ’s quite a long drive from the park entrance to start of the walk, I had assumed the walk would start at the entrance but we saw no one walking along the road. We saw several Sambar Deer though! 

There are bag checks at the start of the walk where plastic is confiscated. Plastic drink bottles had the plastic labels torn off them. If you have food in plastic bags youÂ’ll be given a paper bag instead. This is great to see and it really meant that the park was very clean. 

The walk clockwise to WorldÂ’s End is pleasant with grasslands and bush. There are toilets near little worlds end. It was misty at WorldÂ’s End but the mist came and went so we were still able to see out to some lakes south at times. ItÂ’s a neat spot for watching clouds of mist rise over the 800m drop.

The rest of the loop walk was nice too as itÂ’s through the grasslands with views down to a river. There are more toilets near the waterfall. Overall the walk is fairly easy although there are some challenging areas with uneven terrain and steps.

review_text:
You need to be here early to miss the build up of mist. We arrived around 06.50 and we certainly were not some of the first here. Despite what some people say, this is a pretty tough walk. I'm relatively fit but I'd still call it a challenging walk. My Fitbit recorded 17500 steps and 171 floors.
I hate to tarnish an entire country but we were again inflicted to Chinese tourist hooligans. These moronic individuals who are only interested in taking posed selfies of themselves with 'V' fingers need to be taught how to be a tourist and respect others. We had seen it at religious sites where they run everywhere, shouting and pushing and completely disrespecting other people's religion. Today it was the utter disrespect of nature. Signs ask to be quiet, this is a place to take in the landscape, to listen to the wind. This is not a place to have Timberlake coming out of your I Phone at full blast As no one else was saying anything I'm afraid some Anglo Saxon words about their parentage was uttered and I guess they understood as they put their earphones on!!!!

We were lucky to see the very rare bear monkey, an animal that is incredibly shy. Everyone around was hushed and we were able to see this amazing animal. Despite sushhhing and pointing to the monkey so they too could see it, these imbecilic people started to whistle at it like you would a dog. The monkey disappeared. 

At Worlds End again it was the Chinese that pushed to get the best vantage point to get selfies of themselves. China has just started tourism and this problem will only grow. Everyone appears aware of it but no one is teaching them that there are ways to be a respectable tourist. Our guide said this happens all the time. Perhaps responsible tourism behavior needs to be taught in school? 
The walk as mentioned is challenging, some good walking shoes should prevent slips. We saw people in flip flops. We also saw tourists with small children. This is not the place to take children. It is challenging enough on some of the steeper climbs, but looking after or carrying a child is an accident waiting to happen. It will be completely boring for them anyway and a pain for the parent.
The drive from Nuwara is in the dark and  therefore you don't see much, but coming back its a great drive and you see plenty of local life with good photo opportunities.

review_text: Horton Plains is an important area for nature and conservation this must be it's primary function and restrictions on where you can wander around are understandable. That said, the entrance fee of about Â£15 per person for what turned out to be a half day trip seems excessive. We arrived at opening time to see birds and didn't do the world's end walk, which is what most of the tourists were going for. I saw all of the species that I wanted to and was very pleased. The open air toilets were a great design and odour free. I hope the money spent goes to a good cause. In the UK national parks are free and most other countries that I've visited they only charge a nominal entrance fee. Sri Lanka could get a bad reputation for ripping off tourists. We've regularly come across one price for locals and a much larger one for foreigners. The recent implementation of free tourist visas for stays of less than one month is a great way of encouraging tourists to return after the Easter bombings. We came for two months and had to pay Â£160, we've spent a lot of money in that time. We'd consider returning but please reduce the visa fees.

review_text: We were on a small group tour and the walk to World's End and Baker's Fall has been one of the highlights of our trip so far. You need to start early as otherwise the clouds roll in and you can't see the view. It's cold up there at that time of morning so take plenty of layers as later it gets really warm. I started with a down jacket over the top and ended up in a T shirt! Take hats and sunscreen too and sensible enclosed walking shoes. Quite rightly they don't allow any plastic containers in the park (other than water bottles with labels removed), so be prepared for a thorough bag check on arrival. I applaud this as there was almost no litter on the whole trek. There are toilets strategically placed throughout the park which I didn't use but others said they were fine. Would recommend this if you are reasonably fit. It's 9 kilometres and over quite slippery rocks at times so if you have agility problems you might struggle. I wouldn't want to do it in the rain but we had a beautiful day with great views from World's End.

We left at 5 a.m. and it took us 2 hours to reach the entrance to the National Park. There was already a long queue for tickets. It was quite cold then, and we were glad we had worn our jackets. At the entrance, they checked our bags for plastic. They even removed the plastic wrapping on the water bottles. That was impressive. It was a 7 km trek through various type of terrain. We saw a couple of deer grazing at the start of our trek. We took the route towards the right and were glad of having started early, as it was already beginning to get warm. Half way through we reached Baker's falls which was a wonderful sight. We continued on our way through rocky terrain at times and as we neared the point called World's End,we 
saw this amazing view of clouds coming down. We reached there and felt that we were literally among the clouds. We could not see anything below the cliff. The clouds were covering the view. After this point comes Little World's End and then the hike back is through shaded areas. Here you get to hear the sounds of different birds. Maybe if we had binoculars we would have been able to see them.

Next stop is WorldÂ’s End, which is the main reason to do Horton Plains. Amazing view and take a moment to take in the moment. The final stop was Little WorldÂ’s End which is basically the same view but from a different point. 

The hike back is basically rocky and heading uphill. 

Highly recommended for avid hikers.

review_text: Though this is such a main touristy attraction, it's well worth it. When you first arrive around 6 am, it's full of cars and people running to the ticket booth right when it opens, which makes you nervous about the crowds. But as soon as you get on the trail, of which there are two choices, the crowds really thin and most of the time you are hiking on your own. The hike is not strenuous, with few steep uphill points, and the scenery alternates between forest and open plain which is really cool. The viewpoint at the top is amazing. Get there early- otherwise, cloud cover rolls in and the view won't be the same.

This is a national park and it does require money but I have to wonder where it goes. We were told 3 different distances to the various 'signature spots' and the signposts give a fourth opinion. This should not be attempted by anyone with a hip, knee or ankle problem and hiking boots are almost a necessity. The tracks are not maintained in any way and consist of reasonably steep climbs and descents through deep ruts strewn with boulders, rocks and loose stones. Furthermore it is suppoesed to be a nature walk, and we started before sunrise, only to find around 100 vehicles at the the first gate with several 100 tourists clamouring for tickets. We entered and drove 5kms to the second gate to find even more vehicles and people. Goodness knows what this is like later in the day although when we left at about 9.30 am there must hjave been thousands in the park. As described, walking is difficult and the experience was not helped by crowds of mainly Asian tourists squawking incessantly and noisily with some even playing their radios for all to hear. The result - no wildlife.
When we got to either of the World's Ends we could hardly see a not that impressive view for the crowds of photo and selfie taking tourists. There seemed to be neither control nor wardens on hand and most of the guides were more intent on chatting up their attractive customers than controlling the mobs. Our guide, who was embaraseed by the appalling behavious of the tourists and their mentors, did attempt to quieten the mobs but his efforts were in vain. He did advise us not to attempt a visit to Bakers Falls as that requires climbing and descending by holding on to mangrove roots as the tracks are in an even bigger mess. It is a not that impressive, expensive money spinner but for whom?

Baker Falls on the walk out are well worth a detour.

review_text:
Only 26 km from Nuwara Eliya but a long, steep and winding drive up to the plains. Going up through Pattipola from Nuwara Eliya allows you to visit the Ambewela Farms and view the rolling farm countryside and dairy herds. Pattipola is also the highest point on the railway going to Ella and the road crosses the tracks at the station.
It's best to get to Horton Plains early. Mist rolls in later in the morning and often the views are obscured. It's a 5 km hike to World's End and back via Baker's Falls, also worth seeing. 
Head back out of the park via the Ohiya road for some spectacular views of the World's End gap from the road. Not exactly the same as hiking to the lookout point but stunning nevertheless. 
Viewing wildlife is a hit or miss prospect. We saw nothing. But there are some tame Sambhur deer at the visitor center for a photo opportunity. These animals are habituated to humans due to feeding, unfortunately, but you can get quite close, something that you could not do with truly wild animals.

I imagine when the rhododendrons are in flower the scenery in the rest of the area must be spectacular.
I was surprised how tricky the terrain was though. It was billed as a hike but there are a lot of boulders to navigate and shale surfaces which makes slipping a real risk.Anyone not fully mobile should be aware before setting out. We had a very hot day so take water, you will be checked for plastic items on the way into the trail but are allowed water bottles.

review_text:
We were at the park as it opened.  Already a line of vehicles. Was good to head off early before the heat and the crowds.  We did it clockwise, so shorter to get to World's End and longer walk (via Bakers Falls) back.  It requires climbing up and down some parts of the track so needs some agility. Recommend good walking shoes or sandals. But nothing too bad if reasonable fitness.
Mini World's End was good but World's End was spectacular.  Getting there as early as possible seems to be better before it gets too misty.  Standing on the edge of a 4,000 ft vertical drop is not good for your vertigo!!!
The walk back via the Baker's Falls was also great.
In the end was a loop of about 9KMs.
Be aware that as you enter the walk they search your bags for any plastics and take them away from you.  For example we had a couple of water bottled with plastic labels and they cut off the labels before we were allowed to take them in.

review_text: We hadn't planned to head up to the Horton Plains before we got to Nuwara Eliya, but decided to on arrival and arranged an early pickup (5am) with our tuktuk driver.  Nuwara Eliya is cold at that time of day,and we were very grateful for our padded jackets - make sure you prep well for a cold morning!  The journey over in the dark was, well, interesting - low-lying mist on the unlit roads, speeding drivers trying to overtake at all opportunities (it is Sri Lanka after all!) and low powered tuktuk lights all made for a memorable trip!  After buying our entry tickets ($45 for two people including all fees and taxes) we headed up to the trail head as the sun was coming up, with a few scattered deer out on the plains - fairly magical!  The hike itself is a circular, so you can head either clockwise or anticlockwise - most guides say to go anticlockwise, as you reach Little World's End before World's End but we opted for the latter and didn't regret it at all - it's slightly easier as you get a flattish finish, and you also avoid most of the crowds - once we'd headed out the only people we saw for the first 4km or so were the quicker hikers heading past us (not sure why, this is the sort of place that deserves you take your time to soak in the atmosphere!)  The early start was a killer at 4.30am, but seemed like a great idea now - the light is beautiful at that time of day and there's still the early morning frost on the ground and low-lying mist in the valleys.  Baker Falls are nice (but no Iguazu!) and the views from World's End and it's little brother are great, but for me the real winner was the hike and the scenery - just magical at that time of day, and we felt at times we were no longer in Sri Lanka but maybe south America!  While we didn't see much wildlife on the outward part of the hike we saw quite a bit when heading back after Little World's End - a couple of giant squirrels and a few purple-faced leaf monkeys enjoying a feed in the early morning sun - plus quite a few birds.  The round trip is around 9km or so, but we took our time enjoying the journey.  Very highly recommended if you're in Nuwara Eliya - indeed, probably the best thing you can do here IMO!

review_text:
Living here for two years I can't believe we have never done this before! It HAS TO be on your bucket list of you're outdoorsy, adventurous or just enjoy beauty in nature. 

We left Newara Eliya at 5am and paid and entered the park by 7am. The entire walk took us 3 hours and was stunning. You walk through so many different terrains and get to see stunning sights. I even saw families with young children managing the walk. 

You can choose to go right or left at the Y-bend after entering on the walk. We went left, which takes you to little world's end, then on to world's end and finally the falls. But you can go right and switch the order. I think we choose well as returning by the left route may be more difficult than via the right. Tip: most people turn left to reach little worldÂ’s end first, I went straight to get to bakerÂ’s falls first. This meant the walk back, when absolutely shattered, was way easier and mostly downhill.

review_text: WorldÂ’s End was an anticlimax, and we had good weather there. It is a good 9 km walk with varied terrain, scenery and views but nothing special compared with many walks in the UKÂ’s National Parks and elsewhere in the world.  Not worth the early start and high fees and getting there is not simple.  We were travelling from Nuwara Eliya to Ella, so did the WorldÂ’s End walk on the way. We hired a car and driver for LRK10,000.  The Horton Plains NP fee for two people, plus the car and driver was LKR8,100.  Apart from the first kilometre or so there is no sign of the money raised from foreign tourists being used to maintain the route.  In places the path would become a watercourse after rain, luckily it was dry when we were there. I have no problem with foreigners being charged more than locals but the price charged should be reasonable and it would be good to see the money generated being invested in the site.

review_text:
We were in Nuwara Eliya, Small England of Sri Lanka (elevation 2000+ meters above sea level, average temp 12 degrees). We Started our trip early morning at 5.00 am which will take around 1 hour due to foggy road.
It is 30 kms south of Nuwara Eliya lies the famous Horton Plains (2,100 m) sorrounded by mountain ranges.
It starts about 400 meters from the Entrance Gate. Start off early and aim to get there before 6.30am for the best views over World's End, before the mist & cloud cover the area. 
Take the route that goes to mini World's End first from left. The hike takes about 3 to 4 hours, do not forget to bring water, snack, umbrella (in case if it rains) and wear proper hiking shoes. 
You will first reach to Mini World's End ( 2 Kms from Entrance). 
From Mini worlds Ends to Greater World's End is further 3 Kms. 
Further to reach Baker's Falls you need to Walk 2 Kms. 
On the way you will get a Public Toilet which is not very clean & hygienic with no water tap in it. 
Returning back to gate you will get to see Chimney Pool (1.5 Kms from Greater World's End.
And at last to reach the Gate its 2 Kms 
In rain get muddy and slippery, especially when you go towards Baker's Falls. 
There is only one toilet in entire route inside the Park, so try to use one before you leave your hotel, or else at the entrance of the national park, there is a toilet.
Ticket price is well worth it. Grassland plains, mangrove forests.
There is a restaurant outside the gate were you can refresh yourself .
We paid LKR 7,950.00 for 2 person incl all. for the entrance ticket.

review_text:
We enjoyed our trip to the horton plains and after completing the hike we did an afternoon trip to Ella from the Nuwara Eliya train station. The hike was stepo at some points (we did the "long hike" to world's end) but nothing that children couldn't manage. We saw a pair of chameleons and a lot of playful monkeys which was lovely and the whole hike took about 2 and a bit hours (we didn't walk to fast).

However when we got to world's end there was nothing to see as the views were barred by clouds, so I would recommend if it was a noticeably cloudy day take the shorter route to save time if you would be disappointed if you did the hike and there wasn't any views (whihc wasn't the case for us as we loved all of the wildlife and scenery).

review_text: I didn't find this particularly taxing in terms of fitness, but there is a lot of picking your way over rocky and muddy paths, some quite steep. As advised we got there really early - make sure you allow about half an hour to queue for tickets, then drive the couple of miles more to the actual start of the trail (where there is a toilet and small cafe). You need to make sure you don't have any plastic bags, as they will be taken away at the gate, but plastic bottles are OK if the label is removed. It will be cold when you start (15 degrees when we left Nuwara Eliya at 5am, 12 degrees at the gate to Horton Plains at 6am), but once you start walking you will soon warm up, so only one extra layer is fine, and shorts would have been OK. We actually set off walking at 6.45. Shortly after the start you have a choice of which way round you go. We chose anticlockwise, but with hindsight, I think the clockwise route would have got us to World's End quicker. There is a map at the start, but few signs on the way. The terrain was tricky, with rocky paths to start, and a couple of streams to cross. It then got steeper, and much muddier, which slowed us up. Unless you've never seen a waterfall, don't waste time by diverting to Bakers Falls. It's good, but very much the supporting act, and you can always go back after you've been to World's End. We finally got to World's End at about 5 to 9, and were very fortunate indeed - literally within 5 minutes, the view had disappeared, the mist just rolling up the whole valley - quite a sight to see. So disappointing for anyone arriving after that, as there was nothing to see. The rest of the park is pleasant, but not spectacular. Further along the valley there is Mini World's End, but I can't tell you what the view would have been like! Once past these, the terrain becomes much flatter, apart from one fairly steep rocky path, and the mist doesn't encroach on the rest of the park. There's a toilet on the way back, on the edge of the hillside, open sided with a pretty decent view. I had walking shoes on, but on the way back we passed locals in flip flops!

review_text:
As an obese person with a bad right knee and a recovering strained left upper thigh muscle, I was worried that I could not takÃ· on the challenge that was Horton's Plains, especially after reading horrifying reviews about it. Fortunately, all my fears were unfounded!

Walking at a moderate pace, I found the walk entirely manageable though there were some tricky parts such as the rocky sections of the trail. On this note, do make sure to wear good shoes! 

We were also blessed as the weather conditions were in our favour. It did not rain the day before and neither did it on our hiking day. As a result, the paths were not very muddy and therefore easier to traverse. My friend and I, however, could see why the trail might be challenging should the weather be poor. 

A note on safety precautions to take, do not go too close to the edge of the cliff at World's End. According to our guide, a tourist had plunged to her death just a few weeks before our trip in an attempt to take a selfie.

Some tips: 
1. Check the weather forecast
2. It is preferable to have a guide since some paths may not be clear to the inexperienced
3. Bring some food and water
4. Do not bring plastic bags as there are thorough bagchecks before one enters the park
5. It is okay to bring bottled water into the park. However, do remove the plastic seal and label around the bottle before entering the park. 
6. There are rubbish bins in the park. DO NOT LITTER. 
7. Do not make too much noise as that might scare away wildlife. We had an unpleasant encounter with a group of noisy and rude tourists and had to ask them to tone it down. Do respect the environment and be comsiderate to others. That way, the walk will be pleasant for everyone! :)

Overall, I enjoyed the trail as the views were lovely and it was certainly good exercise!

The best place to view the largest gathering of Asian elephants anywhere in the world. During our visit there were around 150+ elephants near the tank and this can increase to 300+ Elephants in the dry season to drink, bath and feed on the fresh grass from the lake bed. And also to socialize and to find mates. Cost of safari jeeps is around Rs3000-5000 plus park entry fees.   ( we hired our Jeep through the Aliya resort and it cost us Rs 5000 to pick up from the hotel (which includes 20 minutes drive to the park entry)) 
Jeep can accomodate up to 7-8 adults.

review_text:
We came to Sigiriya during our roundtrip through Sri Lanka and stayed for two nights at a local homestay. Our plans were to climb Pidurangala Rock for sunrise and for the afternoon of our arrival we had hoped to do a kayaking trip on the nearby river. However, despite mentioned in Lonely Planet's guide, Rasta Rant does not offer those trips anymore.

So, we decided to return to our accommodation and since we are quite new to Sri Lanka and it is our first time here, relied on the help of our hosts to arrange the Safari on short-notice, instead of booking an offer we had found on Air BnB. The trip for two people was quickly scheduled and a driver showed up in his jeep an hour later. After driving for a while, he pulled on to a gas station, where he asked us whether we were going to Minneriya or some other park. We quickly said Minneriya, as this was what we had asked for from our hosts.

Once we got to the park, the driver (whom we had paid beforehand - 13,000 Rupees for 2 people as agreed with our hosts), went to the ticket counter. While he was gone, a man in what appeared to us as a park ranger uniform approached us and told us that today was a great day to see the elephants. When our driver returned, him and the "ranger" quickly exchanged some words, followed by him also getting into our car, shaking our hands and introducing himself.

During the drive he seemed very knowledgable in terms of the different animals and birds, told us he has been working at the park for over 10 years and that he would know all the best spots to see the elephants. Every now and then he hammered against the side of the jeep to make the driver stop and show us something. Everything seemed fine, until at the end of the drive the "ranger" got up to ask us if we were "very happy" and mumbled something about "I really need the tips." That's when we realised that this man is as far away from an official ranger as possible. 

We passed him some money so he would leave us alone and after again exchanging some words with the jeep driver, disappeared into the woods. We already felt quite embarrassed that we had mistaken him for an official ranger, when our driver made us stop at a local vegetable plantation and encouraged us to buy corn. We kindly refused and were relieved when finally returning to our accommodation. Then, when we got out of the car, he claimed that Minneriya was more expensive than the initial quote and demanded an extra 2000 Rupees from us. We were completely confused, but ended up refusing and walking away from his vehicle.

If you're planning on visiting the park - please make sure to compare prices, and don't make our mistake and fall for the false rangers.

BUT: The park itself is beautiful, we had lots of close encounters with elephants and other wildlife, saw different kinds of eagles, water buffalos and jackals - which overall, was worth the hassle - so overall - we absolutely recommend visiting the park.

review_text: If you wish to observe wild elephants in a beautiful natural lakeside setting, then this elephant reserve is the place to go. It was a wonderful experience. Touring the park in the back of an old 4WD on some pretty rough tracks adds to the excitement and sense of adventure. You are able to get quite close to herds of elephants grazing along the lake side as well as individuals hiding in the thick scrub only metres off the road. Water buffalo herds are also aplenty and were interesting to watch frolicking in the shallow waters of the lake. A storm blew up suddenly while we were out in the parklands requiring the roof of the 4WD to be quickly drawn over us. Then we discovered the mouse living in the rolled up roof and shared the ride with him/her for the rest of the trip. This visit was a truly memorable thing to do and is highly recommended as a must do for anybody whether wildlife enthusiasts or not.

We have been on many safaris, albeit in Africa, and this is the first time we felt uncomfortable viewing wild animals.  The park is small and has limited wildlife (we saw 2 small herds of elephants, a peacock, one empty eagle nest and a wasp nest). On the day of our visit there were upwards of 40 jeeps surrounding a small group of elephants.  One of them, "Broken Ear" was known to dislike jeeps due to one killing her baby elephant in the past.  Despite this the convoy of jeeps surrounded her, and after two roaring past she became increasingly angry. Our jeep was stuck - due to other jeeps blocking exit paths and despite being one of the furtherest away we were in her line of vision and she charged us, hitting the jeep twice.  It was very upsetting to see an animal so distressed and angry, she obviously felt she need to protect her herd which included a baby. It felt so cruel having so many jeeps invading her personal space

It is a beautiful area but I really would caution anyone thinking of visiting

review_text: On our trip back from Sigiriya Rock to our hotel, our guide recommended this National Park to go to, We drove here and it was really an amazing and unique experience. We arrived here at the end of the midday at a big parking. This was the departure point for the jeeps. Here we were seated in the back of an 4x4 jeep. First we thought there will be more people in our jeep, but we got our own private tour. Only the 2 of us. haha. The driver drove into the woods, it's about a 15 minutes drive thru the thick woods before you reach the park area. It's really beautiful and breathtaking. The drivers have their route around the park, and off course there were more jeeps driving around. We were lucky that we were late in the midday, so we had only a few jeeps around us. The driver took us around the water and at some point he stops and shutdown the engine so you really can enjoy the beautiful and silence in the park. When your driver sees an animal, he will point at it so you can take a photo of it. In the beginning we saw a group of elephants in the distance  and this was really amazing to see in real life (not in a zoo). At some point we drove thru a bushed area and when we reached back in the open again we were surrounded by many elephants and other animals, In 1 word.... WOW!! Really amazing and unique, I recommend everybody who is in the Area or is on Sri Lanka, to go to this National Park.

This park is stunning. It is all around the most beautiful lake. Our tour guide arranged a jeep for us and he was very good.We saw a couple of female elephants with their babies in the river and then saw a herd of over 20 with very young babies that came by the track right past our vehicle. I was in elephant heaven.
A big tip is to go at lunch time. In the mornings the elephants don't tend to come to the lake but as it heats up they come and the park is quiet at lunch time. We arrived there at 12.30 and we only saw 3 other jeeps. We came out at about 2.30 and there was jeep after jeep coming in - they were queuing to get in right back to the car park. We had a job getting out due to all the jeeps. It was manic and awful. We were so glad we were early.

review_text:
We hired a jeep and driver from Habanera, their company name was Special Safari, the driver was Giayan Kaluarachchi and their number is 0763101482. They are situated in Habanera, near Cinnamon Lodge. 

We looked on here and took advice to not book in advance, but to go to Habanara and hire a local guide and keep. This was excellent advice. Hire Special Safari as they were fantastic! I read that older jeeps are better as they can go through the water in the park and not get stuck - this was true. We sailed through whilst other newer jeeps became stuck. Our driver was an excellent guide, he knew exactly where to go to see a multitude of animals. We saw: elephants, mongoose, snake, jackals, eagles, deer, herds of water buffaloes, monkeys, peacocks, herons, bee eater, monitor lizards to name but a few. Our driver Giayan was patient, there was never a rush. We set off at at 2.10pm and returned at 6.30pm, giving us 3.5 hours in the park (it's about 30 mins from Special Safari in the middle of Habanara to the middle of the park). We were one of the last jeeps to leave the park as we were having such a great time and our guide was so busy showing us all the animals we could think of!
I can't recommend Special Safari highly enough to do the safari in Minneriya. The other thing to note is that the elephants move between parks, so hiring locally meant that Giayan knew exactly where the elephants were and took us straight to them.
