review_text:
We texted Lahiru 3days before the planned tour date and arranged the safari. The day of the Safari we spent the night at his brothers place. We had great food there. Lahiru picked us up from the hotel at 5am.
The safari cost 100 USD in total for Lahiru, driver, jeep and entrance fee (2 persons). The safari was great, we could take numerous elephants, water buffalos, deer, jackals, crocodiles and different bird species from the closest proximity on remote ways apart from other tourists. Due to the fact that his Jeep was so much better than the others we could go to places noone else could go. This, we were able to see crocodiles as well.
He helped us to take great photos and took a lot of time to explain the animals of the national park to us with humor in love English as well as in German. The safari was definitely worth its money.

Lahiru is also happy to help you plan your onward journey at local prices. He brought us to the next bus station to get our transfer to Tangalle.

So beware of scammers. Someone is steeling lahirus identity due to his good reputation. Just text him:

Lahiru Safari : 076 - 2726799

review_text:
Having come all the way to Sri Lanka from London, we wanted to ensure that we had first class experiences, including this safari. Our daughter has researched the park (here in TripAdvisor), and found excellent reviews for Lahiru (tel and WA: +94 76 272 6799). 

This was not cheap by any means, but we felt worth every penny. Firstly, our guide Lahiru was extremely knowledgeable, interesting, animated and fun.His English was first class and easy to understand. Secondly, we had a separate driver, so Lahiru was concentrating on spotting the wildlife rather than driving.

Then, another hero was the Land Rover Defender - a clear step up from nearly all other vehicles, as it is a proper 4-wheel drive, with the ability to get places the others just could not even think of. That, together with an obviously experienced and skilled driver. At one point, we couldn't get up a muddy river bank, resorting to the front winch to pull us up.

After that experience, we managed to get to an area to enjoy a lake area with basking crocodiles, which was the cherry on top of this excellent experience.

review_text:
We went to this stunning park in between 3pm and 7pm and it took 10 minutes to find some gentle giants! They were so calm grazing near the dirt roads of the park and were not fearful of us. 
We decided to go with just a driver and not a guide as I had heard guides are expensive and do not bring much to the experience. The driver was a great guide explaining what we were seeing and making sure we got the best views without being in danger or stressing the animals. You could see the driver really cared for the animals.

I would highly recommend going in the evening and not first thing in the morning. Tours are advertised as the best in the morning but I guarantee we saw just as much in the evening and there were very few tourists in the park, whereas in the morning hundreds arrive at once.

review_text:
First of all, the park itself is stunning. Tons of open space for the animals to roam freely and filled with lush vegetation and lakes. It was easy to see elephants from afar upon arriving.

However, what really makes the difference is your driver and guide. I had read some mixed reviews about finding a driver upon arrival, so I wanted to make sure I had an excellent driver and guide. I'm a solo budget traveler and I'm very careful about what a splurge on but I read numerous reviews of Lahiru on TripAdvisor so I thought I would contact him.

Immediately, he was helpful, friendly and professional, giving me a clear layout of the price and what was included. I needed transport from Hirikitiya and then onwards to Ella and he gave me a clear breakdown of the price for everything. The transport between cities was the lowest rate I received. And while Lahiru's rates are not the cheapest, they are a very reasonable price considering you have him as a guide with an additional driver as well (not to mention the quality of his tour).

I was hesitant but I decided to book with him and I'm so glad I did. It was one of my favorite days of my trip so far. Lahiru was so knowledgable and an expert as spotting wildlife and giving me information. Upon entrance to the park, we spotted a huge variety of species. Additionally, thanks to the Landrover, we were able to access areas of the park that most other trucks could not. There were numerous times where we were the only truck around. We managed to get so incredibly close to the elephants while still respecting the park rules and regulations. There was plenty of time for photos (which, if you didn't bring a DSLR, Lahiru will help you snap photos with his binoculars and your smartphone!) and to just enjoy as well. I never felt rushed and was always asked if I wanted more time before moving on.

Driving by most of the other jeeps, tourists seemed bored while they stuck to the main road (and drivers asked Lahiru where we had seen animals!). But Lahiru kept me entertained the entire time with info about the animals and his great sense of humor. If I wasn't laughing, I was in awe at all the amazing animals we were seeing. Time really flew by. If I had more time in my schedule, it would have been great to do a camping experience but I'll have to save that for when I return one day!

I've traveled to a lot of countries and almost never write Trip Advisor reviews but Lahiru is one of the best guides I've had and made my time in the park an incredible memory. If you're on the fence about splurging, trust me it's worth it!

review_text:
If you want to see elephants then this is amazing! But if you want the traditional safari big 5 this isn't the place to go, I've heard Yala National Park has leopards but it was closed when we were in Sri Lanka. 

We had a great morning at the park. Meant leaving our hotel at 4am but so worth it to feel comfortable as the temperature was so nice and cool! Such a difference from what we experienced in the daytime! 

My cousin organised this so afraid I don't have contact details for who we used! As soon as we entered the park we could see elephants in the distance. As we drove past a track our drivers stopped and reversed as they'd caught an elephant coming up the path out of the corner of their eyes! Their attention to the smallest creatures is amazing! This elephant was coming right towards us and walked past the jeeps, an experience I won't forget. 

Other animals: water buffalo, chameleons, lots of birds in trees, monkeys in an area we stopped in. Great for kids, we had my cousins children (age 4 and 6) who loved spotting all the animals!

review_text:
We visited Udawalawe National Park by booking a guided tour. Our tourguide was Lahiru and it was absolutly amazing!! We found his contact at TripAdvisor. 

Everthing was well organized (we also booked a transfer from Ella to Udawalawe and a transfer from Udawalawe to Tangalle with Lahiru). Due to the fact that he uses a 4-wheel drive for his Safari we were able to visit also the very muddy places at Udawalawe National Park where other guided tours weren't able to go. So we could observe a lot of animals (elephants, crocodiles, peacocks, water buffalos, monkeys, a lot of birds, etc.) in an undisturbed environmente. Lahiru explained a lot about the animals and the history of Udawalawe and we had enough time to take a lot of pictures. If you ever think about visiting Udawalawe National Park I highly recommend you to join him for a Safari. Just text him via WhatsApp (+94762726799) or contact him by Mail (lahiru.jpdk@gmail.com) and explain what you want to see and he will arrange everything for you!! If we will come back to Sri Lanka one day we will definitely go for a Safari with him again!

review_text:
We went in the afternoon slot around 3.30 P.M but unfortunately didnt see a lot of animals other than elephants. It also started raining heavily about an hour after we entered so we had to cover the vehicle, reducing our visibility.
While we saw lots and lots of elephants, we werent lucky enough to see the other animals that other reviewers have seen. To be honest though, the elephants themselves were completely worth the money and my children had a wonderful time.
A couple of tips - if you get quotes from a few guys and go asking further down the road, you will invariably get a cheaper rate. However you will spend time doing this, which means that you might save 1 or 2 thousand LKR but lose out on safari time, so the savings arent really worth it. My recommendation is to plan ahead, check with a few operators and book a safari the previous day.
Try to go early and reschedule if heavy rains are predicted.
Just for information - the pricing model is like this: the operator will either offer an all-in rate (inclusive of jeep and entrance tickets) or will offer his jeep for a certain price and ask you to buy tickets on your own (you need to specifically ask for the second option). The price of the jeep will be approximately LKR 6000 for 3 hours, which you can try and negotiate. The price is for the whole jeep (6 seater), regardless of the number of people, so you can team up with other guests at your hotel and reduce the per-person cost.

review_text:
Contrary to some of the negative reviews, the actual Pinnawala Orphanage depicted here treats the elephants much better than some of the  other places in Pinnawala where elephant rides are offered with no freedom for the working elephants. 
While here  the elephants are taken twice a day to the river to play and bathe, unchained to enjoy their meals on the premises except for an occasional male who is  aggressive during musth.

There are no rides offered unlike in other places  operated by private owners. 
 The mahoots treated them kindness and care when I visited most recently in February 2023, during which I spent  5 full days staying at the Pinnalanda Hotel. I took the photos from the balcony when they were brought to bathe in the river.

review_text:
The elephant sanctuary in Sri Lanka's pinnawala town is a major sanctuary for orphaned and injured elephants.
The road to the orphanage is perhaps one of the most scenic drive you may come across in Sri Lanka.
The star attraction of the sanctuary was an elephant which has given birth to twins, a rarity.
We were also able to see a few elephants in search of a mate.
Away from the orphanage across the road the elephants were given a cool bath in the river.
There are also a number of souvenir shops near the elephant bathing ghat.
The parking space is spacious and the western style toilets were clean and well maintained.
There is also an ATM near the entrance where the newly arrived foreign tourists can convert their home currency into Sri Lankan rupees.
A fun place for kids to see elephants of all ages at close proximity.
The entry fee is nominal and the place well maintained.
We could not locate a restaurant in the premises.
We could also see a number of birds in the surroundings.
A good place to visit with the kids for a picnic.
Recommended.

review_text:
A bit of a mixed review. I do agree with lots of the reviews here, its not an elephant orphanage, its a tourist attraction. Its clear the Elephants are trained , some of them are chained to rocks in order to tame them around people, we did see some not so nice treatment of elephants, which at times was uncomfortable. On the flip side to this, as someone who has never been close to Elephants before it was amazing to see so many in the river playing. It was definitely an experience and to be honest I don't regret going but Im not 100% sure if I would go again just because of the animal treatment. Also be aware - this is 100% a money making tourist attraction. We stayed in the hotel right on the water (thats another review in itself..) but when we arrived if we wanted to go to our hotel we had to pay an entry fee to the 'park' then if you want a photo or to touch or feed the elephants, its made out this is fine but you're then demanded to pay the staff , and they want more than you give them. 

A tough one to review, as a brit it did seem a little odd and hard to tell what treatment the animals get, but it was an experience we wont forget - so I think you have to make your mind up based on the reviews.

review_text: We landed in Colombo around 7.30am and headed straight up to  the  Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage which was around 2.5/3 hour drive.  Be sure to time your visit when the elephants do their walk from the park down to the river, which happens twice a day, this is an amazing sight seeing a herd of elephants bathing and wandering around in the river area.  As close to them being in the wild and their natural habitat as you can get.  This experience alone is well worth the visit, the rest of the park is average with elephants grazing in different areas.  One highlight was seeing the twin baby elephants with their mother.  There are a few informational boards scattered around the park but apart from this information was lacking.  Wear a hat and cover yourself in sunblock, take water, as there is nowhere to escape the sun.  Be aware of people trying to sell you fruits to feed the elephants on their walk which is frowned upon and of course they can be quite persistent.  Maximum two hours is all you will need here.

review_text:
We reached the Pinnawala Elephant orphanage around 11am- picked up tickets & headed straight to the elephant bath area. Spent the next 30+ minutes watching them in the water- one herd left & another herd of 25 elephants just reached the area. Stunning experience to watch so many elephants up close, enjoying the water & almost natural environment. 
Took some great photos & left to the orphanage area. It was like a pleasant park where you can watch the elephants, read the boards with interesting facts about elephants in general & the Pinnawala orphanage.

review_text:
You have also the chance to enjoy the volunteer project available all year round. 
You can choose your own start and finish dates.
Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is an orphanage and breeding sanctuary for rescued, injured or abused wild elephants which is situated northwest of the town of Kegalle, Sri Lanka. It shelters for over 88 orphaned elephants include about 15 baby elephants that volunteer can gain a wonderful opportunity with the largest land mammal on the earth. This institution caters not only for the abandoned babies but also for those injured and maimed within the jungle. We employ the expertise of both modern veterinary and traditional indigenous medical treatment to cater to these elephants needs. Orphanage provides all foods, medicines, milk for the baby elephants itself. It cost a lot. One elephant usually eats over 150 kilograms a day. Of course this orphanage need volunteers and their donations. That is why we charge a project fee(donation fee) from the volunteers. All these donations are used to take care of these elephants.

Let me start by saying I have visited the Pinnewala Elephant Orphanage many times dating back to 1985. The spirit of the place has certainly changed and unfortunately I now cannot recommend this place to ethically or fair-minded tourists. 

I wonÂ’t comment on the treatment of the animals - there is a lot of info in other reviews about this. My main issue is the price - it costs approximately  $16.50 for a foreignerÂ’s ticket. Bearing in mind that this is approximately what you would pay for an adultÂ’s entry to a large, well-kept urban zoo with adequate facilities in Europe or the United States, the experience falls far short of that. There are far better ways to see elephants in Sri Lanka than to support this racket. Give it a miss and go to one of the national parks instead if you can.

review_text:
We ventured to this Orphanage on a ship's shore ex ... it's about a 2 - 2.5 hour drive from the port on a coach.

I think if you can get here with a local guide you would be better off as you can spend as much or as little time as you like at the orphanage, whereas on a ship's tour the time is shorter.

This orphanage is a government run orphanage and at least paying guests are aware of this when they enter and hopefully all money raised goes towards the elephant's upkeep and setting them free back into the jungle.

I found all the public areas where we went and the enclosures we saw were very clean and tidy.

Take Sri Lankan money with you - although you can use CC at the Orphanage shop and other shops in the town, generally speaking they don't take cash unless it's Sri Lankan money.

There is an opportunity to feed the elephants by hand in one areas of the orphanage however Rupees are required - no USD or other currency and definitely no CC there !!  Luckily our guide exchanged some USD for Rupees but the fruit was gone very quickly.

Yes there were a few elephants chained up in another enclosure but of the three enclosures we saw, this was the only one where they were chained.  The reason we were given for this was because they are wild animals... let's face it ... if they are males and are maturing, they could get annoyed about something and cause injuries to other elephants if not their handlers and / or the public if they crashed through the fence.

Indeed at the elephant feeding area I saw one elephant get grumpy with another one for muscling in on the food I was feeding it - the elephant turned around and head butted the second elephant in its side to show it's displeasure at eating its food.

The third area where we saw elephants at this Orphanage, the elephants were roaming free in a large treed area ... I wondered if this was the first stage of getting them used to fending for themselves before setting them free in the jungle.

We had lunch included in our ship's shore excursion at a hotel by the river and luckily for us, they had quite a few elephants bathing there - a lovely thing to see.

IMO, this excursion is not suitable for mobility impaired people because the terrain to get to the elephant enclosures is not paved and the surface is uneven.  There's also a few steps to negotiate within the elephant orphanage area.  Also, the "road" to the hotel where we went for lunch was not paved either.

review_text: If you are in Sri Lanka and want to see lots of elephants and get up close and feed them, look no further than Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. About 2 to 2 1/2 hours drive from Colombo is this nice, quiet area where they care for orphaned elephants. We could count more than two dozen elephants there. Reach early (I recommend leaving Colombo by 6.30) if you want to capture it all when it's not hot, and get tickets. As is with most places in Sri Lanka - entry ticket prices depend on your nationality. You walk in and the elephants come out and you can get close to the, feed them fruits etc. Then they take the elephants for a shower at a nearby river. I thought it was going to be all natural, but then they opened a powerful hose and started showering the elephants. Oh well.. Sip a cup of coffee or get some juice while watching that at one of the few restaurants there (watch out for those flies!). There are several shops that sell pooper (paper made out of elephant poop) and other trinkets there. I found them exorbitantly priced, so I skipped. But overall a very pleasant place to go outside of colombo.

review_text:
I visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage on 15 February 2020 from Australia. 

This was my first holiday to Sri Lanka even though my parents are Sri Lankan. 

I had heard many stories from my relatives about the elephants at Pinnawala and had always wanted to visit. 

In saying that, making the decision to go was a tough one as I am aware that currently Pinnawala is classed as Â‘slightly controversialÂ’ & I am an extreme animal lover!

Nevertheless after reading many reviews (some from people whom havenÂ’t even visited the site!?), I decided that I needed to see it for myself & make up my own mind. 

My honest opinion was that I was pleasantly surprised and I believe that they are genuinely trying to improve the operations of the park. 

Out of the 90 odd elephants I saw there, the majority were free roaming and appeared to enjoy their free time and bathing in the river. 
The only elephants I saw had chains were some of the males which is more for everyoneÂ’s protection so as not to cause a stampede. There were also 2 that were in pens apparently under veterinary care. 

The only Â“touristÂ” interaction that I saw was the fruit feeding which I avidly took part in - i bought like 4 baskets of fruit to give to 2 beautiful elephants. 

(**And for those people complaining about having to pay for the fruit baskets- get over it! 
It only costs like $2 aud for a basket of fruit! You pay way more than that for animal encounters in western countries and thatÂ’s not included in your ticket price either!)

No tourists (that I saw) were allowed to bathe with the elephants etc at the park and I didnÂ’t really see any Â“exploitationÂ” as such. Ie, I did not see any elephant rides being provided.

It was just a joy to see them down at the river with many elephants enjoying the water or their mud bath. 

At the end of the day people will need to make up their own minds as to what theyÂ’re comfortable with. 

I personally am happy I went there and I donÂ’t believe it is as bad as some people are making it out to be.

review_text: You cannot miss it. It is worth every penny and minute spend to get there! I would recommend to go there very early in the morning before animals hide from heat to the forest. As the jeeps have no windows it is wise to take a hat or something protecting your ears from wind diving along the dam on the lake. I would also suggest to take good camera, binoculars with you as well as something to drink and eat as the trip takes 4 hours. There are so many animals to see that you will enjoy every minute you spend there. As the animals got used to the jeeps they donÂ’t escape Â– we had to stop few times to let elephants, warans, lizards cross the dirt road in peace.

we thought it was part of the ticket which we had purchased.

overall my kids were left very disappointed.

review_text:
I love elephants and was very excited to see, interact, feed and bath them. Pinnawala was a as disappointing as it could be. elephants ill treated, hurt, scared, chained. they were literally poking the elephants with metal rods to make them do things. 

For visitors to be able to bathe the elephants, the elephants must lay down in the water. To make them do this, the handler pokes and chains the elephants. You can hear the elephants crying in pain. All this because visitors want to experience something. 

There are cafes like Elephant bay and others that offer a view of the bathing elephants. 
Strongly urge you to not participate in these activities, which in turn will encourage brutality to animals!

One thing you can consider is buying Poo Paper. it sounds weird but is eco friendly as it is made of elephants poop. The have great shops to buy stationary and painting made from poo paper in Pinnawala

review_text: Today we travelled a long way especially to visit the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage and we were so disappointed. It was 3,000lhr to enter and we specifically went for 1pm as between 12pm-2pm that you can supposedly feed the elephants fruit and see milking time. We walked in and the place was deserted, there was no one to help direct you or advise you, only some signs. There were a few elephants you could see in a small grass area with a couple of trees which you could see from a viewing point at least 15 metres away from the elephants themselves. We moved along to another area where there were 6 males chained up to a tiny concrete area with nothing but a couple of coconuts on the floor and men clearing up the ground around them. They were clearly very distressed and not happy in their environment and it was extremely sad to see this especially as we had believed this was somewhere they look after the animals well. There was no elephants in the fruit feeding enclosure (we also saw this was an extra charge even if there was) all in all we were there for about 15 minutes before we decided we should leave. If you love animals and want to see elephants being treated well in a safe environment do not bother wasting your time.

review_text:
I was more than shocked. On the one hand we only wanted to watch the animals bathing and we were told that we need a ticket for 3000 LKR each (there is a ticket office for tourists and locals. I doubt that they are the same prices) which is not correct. You can just walk down to the river between 10am and 12pm or 2pm and 4 pm and watch the elephants bathing. You need the ticket to see the "orphanage", which was one of the saddest things I have ever seen. The animals have far too little space and no things to play with. 
When we asked why two elephants were chained and kept circling their heads, we were told "their will first has to be broken". 
There was also an enclosure with 3 baby elephants inside, which were made to pose for photos. There were men standing in front of it offering to take photos of us and the elephants. However, this is not a nice gesture (even if the locals are otherwise very nice and helpful), but afterwards the hand is held out again for money. 

 Also the small elephants which are "rescued" are not let back into freedom. Once an elephant is in Pinnawala, it never leaves again. Some of the elephants were chained to the river and many men with very sharp sticks were also on guard. Of course: safety is a must. But I didnt have a good feeling.
 
Better to go to the Udawalawe National Park and see elephants without chains and men with pointed lances. 

Later we also talked to a very good English speaking local, who told us that only a small part of the income goes to the animals

review_text:
Quite a nice place to visit to see elephants free to roam around and do their thing without being chained.

There are about 70 elephants here and most of them are free to roam around the property (there are tied only when under medical care or preparing to mate). Visitors have a gallery from where they can watch the elephants, and also walk around their bathing area. There is a small souvenir shop as well.

They take the elephants at designated times to the river for bathing, but that was not done when we went because the river water level was very high. 

This can be fun for kids.

review_text:
Entry charges were LKR 800 (for SAARC adults), LKR 3500 (foreign adults). We enjoyed the place a lot because it lets you be quite close to the elephants. It's not every day that you see elephants being bathed in a river. In fact, there were more than 20. There were elephants of all sizes. While some elephants were returning to the orphanage, we witnessed them passing on the road leading to the river. We were less than 6 feet away from them! It was amazing! Make sure you check the timings before you go. You don't want to miss the bathing time. 

There was a small little street with some elephant themed handicraft and boutique shops as well. Mainly for souvenirs. One of the shops was particularly interesting because they made products out of dried elephant dung. They had a little processing plant in the back of their shop.

review_text: I was initially worried about going to this place. A lot of reports talk about the elephants being chained up which seriously could prevent any form of enjoyment. We did not actually go into the actual orphanage but merely paid (the full admission price) and watched them crossing the road and bathing at the bottom. Yes, the bull elephants were chained I guess for their and my safety. These were big animals that you would not wish to charge you. The younger and better behaved marched down the road and seemed well looked after and showed no discomfort that I could see. Ok far better that they are free totally in the wild and this would really be the way I would like to see them. They seemed to enjoy their trip and bathe and we did not see any rough handling by any of the Mahoots . All in all a wonderful morning. I would return if I ever get back to Sri Lanka.

review_text:
Visited on 17th Feb 2020

Entry Fee : SLR 800/- per Adult and SLR 400/- per Child of SAARC countries
Timing : 8.30am till 5.30pm (ticket window closes)

Ideal time to visit are 10.00am or 2.00pm respectively when the Elephant herds are taken for bathing to the river in batches, and 12.00noon or 4.00pm when teh elephant herds are brought back after bathing.

We got a chance to see the Elephant herds being brought back from bathing and the walking of the herd in the sandy path is amazing.

Watch towers and pathways are created in the venue for proper movements of the tourists. Also few installations and information boards are provided to inform all about the history of the place and its evolution through years. It also talks about the mahouts or elephant keepers and tools used by them to control the pachyderms.

Duration of visit will be about 1 hour.
Laksala and souvenir shop is available at this attraction. Outside the attraction there are few small shops selling fresh cut fruits and cold drinks and snacks. 

It can be hot on sunny day so please carry umbrella or caps.

Go and Enjoy!

review_text: I'm not too sure what I thought about this place.  The elephants have been 'rescued' and they appear happy enough but I had the vague feeling thye were like peforming elephants in a zoo.  It is a geat expeirence to being down a thoroughfre and suddenly a small herd of elephants (with their handlers) wlk past you.  It was great too to see them behaving quite natrally in the water.  But there were some moments of disquiet.  Some of the elephants are chained, and I accept and understand why, but it does leave an impression.  A couple of the elephants are also forced to lie down in the water for the benefit of the crowd which I was not sure of either.  Still, it was an experience althougha bit expensive, 3000 rupees per foreigner.  If you want the experience of feeding a quiet elephant, you can also do that for 250 rupees.  There are no elephant rides and I was pleased about that.  Finally watch out for a scam with the mahouts (handlers).  They will try to isolate you away from the crowd and lead you up into an area by yourself.  They then offer to photograph you with an elephant by yourself but won't return your camera/iphone until you pay them money.  I was offered this a couple of times but did not do it.  I did see a family forking out a few thousand rupees to one of them so watch out for it.

review_text:
We went here wanting to make up our own minds from reading reviews and have very mixed feelings. On one hand, the elephants were healthy looking (no bones showing) and majority allowed to roam around the river free.

However, around 8 elephants were chained to various spots around the river...the signs say this is to stop harm/danger of the Male elephants. From the looks of things, these elephants were chained for tourists photos as they were dotted around the hotel points and only need the front (of the viewing platform). The elephants are also clearly scared of the mahouts & when one of them began to ride the elephant he was nearly kicked off.

We went up to the Â‘relaxing zoneÂ’ which didnÂ’t look that way for the elephants at all. It sort of looks like an elephant zoo enclosure, however yet again all elephants there were chained up and visibly distressed. A better idea would be to let the elephants freely roam and invite tourists to visit safari style - no touching or contact. 

What we couldnÂ’t understand is if this was an orphanage...why arenÂ’t they let out into the wild, given they are well enough/old enough.

review_text: Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is an orphanage located at Pinnawala village approximately  13km from Kegalle town on the Colombo Kandy Road (A1 turn to left near the 82km post). This orphanage provides a lifeline to the orphaned baby elephants and orphaned elephants lost in the wilderness. You can see them having a bath in the river then crossed the road back to the orphanage where they are feed and roam the ground. The orphanage will be open from 08.30 hrs to 18.00 hrs daily. Normally herd of elephants bathing in the river from 10.00 to 12.00 again from 14.00 to 16.00. Milk feeding starts in morning 09.15, 13.15 and 17.00 hrs. It is the place that gives us unforgettable experience. Elephant caretakers must care with love and respect without being cruel to the elephants will help them grow up with nature.

review_text:
I hadn't done any research on this place before visiting which was a huge mistake.

The young elephants are tamed by being chained up and beaten and shouted at. They were visibly very distressed and making a lot of noise. 
I felt extremely upset when I saw this and angry at myself for visiting. Our guide then took us down to the river where the elephants are taken to bathe. Some are chained up and forced to lie down in the water. There is no need to treat these poor elephants this way. 
Go and visit Minneriya National Park instead to see happy elephants roaming free in the wild.

So disappointed with Pinnawala Elephant orphanage. They advertise saying elephants are Â“semi wildÂ” but reality is, elephants are not well treated, elephants have mahouts to be trained and unfortunately they donÂ’t have a proper semiwild life. Elephants will end working for temples and going to Parahera in some point which makes me really sad. Pinnawala orphanage says there are 84 elephants but visible you can only see a group of 27 elephants + other group of 10 sick elephants. Where are the others? I would say, chained, because they refuse to be domesticated* I paid 3k rupees for the entrance expecting to see elephants having a better care. I am the person who would pay more if elephants are well treated. Elephants only eat once per day (kindly note elephants of Pinnawala are well fitted), but still, the nature of elephants is to eat several times per day. Sri Lanka government, please do something to improve the programs for elephants, I understand your mindset, culture and religion and most important I respect it, I understand the value and meaning of Parahera, but donÂ’t advertise lies. Please give a better care for them. Elephants are humble and loyal animals we should be better for them. 
*Note: some elephants are on their Musth period, is understandable that they remain separated from the group, but, are 50 elephants on their Musth? DonÂ’t think so. 
Note 2: tourism is an income that Pinnawala orphanage needs to give elephants a better life. I wonÂ’t say donÂ’t visit the place, I will say: go and see for yourself, raise the voice and ask Sri Lanka Government to improve the programs.

review_text: We arrived in the late morning and found most of the elephants down at the river bathing.  As we walked down the street to see them, we passed several shops selling souvenirs and then suddenly were treated to a few elephants being ridden back to the orphanage from the river.  It was a bit scary, but also exciting as they walked right past us.  We got down to the river and there was the rest of the group bathing and playing.  We took a few pictures and then went to the orphanage where after a short walk inside we came to an area where one can feed the elephants.  I didn't see any mistreatment while we were there, but our experience was limited to about an hour and a half.  It's a long drive to get here, but if you like elephants, it's worth the drive. review_text:
If you short of time and/or money, you can easily avoid this place. This is basically a zoo (even worse than a zoo) than an orphanage. How often do you see children in orphanage tied up with chains and made to walk a long alleyway just so that a few tourists who paid exorbitant prices for tickets can watch them walk and feed them coconuts?

The elephants take bath in the pond which is at the opposite side of the road from the orphanage, twice a day. We were very excited that we reached just in time when the elephants were getting ready to walk through that alley to go to the pond to take bath. What we saw was very disappointing. Almost all the elephants were chained to their teeth. Most of them were missing their tusks (don't know when it happened) and almost all of them just sat in the pond and did nothing.

Inside the orphanage, it was the same story. You can see them grazing or can give them bananas or other fruits (there are extra charges for that as you can only buy the fruits from one of the shops inside the orphanage).

We were from the SAARC country so we paid 750 LKR per person for entry but I think for foreign tourists from other countries the fees is around 3000 LKR. It is highly overpriced and it's better to actually go to Marissa and watch whales in their natural habitat instead of seeing chained Elephants sitting in water.

You can do all the things you can do here at Dehiwala zoo in Colombo, including seeing Elephants taking bath.

review_text:
We visited this place in February as part of a tour with Mercury Holidays.  We were hoping it would be the highlight of our trip, sadly it left us with bad memories for this part of the trip.  
We started watching the elephants in the water from an adjacent hotel veranda, the elephants certainly didn't appear to want to be there, they were corralled to stay close to the hotels so that visitors could see them.  We then went to the land site on the opposite side of the road, again elephants are corralled for the entertainment of the viewing public. A very heavily pregnant elephant was trying to get to a water hole at the top of the paddock with some other elephants following, however the mahouts would not let her rest and drove her and her followers to the part of the paddock closest to the tourists.  In another part of the paddock one of the mahouts was repeatedly hitting an elephant in the leg making it squeal, a sound I don't want to hear again.  One of the staff stood near me kept saying 'happy elephant'. I'm not David Attenborough but I would say that the elephant was not squealing with delight.  There were also other elephants under shelter which clearly had mental issues and were heavily chained, I do however appreciate that where they have been rescued from may be the cause of their problems and not the place they have come to. 
I have read through some of the reviews and they do vary widely and of course they're all personal assessments, some cultures approach animal care differently, for instance some have referred to being able to ride the elephants which I personally don't agree with.  I would strongly recommend you think seriously about visiting this place, yes there are a lot of elephants here which is great, but the evident lack of care for them is distressing if you are an animal lover.

review_text: Despite all the positive recommendations for this elephant 'orphanage', it seemed more like an elephant medium security prison. There are many captive elephants that are kept in large fields. In some areas the visitors can come close and even touch the tamer elephants. Around mid morning (10:30 to be precise), the elephants are paraded down to  the nearby river and encouraged (or in the case of some of the young male bulls, forced) to bathe. The male elephants are chained up and pushed and prodded, and appear and sound unhappy. The females and children though are allowed to roam and appear less anxious. In comparison to elephant sanctuaries in Thailand or free roaming African elephants, many of these Asian elephants appeared to be distinctly unhappy and uncomfortable. We went with two teenage girls and they were distinctly unhappy with the elephants' circumstances, as was I.

review_text:
We visited this elephant orphanage and quite honestly didn't see any ill treatment of the animals.  It was lovely to see the elephants walking to the river for  a bathe. We got quite close to a few of the cheeky ones who came up to the chain where we could stand. 
Yes a few of the males have a chain to a leg but we were told they were the "frisky" ones and it was to help keep them under control. 
The older  males are separated from the females as in the wild . They even have a "murderer" male which is kept apart from all the others and needs a few members of staff around when cleaning his area. He apparently has killed humans when he was in the wildlife reserves-  so nice to see he has been given a chance to life as his rages were probably instigated by humans  who didn't behave appropriately around him. 
We were told not to buy fruit from the street sellers and were always reminded to behave appropriately.

They use the sticks to apply pressure to vital points ( acupuncture points) which do not harm the elephants - if youÂ’ve ever been struck in a pressure point you will know a slight jab doesnÂ’t hurt but does encourage the body to move in a certain way. This is what they do with the Sticks. You couldnÂ’t move an elephant with a shove or a little stick otherwise.

If youÂ’re concerned with the treatment suggest research first before judging. 

Many of the elephants come from farmland where theyÂ’ve been trapped in holes dug by farmers to collect water. They often have broken limbs when they come to the sanctuary. 

Once recovered, most are returned to the forests. Some pictures attached of the time we watched them bathing.

One thing to note - from wherever you are you will likely take some time to get there. For us it was worth the journey.

review_text:
We visited this tour part of what Mercury Holidays offer, I did at the time question the rep about the chains on the  elephannts as I had read about this, and aware this is a cultural difference, but at the end of the day it should be about the elephant not a zoo or making the elephant perform for you.  The Rep advised the chains were required as the Bulls do get aggressive.  What I donÂ’t understand is elephants should be able to roam freely, however when we visited I was sad to see these poor animals in such distress.

When you approach the orphanage you are advised not to purchase any fruit but to buy inside, the place was heaving with local school children coach loads - not sure if this is part of their school curriculum but vast amount visiting.  The elephants in the watering hole seemed dazed and when one elephant approach the handler who has a stick with a hook to control the elephants came close she quickly reacted and walked away - the elephants seemed lifeless and bored.  One elephant was showing signs of distress side to side shaking her head and body - not nice to see.  We then visited the feeding stations and walked passed where the elephants are seen my the public - makes you wonder how much space do these elephants have to roam - not a great deal.  I saw the bull elephants chained and what was so shocking was the behaviour again rocking back and forth - this is where he remains all day - and the phrase for the wealth and safety of all elephants was the reason - this was utterly sad, such a beautiful animal chained. Again aware the cultural differences but, somehow human instinct should kick in for anyone to see these elephants are anything but happy. We then visited the feeding station once again for the elephants to perform - one of the man handlers asked if I wanted a picture of the elephant raising its trunk - he called the elephant over and used this stick to control her - just like a circus act, and she had chains around her neck.

Please think twice about contributing to this orphanage in hindsight I regret contributing, and my advice would be be go on the safari - this is where you see elephants roaming freely and happy but the choice is yours.

review_text:
Spent 2 hours at Millennium Elephant orphanage. The pre walk information sessions was really informative and revealing!  Walked with the first elephant born there "Rani" - just a wonderful experience as she accepted food and gently walked around with us. Her mahout was gentle and you could see the intense relationship. The helped washed her in the stream and scrubbed her with coconut shell.  I swear she winked at me!  She lay there as we all had turns. Then she showered us with water from her trunk. These are just beautiful and serene creatures.
Next door is the only elephant poo paper factory in the world. It's free and fascinating how the elephant dung is used to make paper in a very simple and environmentally friendly way. Nice gift shop as well with the final products for sale, all reasonably priced.

I have mixed feelings about my visit to Pinnawala. Having read some disturbing reports I was nervous about what we would see. We visited early in the morning and saw the elephants bathing and then went back to the reserve and saw some elephant there in the enclosures. Did we see cruelty? No. Did we see chains? Yes. Was I impressed? I don't think so.

Now, I have to confess to not being a fan of zoos on the whole but I can really appreciate a zoo that has a conservation ethos (Twycross for instance) Pinnawala felt like a poor zoo to me. A few elephants paraded for public entertainment. Thats ok I guess if there is a greater good but I'm not sure there is. 

Overall this was an ok experience but I wouldn't go again.

review_text:
I visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage just over a week ago and I must say that I was on high alert after a few derogatory articles I had seen written about the facility and its treatment of the elephants. Happily, I found nothing worthy of a complaint.

The elephants parade down to the river and anyone who knows animals can see that they are intelligent beings who are used to the routine and are not at all stressed by the watching crowds - in fact, some clearly loved it and were happy to participate and be patted or fed a morsel along the way.  Once in the river they splash, roll around in the water and clearly enjoy themselves.

Yes, some did have a loose chain around their necks, but this didn't bother them. When you consider the size of an elephant and the general havoc they could cause to a community when aggressive, it's not difficult to understand that there are times when they must be prudently restrained or separated. 
As for returning them all to the wild; these elephants no longer have a place in the wild as they have formed new family bonds within their new herd. Many have already been rescued from the wild where they were close to death and others are on medication or special food.

So if you want to truly help elephants and not just have a pompous rant about turning them loose, visit Pinnawala, spend a few dollars towards their support and watch them happily splash about in safety.

Very ordinary. 2 stars only because you can go across the road and see some elephants bath in the river and then walk back up to the orphanage. They walk straight past you and across the road. Pretty cool. The traffic is stopped by the police each time. I think you need the ticket to get to the river, our driver organized that.

Overall pretty poor. Save your money and time.

review_text:
Reviews of Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage praise and condemn so our only choice was to see it for ourselves. The stamp of the countryÂ’s Department of Wildlife Conservation on the park was the deciding factor.

Over a twenty year period, Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage hand raised abandoned babies, treated the injured and integrated displaced elephants into a growing herd.

Currently, 88 elephants are part of the Pinnawala family on their 30-acre property, making it one of Sri LankaÂ’s largest tourist attractions.

At Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage you will see chains. This is precautionary for large males while bathing, wandering the park Â– river path, and when a femaleÂ’s seductive pheromones spike.

A full grown male can stand more than 2.5 metres weighing  5.5 tonnes. A force to be reckoned with when they want to get down to business.

You will also see mahouts rounding the elephants to keep them in one spot. This is also precautionary to keep them from getting too close to punters.

A disappointing observation was people paying some entrepreneurial mahouts to bathe the elephants. The elephant is chained and made to lie on its side during the encounter. This is not approved and is something the orphanage is trying to eliminate.

Elephants eat an average of 250kg of food per day, multiply that by 88 of them and you have an expensive grocery bill. Modern veterinary equipment and traditional indigenous medicine come at a price and the gallons of milk required to raise a baby elephant is also exorbitant.

Sponsorship programs, donations and your ticket price all contribute to the cost of feeding and caring for these adorable creatures.

Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is not perfect, but the care for these elephants is obvious.

This is a heavily tourist-trafficked attraction. Vendors take advantage of the captive audience and sell everything from elephant poo paper products (quite an interesting process) to every form of elephant printed clothing you can imagine.

Away from this retail madness, however, is picturesque countryside, a meandering river and comfortable accommodation.

review_text:
This place was first in our itinerary in a 10 day Sri Lanka tour and were very happy to see how the Elephants are treated. We were on time to witness the elephant bathing session on river close to main entrance gate. I mean accross the road. Local seller sell food stuff to be fed to elephants and it was really great experience. There are more than 40 elephants taken care at this place and whatever I saw I felt they are really taken care by staff.
If you have time you can also plan to give bath to elephant at extra charges.
Do visit elephant poo paper factory to experience the making if paper from poo.
Overall a great experience

review_text:
The orphanage is great and the vast majority of the Elephants appear to be enjoying life.

They have various areas and pens and so some are chanied. But without knowing why, you cannot really judge on it being cruel, given that so many are roaming free.

If you go mid morning around 1030 or at 1430 in the afternoon you can see the elephants walked down to the river to bathe. It really is a beautiful sight and they appear to be thoroughly enjoying themselves.

We enjoyed our visit and these elephants appear happy.

Unlike the elephant tourist spots before or after Pinnawala which offer close ups and rides with the elephants. They are nothing but a rip off and it's distressing to see the elephants. We did stop off at the advice of our guide and wish we hadn't. A complete rip off. 

DO - Visit Pinnawala Elephant Orphange 

DONT - Visit any other tourist elephant spot before or after

It's not often that we get to see wild animals close up - least of all endangered  species  like the Asian elephant. But to see 75 of them in one place is incredibly privileged. 
This is the largest herd of Asian elephants in the world today in controlled ,protected surroundings.
The orphanage  has been running since 1975 and the work it is doing is helping  to keep the species alive and all monies raised goes towards the continued  work of looking after these magnificent beasts.
A MUST SER. Very highly recommended.

review_text:
Spent 2 weeks volunteering here as a family so gained some insight into the orphanage.
The orphanage would love to see all elephants in the wild, unfortunately this is impossible with pressures on land use by a growing population.  They cant introduce elephants to an existing wild herd as they would not be accepted.  All elephants in the orphanage have been raised in captivity so would seek out people if released and this would in turn create conflict risking the elephants life.
The mahouts do shout and use ashoks with elephants to ensure public safety.  To see behind the public face and watch them tenderly go over the elephants skin for 2 hours looking for problems shows their true feelings towards the animals.  They shout at the cleaners if the elephant houses are not sufficiently cleaned.
The prices are fair for tourists and cheaper for locals to encourage locals to visit, learn and take an interest in their own wildlife.  This is a government run organisation so the prices are set in Colombo, not by the orphanage.  The extra fee for feeding or bathing 
elephants is likewise set by the politicians.
The Elephant in the Room - chains.  These are necessary to manage the herd in a small area to keep public, staff and elephants safe.  Injured, sick and pregnant elephants are kept separate, but still taken for free time at the river away from the main herd. There are 19 elephants housed here which have been seized from illegal owners and are awaiting court cases so can't be put with the herd.  
In all we really enjoyed our 2 weeks here giving us an insight not gained during a short visit.  Volunteering is hard work and not for everybody.  We learnt about the politics behind a lot of decisions and saw the love held for these wonderful creatures by all the staff at the orphanage.

review_text:
I wish I had done my research before going to the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage because it was honestly more like a prison than an orphanage. The second we got there we were bombarded by a man who said after we see the elephants eat we need to get in a tuk tuk to see the elephants bathe and then go to the spice factory. You do not have to do this! All you need to do is cross the street to see the elephants bathe. 

Now back to this horrible place.... once we entered everything just seemed like an amusement park. It seems this place is more for making money than helping animals. Most of the animals were chained up not able to roam free. There was also an area for I guess the elephants that could not be with the rest of the population and they were chained in an area that was dark and smellyand they were weaving back and forth. This is a sign of distress which many of the elephants exhibited. Once it was time for the elephants to bathe in the water they walked them down in chains while the handlers prodded them with their bull hooks. I was shocked to see how aggressive they were with the elephants. If the wanted the elephant to move or stand a certain way they would hit it with a wooden stick then take the hook part and stab the head of the elephants. You could see when the handlers came around the elephants were scared. I also saw them prodding elephants to pick things up and move them. They were using them for work abs using the hooks to get them to do what they wanted. 

It was an extremely sad and disturbing place. If you love animals do not give your money and support this torturous place. This is just a place to exploit elephants and make money. I have to give 1 star to post this but it would have been 0 stars.

review_text:
I had read up about Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage before I visited Sri Lanka and from what I'd read, I was honestly considering skipping the visit due to claims of animal abuse and unnecessary confinement. But as it turned out, I was part of a group and because the group wanted to go, I had little option but to tag along.

What I saw there truly horrified me.

1. Elephant calves were confined in a circular pen and their legs tied with metal chains that left little room for manoeuvre or free movement.

2. There was a tusker displaying a classic case of depressive symptoms - head swaying incessantly and bobbing up and down. Like the calves, he was also tied with a short metal chain in a small shed. 

3. A herd of elephants we saw there was so scared of the keeper that as soon as he entered the enclosure with his bull-hook, the terrified elephants literally fled away from him. The keeper was careful not to display any aggressive behaviour in front of the tourists but it was obvious from how scared the elephants were, that terrible things go on behind the scenes. 

4. While there, we saw a keeper repeatedly strike a pregnant elephant with a huge pole that had a metal spike at its end. He poked and struck her hard despite the presence of tourists there. I cannot imagine what must be going on once tourist hours are over.

We then headed off to the river adjacent to the orphanage where they take the elephants for a bath - hoping that at least there, the elephants must be free. But they were not. Even here, the elephants were tied with short chains while tourists threw fruit at them.

I would've compared Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage to a zoo but most zoos treat their animals better than this 'orphanage' does.

Pinnawala is not a place I would ever visit again. My money isn't going into a place that has made a business out of abusing animals that should've been returned to the wild. Plus, they breed elephants in confinement at Pinnawala. Real orphanages don't typically do that.

Instead, I would strongly recommend visiting the Elephant Transit Home near Udawalawe National Park. I haven't been there but from what I've heard, they are much more responsible in caring for orphaned elephants. Plus they return the elephants to the wild once they are old enough - unlike Pinnawala.

Animals are chained and beaten with long sticks with spikes!

review_text:
The actual sanctuary area is a bit of a let down,  not much to see,  we were out within 15 mins.  The walk down to the river was easy, the road is lined with shops,  including elephant poo paper shops (the first one you encounter is much cheaper than the other one). 

We got to the river and went into the cafe on the left,  got a front view table and ordered a couple of drinks.  

It is great seeing the elephants walk through town and into the river.  We sat and watched them for over an hour.  Did not see any mistreatment at all.  

I would recommend going.

review_text:
The orphanage has three broad time slots: milk feeding to calves, fruit feeding to elephants, elephant bathing, so you should try to plan your arrival at beginning of one of these (picture has details, zoom in). You will be shuffling between hold area for feeding and river for bathing. One ticket (Rs. 700 SAARC country, Rs. 2500 for other countries, 50% for children) gets you multiple access to all events. You can easily spend 2-3 hours here watching elephants eat, play, relax, dance, and what not. They even have huge hose spraying elephants in the river, though we expected more frolicking in water it was still good experience. There are various souvenir shops and elephant poo paper shops around, and few mid-range restaurants.

Story behind orphanage is that it takes care of abandoned calves and tends them to youth, though for tourist purposes you can consider it open zoo. There is also separate zoo nearby and you can also take elephant ride.

Lot of negative reviews are from people who are aghast seeing animals in chains. It's not a jungle safari, and (some) elephants are in chains (some of the time). Go for watching elephants doing various things, as extended version of zoo. Don't go thinking it's natural habitat. It's always ironically funny to see bleeding heart of meat eaters for animal cruelity.

review_text:
Both my partner and I are animal lovers, and we deliberated long and hard whether to visit here due to some of the Trip Advisor reviews. However, after doing more research and reading some independant travel articles, we decided to visit - and I am glad we did. 

Yes, there are chains used to anchor, help control and keep the elephants safe as well as the many visitors this place has. In addition, the males - especially when in musth - need to be controlled and seperated. These elephants can never be released in to the wild, so ensuring they can not wander off when in the river is essential. I did not see any evidence of distress, and I saw some lovely interactions in the main herd with some of the younger ones playing. They genuinely seemed to enjoy their time in the river, and seeing them walk through the main street was an experience! 

This place is not perfect - however people also need to remember this is a poor country. It seems to me like they try and do the best they can with the money that is available. The only thing that stood out to me is that the Mahouts seemed to over use their hooks and shout when it did not seem necessary. This could be my ignorance of course, but it seemed over the top at times like they were showing off to the crowds.

I donÂ’t even handle an orphan baby like this.
Elephants are most brainy animals in this world and when you see elephant babies with their herd, you can figure out how they are protected by other elephants.

The initiative is very good by the government, but commercialising this Is not a fair approach to that baby elephants. Animal lovers especially those study about elephants and its emotions will understand this.

The elephants are not treated as babies or orphans. They are mainly managed to attract the tourist who visit that place. Locals who belongs to this place, including the management and staff should at least show the attitude of their loving approach to elephants.

As a human if you have never seen elephants closely or interacted with baby elephants, you may find this place interesting. 
We have lived in a culture (Southern most part of India) which is very much similar to Lanka, with elephants on day to day life. In timber depot, temple festivals, local rich guys house, but baby one is always attraction for us.

We arrived around 1030 by the time the Babies were at the river playing, some were afraid of the crowd being gathered, some are weak to even taking bath/ play.

We also saw while they were taking back to the so called orphanage from river.

Pros:- you can see herds of babies in one go.

Cons:- you wonÂ’t see the feel of orphan baby elephant being well treated.
More of a commercial establishment to sell substances, gift items with elephant name or photo somewhere.

But a place one should visit at least once, best time is while they were going to river, taking bath and coming back. Timings are displayed and published in their web page.

Avoid buying souvenirs from their, as the prices are sky-rocketed for tourists. You will find same items in cheaper rates outside.

review_text:
I've got very mixed feelings about pinnawala. 
On the one hand - beautiful to see so many elephants together in safety. Some reviewers have stated that ALL the elephants are in chains - they are not. The information boards clearly explain that the male elephants are chained when in the public areas for the safety of everyone around them. 

However, I did see an area with two baby elephants who were chained front and back, unsupervised, surrounded by noisy tourists. I didn't stay long to see this, it was too upsetting.

Things that bothered me were - what happens to the adult male elephants? Where do they go? Are the elephants ever released back into the wild?

Regardless, this is a beautiful place, surrounded by hills, with the most elephants you're ever likely to see in one place.

review_text:
There are clearly divided opinions about places such as these. The elephants here are either orphan elephants, those born in captivity or ex-working elephants in retirement. They are cared for at the orphanage their whole lives and are not planned for release back into the wild,  as they probably would not survive  by themselves, having become accustomed to human handling. We saw them taken to the river for their daily bathing,  and clearly they enjoyed the experience, playing and splashing around with each other (and even trying to mate!) in the water for several hours.. 
Some in our group objected to the chains the elephants wear and the actions of the mahouts prodding them to move. We learned later (contrary to appearances) the elephants are not chained up back in the orphanage - they only have the chains on for use in an emergency and for public protection if they get spooked. 
But as one commentator has already said, if you want to see elephants in a free and natural environment, visit one of the many national parks -  not the orphanage, or a sanctuary.

review_text:
Before our trip to Sri Lanka I did a lot of research online into Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. There are lots of contrasting opinions online so in the end we decided to visit.

I regret going here and giving this company my money. The elephants are not well looked after, they are paraded around like zoo animals, and patrolled with bull hooks and chains and it is a massive money making exercise. The elephants here are not happy, and there is no program to release the orphans back into the wild.

I came away feeling really sad and sorry for the elephants at this place.

If you are thinking about visiting - please do not! Instead save your money and go on a safari at Minneriya national park, where you will see hundreds of happy elephants in their natural habitat.

review_text:
We got there at bath time. Elephants seemed to enjoy being in the river. They were given reasonable room to roam, a 30m x 10m section of river. A few wandered past the handlers to forage on the far side of the river ... it seemed that they could have made a dash for freedom into the forests, but they didn't.
Of herd of 30, only 2 or 3 had chains. Handlers had hooked poles but although they were waved around, I did not see any physical abuse or contact.
We enjoyed seeing them close up and being relatively free in the river.
These are not wild elephants.
Not sure what happens at other times or the conditions in which they are kept. Would be sad if they were not treated well then.
Although we sat on the hotel balcony, there was no pressure on us to buy drinks etc.

review_text: Certainly one of the most avoidable experiences.. the elephants are all chained up and seem pretty afraid. There is a place inside where you can feed fruits to the elephants, provided you pay money (and can also pose with the elephant). Those tourists who decided to pose without paying for the fruits were rudely told to stop clicking photos.. later our driver took us to the hotel where the elephants come close by to bathe. Some elephants who were afraid of getting into the water were whipped so they would enter the water. Again, here, when some tourists decided to touch the elephants trunks, the mahouts immediately helped them click pics and asked for money. It is a money making business for the mahouts rather than being an orphanage.. avoid at all costs!

review_text: I had been here 15 years ago, so had some idea of what to expect, but still went in two minds about whether it was worthy or not. The development has been enormous, with two hotels now overlooking the bathing area, and a street lined with proper shops. No doubting where the focus is. It's still tempting to go to see the elephants close up, and their handlers will happily take photos of you with an elephant (and then expect 1000 rupees +), but the pictures are kind of spoiled by all the chains..................

review_text: So we visited the orphanage during our honeymoon Sri Lanka tour. We knew what to expect and our guide confirmed it. It has nothing to do with an orphanage. It is a pure tourist money making machine. The animals live on a fenced area with no shade to hide from the sun and no water place. A bunch of them are chained, for the safety of the tourists. Having visited previously elephants in one of the national parks, where they live freely and feed from the jungle, it is a very sad image to see the orphanage. If you are looking for a nature friendly experience, rather visit one of the national parks instead of the orphanage.

review_text:
There are a lot of misleading reviews about Pinnawala. I've been twice - earlier this month and 21 years ago - and I've enjoyed the experience both times. The price of 2500 rupees (about Â£11 per person) is quite high but much lower than I've seen online where it's often stated at $20 per person.

There's not too much to do. Our driver went in with us which we thought a bit odd until we realised he knew exactly where to go and when to make sure we got the best experience. We went first to the elephant 'paddocks' where the ladies were hanging around eating and waiting for bath time. In a separate area, the boys were getting ready to go the river.

Nothing can really prepare you for seeing a massive herd of elephants on the move. The boys went first, strolling through the orphanage, out to the road and down to the river. Some are chained - for their safety and everybody else's. I don't think it's a bad thing. Once the boys were on their way, the lady elephants followed.

We watched the bath time for nearly 2 hours. Our driver urged us to a brilliant watching space in a cafe which we really appreciated. In two hours you have plenty of time to watch and observe the different personalities amongst the elephants. There are the cheeky younger boys, the stubborn old ladies, the frisky and the laid-back all hanging out together.

People have commented on the use of 'spikes' or 'guides'. We was the metal guides being used by the mahoots but always very gently and never with any violence. The love of the handlers for their pachyderm pals was clear to all.

One old lady - quite possibly the grande dame of the herd - spent an hour standing knee deep trying to avoid a wash. Her mahoot gently urged her into deeper water, taking his time and using his 'guide' to help scrape old mud off her head and back. Eventually she gave in and rolled over in the water to let him clean her properly.

Some are chained in the water but didn't seem distressed about it. A couple of young females made a jovial bid for freedom on the far banks and were laughingly chased down and returned to the herd.

If you're looking for lots of action, this may disappoint. If you have the patience to watch and wait, you'll probably love it as much as I did.

One comment. I think the management should consider rebranding this as an Elephant Home rather than an Elephant Orphanage since it seems to create elevated expectations of lots of babies and at present there really aren't many at all. The purpose of the home is to give safe haven to elephants, not to go looking for unwanted babies. Back in the days of the Civil War, a lot of babies were orphaned by their parents being killed (accidentally or intentionally) so there were more little ones to see. These days they do have a few babies but I suspect that's more an outcome of boy and girl elephants getting friendly rather than any kind of captive breeding programme.

i was expecting many happy elephants being helped by loving people and am absolutely gutted that i have given this place my money and come across this.

After landing in Colombo, we headed to Kandy & this orphanage was the first stop en-route to Kandy. 
Visited with family & my 4 year Son enjoyed the elephants bathing in the river. It's fun to watch the elephant parade when all the roads are cleared of public - so the elephants can go back to the orphanage after bathing in the river. There is a restaurant overlooking the river & the entire lane has a lot of road shopping stuff in terms of clothes, souvenirs, etc. 
They have time slots reserved for the elephants to bathe, be fed, etc. One can pay & feed the elephants.

We visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage again, the first time was 2007, certainly another highlight was According to our guide there are nearly 100 orphaned elephants here and we got to see them be playful with each other, walk through the sanctuary, saw them being fed milk (members of the public can do this but there is only a limited number of tickets available, if I recall rightly its only 30), What an unbelievable sight it is to see them walking down the street towards the river for their bathing (10-12 and 2-4).
They blow a siren warns of approaching elephants to signal that the elephants are on the way, you can stand within 2 feet or so of the procession. Once safe, make your way back to the rocks by the water. This is an excellent vantage point to enjoy the spectacle. when all merchants guided all tourists inside and took their merchandise inside as well. Then dozens of elephants marched through the 200m market street and some bags and t-shirts feel down to the ground as they had passed by so close to the shops including the poo shop. 
The keepers or mahouts also carry "guide sticks" to help direct the elephants to the bathing river etc. They never hit or hurt the elephants with these sticks, they just use them gently to guide them safely across the roads etc.  Then we positioned ourselves on the verandah of the Hotel, where to also had lunch overlooking the river & got a really good view of the Elephants being washed & playing in the water.

review_text: It was very sad to see some of the elephants chained in solitary confinement. The reason that they are adults and may pose a threat to others at certain times does not seem a true statement. This as supposed to be an orphanage but it is clearly also a breeding program. We were told that the animals are never released into the wild, surely other species can be rehabilitated so that seemed so wrong. We went to see the animals bathing in the river and were disgusted to see a young elephant walked down the road heavily chained and tethered to a rock when in the water, It was clearly distressed and only settled when an older one was allowed near it. Many of the others were chained to rings embedded on the rocks. Most of them didn't seem too stressed by this but I suppose they don't know any other life.

review_text:
Read a lot of extreme comments of this site beforehand. This place was highly recommended by the agent and was a midpoint from capital to Dambulla. 

We spent an hour here for a short walk with the elephant, feed with fruit, and watched it at bath in the river. Each elephant had an assigned caretaker to look after and as per the guide, the elephant would only be chained at night during sleep and no wounds or marks could be found at the elephant leg which caused by the chain. Literally there was no evident to prove if they treated the elephant in a proper manner or not in just an hour stay. 

To us, this spot could be omitted as we would visit Minneriya National Park seeing the wild elephant 2 days after this. Recommend to go for the wild elephant instead of seeing the caged.

review_text:
First things first, I saw no evidence of any physical abuse of the elephants during my visit to Pinnewala Orphanage. The elephants look well fed, clean and have no scars from chains or sticks as far as I could see. The keepers used goads to guide the elephants and to prevent the bulls trying to mix with the main herd of females/younger elephants, but I did not see a single one being hit. The chains used on some of the bulls look unpleasant, but they seem to be loosely fitted and not particularly irritating to the animals. Keeping such large and potentially aggressive animals under control is essential when they are in such close proximity to one another (bulls generally wouldnÂ’t mix with the herd in the wild) and to humans. The animals are corralled to be fed and kept in a certain (quite large) area of the river to be washed, but otherwise roam around a large natural reserve. 

Some of the Â‘extrasÂ’ put on for tourists (photos with the elephants, feeding/washing them etc) arenÂ’t acceptable. The elephants are wild animals, not playthings or props, and they should be treated as such. A couple of keepers rode some of the bulls back from the river, which again I donÂ’t agree with. Additionally, perhaps more effort could be made to return some of the animals back to the wild, however I donÂ’t know anything about the practicalities  and of course this runs the risk of them being killed by farmers (the main threat to wild elephants in Sri Lanka).

All in all, as far as I could tell the Pinnewala Orphanage is not abusive to the animals in its care and is no worse than Western zoos. Keeping animals in captivity is never ideal, but the fraught relationship between farmers and wildlife in Sri Lanka make it impossible for all elephants to live in the wild. Perhaps in the future with better education, people all over the world will be better able to co-exist with animals and places like Pinnewala will be unnecessary. However, for now this place is the best of a bad situation.

review_text: We stopped off here on the way from Kandy to Negombo in time for the 2pm bath time. ItÂ’s the last thing we have done in Sri Lanka and has left a bitter taste. As this wasnÂ’t part of our planned itinerary, I did not do any research beforehand. Wish I had. YouÂ’ll find plenty of articles which will dissuade you. The word Â‘orphanageÂ’ is a well chosen one; it fools you into thinking this might be ecotourism. There are no Â‘success storiesÂ’ about these elephants being released back to the wild, only a brag about how this is the largest herd of Asian elephants handled by man. Twice a day the elephants are walked across the road down to a river where masses of people crowd around taking selfies. One man sprays them from a water cannon. If they donÂ’t want to get wet, then tough. I watched several try to avoid the spray only to be herded back into its path with shouts and the bull hook. It is sad to see them just standing there not playing at all. It is not their choice to be at the river and they look unhappy. Some of the handlers were interacting nicely with them, washing and scratching them. But others just sat on the rocks. I fail to see how the animalsÂ’ well-being is put first - a complete money making scheme (2500 rupees to watch at the riverside). In penance for participating in such unethical tourism I will be donating the cost of our tickets to Save the Elephants. IÂ’m hopeful my review will deter at least a few people from visiting.

review_text: I read a whole bunch of these reviews before we travelled to Sri Lanka. I really wanted to see the elephants and it was our honeymoon after all. We visited Thailand last year and refused any elephant visits as they are so mistreated over there and we are very against elephant riding. Our experience of Pinnawala was delightfully reassuring and I felt relieved. The elephants are treated very well and no one was riding them or beating them with sticks - as some of these reviews suggest. They were free to walk around and were fed very generously. You can tell that all staff members look after them very well. Yes - there some that have some chains around them. This is unfortunate but we asked why this was and didn't just assume. As this is an orphanage, a lot of these elephants wouldn't survive the wild because they are unwell or have certain illnesses. Naturally, some are also a bit aggressive and therefore, to protect themselves and the other elephants they have some with chains. It's the best of a bad situation for them but they are bathed separately and have the same amount of love and care as the others. The keepers also carry "guide sticks" to help direct the elephants to the bathing river etc. They never hit or hurt the elephants with these sticks, they just use them gently to guide them safely across the roads etc. I think the people here are doing an amazing thing and we loved seeing them. We didn't need to ride them or anything - it was just amazing to see them. What a wonderful place for them.
