On arrival at the orphanage we saw young elephants being fed by the keepers with large bottles of milk.
We crossed the road towards the river, a siren warns of approaching elephants, Jack took us up some stairs to a restaurant overlooking the river, what a view we had,and then they arrived at least 20 elephants, some to the left and these were chained as they were being trained for religious ceremonies. The rest just played in the river, washing and shooting water out of their trunks, an amazing sight and a privilege to be part this tour. Thanks to Jack and our new friends this is a trip we will never forget....

review_text:
Maybe the intentions of this 'orphanage' were once good, they are definitely not now. 

This is a commercialized elephant breeding factory. Most of the elephants are bred in the park, for the sole purpose of entertainment for tourists. 

Caretakers are encouraging everyone to take photos and touch the elephants in exchange for tips. 

You can pay extra to feed a baby elephant, who is chained by itself in a cage surrounded by tourists. When we were there, the baby was freaking out, trying to get out of the chains and hurting herself. They get fed whenever a tourist pays, not only during feeding times.

Many elephants are chained up all day in the same spot. They get to go to the river 2 times a day (you have seen the famous photos). Even there many are chained up under water and caretakers push them underwater with a stick so they look like they are splashing around. 

Many of them are showing signs of distress, rocking back and forth for hours at the time while being chained up. This does not happen in the wild. These compulsive movements cause life-threatening damage to the feet and joints of the elephant. They are in severe distress and don't let them tell you otherwise. 

People saying that there is no other way to treat them and the elephants would not survive in the wild are wrong. There are way more humane ways to treat elephants in an orphanage and this is not one of them. Please don't participate.

review_text:
We went to the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage with our driver as our guide - if you didn't have someone with you who knew how the place worked you would be at a loss as you are not given any information when you purchase your tickets.
We were in time to see the elephants herded together to be fed and then followed them down to the water for them to bath.
This is 'put on' for tourists twice a day and even though it was wonderful to see these magnificent beasts it really felt like a show.
It is expensive to get into the park and we are hoping that most of the money goes to caring for the elephants.
The tourist shops on the way down to the water are fairly expensive but you can get a last minute gift if you need.
We preferred seeing the elephants in the wild on our safari tour

review_text:
We were on time to see around 30 elephants bring given a bath through a high pressure pump.
After the bath, they orderly walked one behind another to the orphanage across the highway.
We saw many more elephants including one with very long tusks.
There were many curio shops near the river where they sell a lot of elephant related curios as well as stationery and other items made of elephant poop. There was a demonstration too to visitors showing the process making paper from elephant poop.
A must visit place in Srilanka.
Ganesh J

Its a good 3 hr drive from Colombo. This place is famous for the elephant sanctuary.

We could see the elephant bathing at the river and in the orphanage could see a lot of elephants especially the baby elephants. It was a bit hot so did not venture too much.

review_text: The first thing to note is the orphanage is more Zoo like than I expected. I was also not really prepared to see some of the elephants chained to posts, however I also didn't expect one to walk past within ten feet of me either. The park is split into three sections - there is an area where you can feed fruit to an elephant, there is a holding area where the elephants are chained and fed; and then there is a large 'paddock' where they roam free. There are keepers who patrol the perimeter of the paddock, but other than a smattering of rocks, there is nothing between you and the elephants. Whilst we were at the paddock, the elephant who had been at the fruit station, was walked back to the field in front of where we were stood. It was quite amazing. Later on a group were walked down to the feeding station and again were no more than ten foot away from us. There is a daily milk feed for the orphans, and a walk down to the river for a bath, but on the day we were there, neither took place. Unsure as to why the feeding didn't happen (although I expect the babies would have been chained too & not quite the romantic image I had), but the bathing was cancelled due to the rain causing river levels to be too high. Would recommend as an opportunity to get close to the elephants, but not as one to view them in their natural habitat.

So we had read so many mixed reviews and were debating whether to go or not. We decided to go and see for ourselves and make our own minds up & in all honesty seeing these wonderful animals at such close proximity was amazing, would we prefer no chains - of course, but you can see in most cases it is for the Elephant & public safety as most do not have such chains when back in the ample enclosures. They seem to be well fed and love the water playing.
Bearing in mind that this place started with two elephants and takes in sick or injured as well as releases some back to the wild on balance they do a great job.
Seeing the keepers with hooked poles is not nice but we saw no ill treatment and more love than anything.
Cost for us foreigners is 2500 rupee (around Â£12.50) each and bearing in mind that the money goes to help I see this as good value plus I paid 750 rupee for my wife to wash an elephant in the water - clearly enjoyed by the elephant and my wife.
I do have issues with the elephants being ridden by the keepers & also on the road into the orphanage a place offering Â‘ride an elephantÂ’ Service - this to me is totally wrong and should not be allowed! 

Anyway in my humble opinion it was a wonderful experience

review_text:
We were taken to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage by our tour guide on our way to Nuwara Eliya from Colombo. I had heard and read so much about this place that I definitely wanted to visit it.
As soon as we entered we were pleased to see so many elephants in the river  which was quite a sight. But after standing and looking at them for a bit, we realized that some of the elephants were chained up and forced to spray water from their trunks or were being forced to lie down. If they tried getting up the so called caretaker would pierce them with these long sharp and pionty spear/rods in their hand. It made the the elephants scream loud(could be heard at a distance) in pain and the care taker seemed to enjoy it. I really felt bad and we all decided to leave immediately. review_text:
Elephant parks can be found at several place in Asia. They differ in offered service, exposure and elephant treatment, At the Pinnawala Orphanage in Sri Lanka you can see the herd walking to/from the river and watch them inside the the orphanage, being fed. 
Part of the herd is on the background (furtheraway from the public) and others are more upfront. The entrance ticket is also required for the riverwalk, as the authorities close off the street, to secure the elephants from traffic. Inside the park, I saw 2 elephants chained on 2 legs (according to the staff because of behavior). There are no rides possible, and no tricks/acts are presented. Mahouts offered me to take a selfie with the elephant (for money), which I declined, The mahouts are using the sticks with metal points,

review_text:
This is a place that has many controversial reviews and so we pondered to whether we wanted to go or not. It was a tossup and I am glad we did go but it did leave some questions unanswered. 
We missed the elephants walking from the park over the road and down to the river. So we purchased our tickets from the ticket office and then headed over. You have to give your ticket to the ticket man at the start of the road so unpaid people cannot get down there to watch the elephants. We got down there and it was quite a sight. All these elephants standing in the water. The group of elephants was split and I did notice the ones that were chained in place. I also noted a small group that kept trying to get out of the water. The mahout would let them go for a while and then he would yell and wave his hook and the elephants obviously fearful of him would get back in the water. I got talking to another visitor who said she had been a number of times and that the river was really low and when it is low they seem to be lethargic. It was the first time she had seen them so disinterested. 
The mahout to me seemed to be a bully. Later on when they were prepping them to leave, this particular guy caught my eye and smiled. I gestured to him that I was not happy with his behavior and proceeded to photograph him. I believe there is a difference to being in control fairly and being a bully. Out of all of them he definitely was a bully. The elephants were swapped  around a bit and it was fascinating to be so close and to watch them for a reasonably long period. It was extremely hot that day so we sat up in the restaurants balcony and had a beer etc. to get some respite. They then moved the elephantÂ’s to the water cannon by the exit to the river which they seemed to enjoy and then the main girl elephant, she led them back up the road. They knocked over a hat stand in a store which was funny and they seemed keen to get back. 
We followed them closely and when we got back they had taken them over the back of the park and they were being fed. We stood for perhaps half an hour and no one told us what was happening- we just stood and hoped there was something more. Eventually they told us we could go over which we did. 
Yes they were all chained by a foot and they all had piles of food. We stood for a period watching how they ate soft wood, palm leaves and observed what they seemed to prefer to eat, and how they manipulated the food to eat. 
We then went back to another area where they had younger elephants still on milk. We got talking to the assistant curator and it wasnÂ’t until he answered my questions about containment, feeding, punishment, medical care, that it made any sense. He said there was a lot of misunderstanding and therefore there are negative reviews. I asked why they seemed to be not enjoying themselves in the water and he said, they are just so keen to get back to eat.
The main reason for containment is to stop fighting. In the wild the elephants form packs where there is a boss and they will fight if they encroach on other elephantÂ’s territory. They are working on a big open area for them but at the moment containment is the best for them. So this parks environment is not normal, but it is the best they can do and they do their best to stop the animals hurting each other. He said that the elephants do not have to work for their food there and life is quite easy and the care is excellent with medical care etc. and it is a good alternative for the orphans. I suggested they educate the visitors more. There was very little education of the visitors and when you donÂ’t know why things are being done, you come up with your own theory. The experience is not interactive enough. 
I also complained about the bully mahout and he knew who I was talking about and he has been pulled up before about this. I appreciate what this place is doing but think it is a shame that there are even orphans that need care. If they were just left to their own devices, and humans didnÂ’t interfere, there would be few orphaned anyway. 
I think they actually do really care for them and give them great care, but they need to connect with the visitors more and explain what and why and how they do what they do.

review_text:
We stayed at Hotel Elephant Park. This is an excellent place to get up early, have breakfast and have some of the best seats in the house to a fantastic experience. Photographs of the experience are readily available... the actual experience is way better. From the eyes of my 8 year old granddaughter, it was magical. You want to be done with breakfast by 830am when the first group of about 7 elephants come. You can move off the balcony of the hotel down to the rocks to get really close to the elephants, If you move down early you will beat the crowds and get pics you will treasure. Once the elephants are guided away from the river, take an hour or so shopping the row of shops leading to the river. Make sure you begin to make your way back toward the river just before 1000am. You will be able to see 40+ elephants guide toward the river. You can stand within 2 feet or so of the procession. Once safe, make your way back to the rocks by the water. This is an excellent vantage point to enjoy the spectacle.

Unfortunately I don't have anything positive to say about the actual orphanage. I imagine and believe that they are doing good work, but I can't personally vouch for it. We went before the 40+ elephants were guided back to the orphanage, and I can say that within 10 min, the overwhelming impression my family got was: depression. I would NOT recommend entrance to the Elephant Orphanage. Enjoy the elephants while bathing.

BTW,if you are looking for an extremely high quality experience from a personal driver,  I had an opportunity to work with both Gamage Asanka from Gamage Tours, gamagetours.com, asankamail2@gmail.com. I reached out to him because of a good review on Trip Advisor. From the first email, it was obvious he was responsive, quite courteous and professional. We began to work on an itinerary together, and received what I thought was very reasonable pricing for what I was asking him to do. When it came down describing our vehicle needs he was quick to note that since we had 4 people in our party, his vehicle would not be the best option. I appreciated his candor. 

He recommended a personal friend and colleague, Gihan Thissera, from Sinethi Tours, sinethitours77@gmail.com.  Gihan took us on 7 day tour of central/southern Sri Lanka. He was prompt, kind, attentive, and professional at all times. His driving was safe and at no time did I feel any stress on behalf of my family. He asked him to meet us at a railroad station after a 5 hour train ride, and he was there exactly where and when he was supposed to be. He pointed out fruits in season, and bought us fruit to sample. He was especially attentive to my grand daughter. His vehicle was utterly spotless at all times. I thought I was getting a driverÂ… what I ended up getting was a guide who became an integral part of our group. My family and I could not imagine a better experience than the wha we had with Gihan.

review_text:
This was booked by our tour company for us.  We did not therefore have to deal with getting tickets etc as our guide did all this for us and showed us were to go.  First of all we went across the road from the main site towards the river where we watched the lephants bathing in the river.  It was a lovely sight to see, I know some had chains on them but this we were informed was for safety reasons related to the behaviour of the specific elephant. The elephant hotel is an ideal spot to having a drnk and some lunch as they have a balcony area overlooking the river.  We were fortunate to be browsing the shops down towards the river when the elephants were being brought back to the main sight.  Boy were they lively with a slight incident with one not behaving!!!

Back on the main sight we were able to see the elephants includiing a couple of tuskers (we learnt that not all elephants have tusks).  There is the chance to hand feed a elephant fruit which was 350 rupees and this was certainly memorable with the chance to touch them under the supervision of one of the keepers.  There is also the chance to bottle feed a calf again under supervision - if you're going to flim or take pictures of this be quick they drain a large bottle of milk in the blink of an eye!

It certainly was a bucket list exerience and lovely to see how they have taken them in for various reasons ad how well they are cared for.

review_text:
This place has something quite magical about it - the elephants of course. Split across a road (really) it is a little bit complicated upon first arriving as you feel you shoud go into the actual orphanage but then a siren sounds and the elephants leave the grounds to cross the road, parade down a street full of shops (!) and into the river but this is something you must see! It's amazing to watch 40+ elephants happy, frolic and even scrubbed by some of the orphanage workers. You can enjoy the view from a cafe or just from the pavement. Proceed back up past the shops selling elephant dung toilet paper ;) to the orphanage where you can enjoy feeding them or just watch them roam about in wide open spaces. 

Some elephants are with chains which can be a little upsetting to initially see but it appears its only for those that are a bit unruly and could charge off. None are actually shackled to the ground although we did feel a bit taken advantage of by the river as a young elephant with a chain was used to pose for photos with tourists as workers pressed for money for each photo. Try to avoid this if possible as you will have many opportunities to take photos of them in the river, on the road and in the orphanage without lining the pockets of opportunists using them for a photo opportunity. Who wants a photo with chains in it anyway?

review_text:
We visited as a part of a day trip from Negombo to Kandy.

We arrived early morning, at 0930 and were able to watch the baby elephants being bottle fed. You could also give it a go yourself if you asked.

The elephants looked well treated and after  walking around the orphanage, we were pleasantly surprised to be guided across the road by our tour guide to a local restaurant overlooking the rivers. The street was full of shops and people asking us to come in, which seemed decent if your into that kind of thing.

We arrived at the restaurant and ordered some food (Western prices) and after a few minutes, saw a huge herd (50+) elephants coming down the streets into the large river to bathe. It was particular great to see they were completely free to play and wash (no chains of ropes) with a few of the handlers simply sat by on the rocks.

Absolutely fantastic to see and definitely recommended.

review_text:
Having read some negative reviews on here about entrance fees and paying extra to feed the elephants I was pleasantly surprised to see the entrance fee clearly displayed on arrival. RD 2500 for foreigners and RS 100 for Sri Lankans and RS 700 for SAARC nationals. 

Twice daily you get the chance to bottle feed the babies or fruit feed the adults, who clearly love the attention they get. The elephants are kept in wonderful surroundings and are looked after very well. This is a tourist attraction but it has expanded to rescue elephants injured in the jungle and offer them a safe home for the rest of their lives with medical attention when needed.  

It is an amazing sight to see the elephants being led down to the river to bathe, some are tethered in the water, this is to protect the human visitors and also to stop the males harassing the females. There are a couple of hotels/tea shops on the banks of the river from where you can sit and watch the elephants bathe and the road leasing from the river to the main park is lined with souvenir shops which are fun to browse. 

We thoroughly enjoyed our trip to the elephant orphanage, it is as close to seeing elephants in their natural environment as possible. I would recommend a visit, even for those who do not like to see animals in captivity, they are well kept and far better off here than in the places they were rescued from.

I was a little unsure of how I felt about this place upon arrival. My driver dropped me off at the foreigner ticket booth where I paid maybe l35 USD for my ticket. 

When I went in there was a spot where people were paying to feed fruit to elephants. Then an open area in the back were some elephants were just standing. It seemed like occasionally the staff were trying to corral the elephants closer to the tourists.

I wasnÂ’t feeling great about the place. I walked down to see the milk feeding and again, people were paying to hold a bottle of milk for a single elephant in a caged in area while so many people made noise and took photos. It felt so commercial and unkind for the elephants.

I left disheartened, not knowing that there was another area across the street where the elephants were taken to bath. My driver then showed me the area across the road, and for me this for me was magical. I watched maybe 30 elephants walk their usual path down to the river where a giant hose has been built to facilitate their bathing.

IÂ’ll admit, I was slightly distraught to see that some of the elephants had chains tied on their ankles that were then hung over their backs. They were not being led by chains and a near by sign explained that the chains are precautionary for the safety of the staff and tourists. I watched the elephants bath for almost an hour before deciding to have lunch at a restaurant that overlooked the bathing elephants. I did not once see the chains used.

My only qualm is that some of the staff ride the elephants. I have heard that this is very bad for the elephantsÂ’ spines. I am no zoologist, and I welcome any additional info on the harm this may cause to the animals as I do not like to see animals being mistreated.

Yes, even for 1500 rupees per person (for foreigners like us), it is worthwhile and a very good first impression of Sri Lanka.

review_text:
We visited this last week with our family. Childrens love it when they see elephants so close by. However one of the fun activity here was feeding the elephants. Now for this to happen you need to 
a. Know the feeding times
b. Be a little earlier than feeding time, as there are only limited tickets available and its first come first serve. So, if you are with kids, highly recommended to plan it with your tour operator. 

Overall nice place for kids. 

You can also buy some handmade paper made out of "elephant poo" . They show you the complete process which is amazing. Then when the elephants are taken for bath, it is also amazing to see. 

Vegetarian restaurants nearby are not so much, so please be prepared to eat French fries , sandwiches only.

Overall a nice place to be. 

If you are holding passport from one of the SAARC countries, ticket is discounted. So indian have to pay only 700 Sri lankan rupees.(approx)

Now en route from Colombo to Sigiriya one cannot... rather should not miss the Pinnawala elephant orphanage. 

These are rescued elephants and are not tame, you can see them take bath . Its more of an elephant rehab. If you are here to witness the wild and the wildlife this is it.. now there are plenty of private farms here catering to tourist needs of elephant rides and baths.. not these are exact opposite to the govt run which is a rehab and the private ones are only for tourist and making monies with elephants rides of different rate cards i.e. by the time you wanna ride them, there will be a mahout who will walk along and will take thru the mad and wild made wilderness.

there will be a place for quick bites and buy souvenirs too. So its practically ones own decision what they want and do. If you are Asian, you will not find anything amazing what you have not seen in your own home country.

review_text: The Pinnawala Elephant orphanage was first set up as a tourist spot but is now known for its rehabilitation of elephants. While there we saw herds of elephants in tranquil like conditions and free to roam with extra feed being trucked in. There is information posters explaining the difference between the Asian and African  elephants which was very interesting. There is a small gift shop which sells lovely fold up umbrella's with elephant designs for $7.50 all which helps finance the orphanage. One small elephant was chained by the leg and a bit distressed but we were told it had recently arrived and was being assessed and its feed monitored . On the way back to the bus we had to stop as did all foot traffic and auto traffic for the herd of elephants returning from the river following their bathing, There is a platform to watch them in this process

review_text:
We visited the orphanage on the way round to Dambulla. We had read reviews on tripadvisor but we were undecided whether to visit. In the end we felt that perhaps our entrance fee would contribute to the elephant upkeep so we proceeded to visit.
On arrival and purchase of tickets we were taken down a small shopping street opposite to the orphanage which takes you to the river where the elephants bathe daily.
We arrived to see at least 30 elephants enjoying the water with some "snorkelling" and a couple of younger ones being a little cheeky. This part of the visit was great.
We did not wait to see all the elephants make their way back past the shops and street stalls but that might have been fun.

Back at the orphanage the pens, albeit large, just did not offer any stimulation for the elephants. Even though they are trying to make improvements the orphanage itself was not what we expected or would like to consider as acceptable for keeping what are wild elephants. We were saddened by what we saw and it left us thinking why not take them to one of the national parks and releasing them back to the wild. Probably not that simple but thats how it left us feeling.

review_text:
Visited the Orphanage's bathing site at around 10.30am. The elephants are already in their natural bath. Honestly after walking through the street full of souvenir shops and suddenly this open space appear, seeing the elephant against the greenaries and blue sky is quite a sight to behold. Do look out for the men enticing you to feed the elephants with the oranges they provides, it willcost 100rupee. I next visited the Orphanage itself but only a handful of elephants are there. Do wait till 12noon when the elephants walk home from their bathing site. This is where the elephants walking by the souvenir shops and crossing the busy road to return to the orphanage. There are some reports that saying this Orphanage is ill-treating the elephants.  Yes I do see some elephants been chained at the leg but there are also signage to explain that they need to chain some of the more agressive male elephants to prevent them from attacking.
So is it ill-treating or disciplining - I guess it's up to individual to decipher.

review_text: Before we came here, we did much research on the humane treatment of their elephants.  The primary objection that most people have is that male elephants have a chain on them when they are bathing.  This is to prevent them from attacking other males.  The elephants and their trainers had a grand time taking a bath and there was nothing cruel about it.  If they were released to the wild, they would die.  What other solution would you offer.  Seeing 40 plus elephants was a once in a life time experience and we would highly recommend it.

review_text: After visiting the wonderful Elephant Nature Park in Chiang Mai a few years ago, this was a poorly executed excuse for a rescue park, where in truth the Elephants looked stressed and far from happy. At the feeding station, we declined feeding an elephant on the grounds that its keeper had a big stick with sharp end to keep the elephant in step. It may be needed, but it looks as if the elephants are are not treated nearly as well as in Chiang Mai. We then crossed the road to watch the elephants bathe, only to find that they are are chained in the water and literally unable to move, does not look like fun to me. I totally get why some people love this place as its the closest they ever get to seeing elephants in a wild setting, but I would say better to do a safari, which is close by.

review_text:
We visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage on our way to Kandy from Colombo. 
Initially I did not have high hopes of seeing anything extraordinary. 

After entering we had to walk for some distance in the hot sun seeing only one or two elephants chained inside their enclosure. 

But at the end of our walk, we were treated to a fascinating sight of more than 50 elephants roaming about in an open area enclosed by rocks and railings to prevent them from coming out. 

Then we watched some elephants being fed and some people were allowed to feed milk to baby elephants in bottles. 
After coming out, we were told that the elephants would come out, cross the road, walk into the street and take a bath in the river. 

We waited outside for some time and then the gates opened and more than 30 elephants came out, crossed the road and walked into the street within 5 feet of where we were standing. 

It is both awesome and scary to have 25 elephants walking right next to you, trumpeting and swaying and one elephant swerved dangerously close to where I was standing. 

After they crossed us, we followed them to the river by paying the charges and were again treated to a rare sight of so many elephants bathing together in the river. 

All in all, it was a wonderful and unforgettable experience and I am very happy that I paid a visit to this place. 
I have no hesitation in recommending this attraction to all of you who are visiting Sri Lanka.

Honestly. I thought I would write something that will help guide your decision about whether to go or not, however it isnÂ’t straight up and simple. IÂ’ve tried to bullet point my thoughts to try and help.

1. Yes there are chains on some elephants. I believe some have shown aggressive behaviours. There are some very not well looked after elephants in extremely worse situations I have seen across the island. 

2. The milk feed I am in two minds about. It is done to obviously provide money for the elephants. The two we saw were not in shackles, were boisterously playing around the site and seemed more than happy to keep drinking away, and were more teenager-ish stature.

3. The River. They seemed more than happy to splash about in the river. Some elephants were having their keepers wash them, one elephant didnÂ’t want him to stop, encouraging him when he stopped until he carried on again. Two elephants were chained on a long chain, they had enough room to play and their keepers could leave them safely there. It didnÂ’t seem any different to when you nip into the corner shop with your dog tied by its lead to the lamppost outside.

4. I did see one keeper prodding an elephant with a sharp pointed spear type implement at one point when it appeared to be going off track. This concerned me a little, however no elephant I had a good look at had any wounds, there were happy calves with their mums. They kept the bulls separate to the rest of the herd as they generally get territorial and violent.

If you do not like Zoos, do not go. Minneriya National Park is nearby and has wild herds.

review_text:
After some initial concerns, we decided to visit Pinnawala Orphanage and we enjoyed it yet it did raise some concerns. The ticket for locals is a bargain. Foreigners pay much more, but I guess you need to maintain such a place and it's be unfair to overcharge locals. The place is indeed huge, beautiful and well-kept. It's all surrounded by the jungle. The orphanage enclosure is all done with wood and trunks and there is varied and typical vegetation (there are signs for the trees).
The fruit feeding of adult elephants and milk feeding of the young ones has a little of a show feeling, but if you try (paying a somehow reasonable price), you'll get the chance to have a unique experience, get close to the elephants and touch them. The unruly young ones were cute and insatiable. The adults seemed to enjoy the fruit and none seemed to be forced to eat.
Across the place there are lots of signs with information about elephants and their care and feeding. 
In a world where human beings are taking space from the wildness to build towns and roads, Pinnawale has a caring aim. Seeing a few unruly young ones chained was cause of concern, yet I want to believe that's the only option to keep the most unruly ones and that at some point, they are unchained and allowed to be in other open areas. 
It's a different experience from a zoo and a from a circus. I have heard otherwise yet I don't have those strong opinions. These elephants were separated by their own herds so at least they appear to be looked after and they may not have had many chances out there alone.

review_text: Came here with my partner and our three youngest.  Firstly, it was enlightening to read the information at the entrance regarding the welfare of the animals, apart from which they had such vast grounds to roam in and the wonderful river to bathe in.  We only saw two elephants with chains on their ankles, but the reason for this was explained - apart from this all the elephants seemed well cared for and had plenty of freedom.  Watching them frolicking in the river was awesome and provided excellent photo opportunities. We then all had to stand back whilst they walked back up the road the the other area.  We spent ages in awe just watching them walking around and the babies playing and then moved on to the feeding area.  We were too late to purchase a milk bottle, but, that being said we were able to purchase some fruit to feed to them - what an amazing experience for the children.  I firmly believe that this orphanage works to help elephants and I am unsure as to why some people have a different view.  A wonderful day was had by all!

There are about 8-10 elephants and you take turns with 2 people riding the elephant at the same time. 

There is a river and you can bath the elephants in cool water. 

Also can make some shoping to donate/help the orphange.  

Once in a life time thing to do while in Colombo

review_text:
This was one of our favourite days in Sri Lanka. Definitely worth a visit.

As others say below, you can go with or without a guide. We had a guide from Ella whose company we really enjoyed, so we went up with him Â– but you could definitely find your way without a guide if you wanted to, maybe with a wrong turn or two along the way.

We took the short 20-minute walk rather than the 2-hour hike, and didnÂ’t regret it.

The bottom pool is the busiest with tourists Â– but we found it was only really worth a short stay. The views are beautiful, and this is where everyone gets their photos Â– but thatÂ’s pretty much it.

The second pool, a very short walk away, is good for a swim, and the view of the falls above you is pretty special. 

The third pool, directly above the second, and a short 2-3 minute hike up, features an 8m cliff jump. We did it and were perfectly safe Â– but I wouldnÂ’t do it without being shown by a local guide. There are plenty around the first pool who can show you. We did it a couple of times Â– every time, my feet hit the bottom of the pool at the end of the jump, but not hard enough to be of any concern Â– just a surprise first time around!

We then had a lovely time at the top of the third pool, sitting in the sun and relaxing. Well worth a trip.

Wow. Could not recommend going to Diyaluma Falls more. It was an absolute highlight for not just our trip to Ella, but Sri Lanka as a whole. Such a beautiful waterfall, amazing views, you can swim (definitely recommend as itÂ’s a lot of fun!) and the hike isnÂ’t too hard to get there. 

The only thing is, you do need a guide to walk you to the spots to go. When you arrive by tuk tuk, there will be guides there that will offer their service, at first you donÂ’t think you need them but IÂ’m telling you... you definitely do. So many turns and thereÂ’s no clear path in the slightest, and they take heaps of photos for you ! We went with a guy named Dennis (071 988 1825 if anyone wants to get in contact with him) and he said we decide on a price at the end depending on how happy we were with his service. We ended up paying 2,000 rupee for 3 of us which I think is very reasonable. 

Also, a tuk tuk from Ella to the falls was 4,000 rupee, they all say 6,000 only but you can definitely find someone who will do it for 4,000 just takes a bit of bartering and searching !

After thoroughly researching the falls we were confident on how to get to them with clear instructions saved on our phones. after parking our Tuk tuk at the top carpark we were asked multiple times if we would like a guide. After saying no and following our saved directions we set off to find our path only to be followed by one of the "guides" from the carpark. 

We were told we were going the wrong way and he directed us down some path in which he said was the right way. We trusted this advice as we thought he was being genuinely helpful. This path was overgrown and full of leeches (have a bottle of insect repellent and lighter ready to spray/burn them off as soon as you feel them) after eventually reaching and exploring the waterfalls we found a much much better path back. we popped out (surprise, surprise) where we were originally headed before being led astray by the guides advice. 

After returning to our Tuk Tuk and confronting the guide we asked him if the path we were going to follow was were the guides go and he laughed in our face and said yes. We expressed our disappointment at his actions and said in Australia or New zealand we would never do this to tourists or deliberately lead them astray simply because they chose to make their own way. 

Below are clear instructions how to get the falls without utilising the guides who take advantage of tourists and deliberately confuse them or make up that google maps wont work or that its extremely difficult to find the falls, both of which turned out to be lies. 

Follow this reviews instructions - however after walking past the green and white gate walk for about 50m then take a sharp right onto a wide path. From there traverse around the hillside towards the sound of rushing water and you'll find the various waterfalls.

review_text:
We are a family of 4 (2 kids age 10/13) and spent the day around the falls. We took a bus from Ella to Wellawaya (45 min, 300 rs). From there, our guide for the day (Tharindu, +94 719702456) picked us up by tuktuk. Of you have a car, you could also come straight to the falls on your own. Tharindu lives at the base of the falls.
We first spent half and hour climbing and playing on the boulders at the bottom of the falls/river.
Then Tharindu brought us with the tuktuk halfway up the mountain, from where we hiked 30 min to the falls. We recommend bringing a guide, because it saves you a lot of walking and you wonÂ’t get lost (which is easy). When we got to the top of the falls, it was a bit crowded with locals because of the weekend. We hiked 10 min further up to Upper Diyaluma falls, which where even nicer! There, we swam in the pools and climbed up to the top, from where our kids jumped off from a 8 meter rock in the pool! Awesome!
Tharindu was really nice and helpful and encouraged the kids with the swimming and jumping. He also makes really nice pictures (and loves the panorama setting!). 
We had a great day all together. DonÂ’t hesitate to give Tharindu a call.

review_text:
Diyaluma Falls is the second highest waterfall in Sri Lanka at 720ft high. Located about 6km from Koslanda in the Badulla District, and 38km from Ella, this horsetail waterfall has multiple falls and natural pools for you to dive into, refresh yourself and explore. Diyaluma Falls can be explored from both above
and below, as the base of the falls also has a pool you can dive into! The best time to visit would be for sunrise as you get to see the rising sun shine upon the waves crashing down, however, sunset isnÂ’t a bad
option either, just be weary that you may need to travel back towards the main road in total darkness.

I gave it 4 stars because of the tough climb to get to the top. Otherwise, it is indeed a multi-level beautiful waterfall with a number of pools to sit or have fun in.
We rode a motorbike from Ella, took about 1-1.5hrs. Fairly good roads  except for the last 15min stretch which were bumpier. At the base of the waterfall (some distance away from the actual waterfall), there is a small parking area and an inn. 
There are a few local boys/ young men waiting and will offer their service as a guide. We could have bargained to 1500lkr but paid the 2000lkr asked, after hearing from other travellers at our guesthouse how they topped up 500lkr in the end after experiencing the amount of walking and the guide waiting to bring them down at the end.
The walk up starts with a fairly straightforward dirt path through rubber trees and a small cluster of houses. However, the rest of it is a climb up the mountain, on uneven, scrabbly rocks, large and small, and cut-in steps in the ground. You should be young or of moderate fitness to do this. Definitely wear proper shoes and have sunscreen and water. Preferably start early in the day and wear longer pants, as the tall grass growing towards the path for much of the climb can get itchy after a while. You will also appreciate the helping hand of the guide as you climb..
At the top there is a coconut seller, then slightly downhill to the actual waterfall. 
It is fairly easy to get to the various levels of the waterfall. Be careful stepping in and out of the pools as the rocks are slippery with moss.  
There is only a roti and coconut seller at the waterfall itself. Bring some snacks or you can buy them from the few village grocery shops on the road in. Very friendly locals, we smiled and waved to everyone.
From the bottom of the waterfall, you will need to climb back up again to the top where the coconut seller is, to go all the way down again. It takes about 1hr each way.

The road to get there was in good condition and picturesque. 

The Diyaluma Falls are easily seen from the road which makes it easy for pulling over and having a look.

review_text:
It is a long drive along a terrible road to get to here, which is why you don't get many foreign tourists. I saw coach loads of Sri Lankans, though. Not really worth walking up the track to the foot of the waterfall -- you get a better view from the road, especially about 500m toward Wellawaya.

It is rather puny if there has been no rain, but after a decent rainstorm it is stunning.

review_text: We returned here after a year away and the falls were not so spectacular as we have seen on previous occasions, but we were not in the heavy rainy season. At all times of year these falls are impressive being some 220m in height. They are very easily accessible on the highway from Belihul Oya to Wellawaya and one can easily park, enjoy a splash in the water and take advantage of the road-side vendors who sell water, corn, nibbles and so on. As with all falls, the rainy period is by far the best time to see them at their spectacular best.

review_text:
So everyone can enjoy the beauty of Diyaluma easily by the Koslanda - Wellawaya road. There is a way to get to the top of Diyaluma with a short and enjoyable hike. You have to travel  bit further towards Poonagala and find the foot path by the makaldeniya bend. On the way to Poonagala also you will find several beautiful rivers. Ask a local they will show you the road. 

Then there is a hike to go to the top of Diyaluma. Go to there around 9-9:30 in the morning because a local warned me that there are elephants around 6-7 in the morning. 

 At the end of the hike, you can get down to the point where the water finally descends the 200m. You can peep over the edge the look down at the main road. Be care full. The pool created by the first cascade is good for bath. The view over the edge is amazing and worth all the steps in the hike. See the pictures.

review_text: Although we came from the other direction and it took 45 minutes each way, the falls were well worth the trip, even the hold-up on the way back as they were renovating a large bridge!  The falls are 220 metres high and tumble in long silvery plumes against a dark brown rock-face. There are also small refreshment places nearby.  You may do a bit of rock scrambling to get close if you wish, but the best view is from the road bridge. Of all the falls that we saw in Sri Lanka, this was probably the best.

review_text: The Diyaluma Falls can be seen from afar as you approach them travelling from Wellawaya to Beragala. We have seen these falls on many occasions but strongly advise, if possible, to visit during the wet season when they are spectacular. On this occasion (January) we remained impressed by the incredible height of the falls but the volume of water was very low. There are places to get water, drinks and snacks on the roadside at the foot of the falls. If travelling this road, it is worth stopping to enjoy the incredible power of nature.

The majestic Diyaluma Falls drops 220 metres and is best seen during the rainy season when there is a lot of water flowing. It has been called the "waterfall of smoking water."

It is on the Beragala to Wellawaya road, a short distance from the small town of Koslanda. The road is narrow, potholed and has some mud, so be careful when driving or riding, especially in wet weather.

review_text:
We visited here on the advice of our guesthouse in Haputale. We hiked up and down Lipton's Seat in the morning and then caught the Wellawaya bus at about 2pm. Bus was mega full (it was a Sunday) and we didn't get a seat. It was hot and bumpy and we were happy to get of the bus after 1hr and a half. 

It was dry season so there wasn't much water, but the falls were impressive nonetheless. We didn't hang around too long at the bottom because it was a bit touristy. Instead we attempted the hike to the top, as described in the Lonely Planet (2012 edition). A young boy from the village volunteered to guide us along the way. To be honest we would have struggled without him, so we gave him 10Rs. ostensibly to buy school supplies. He put us on the right path and we scrambled up for 20min to the top. You should make sure to take plenty of water for the hike, and don't wear flip-flops. 

At the top we hoped to have the pools to ourselves, as we were hot and sweaty and just wanted to jump in the water. Surprisingly there were a few groups of locals (one getting a bit boozy), and some German girls attracting attention in their bikinis. We just took our boots off and cooled our feet off while chatting to the locals (apparently a family of wild elephants come here for a drink most days at around 6:30pm). 

Sadly we didn't go to the top of the actual falls, because we had to get the bus back to Haputale. It looked really cool and would probably make a great photo. 

The REAL HIGHLIGHT for me was in fact the bus ride back up to Haputale. Buses going up come approx. every 30min, and the last one is at 1830. It took us just over an hour to hike up, 20min at the top, and 45min to get back down, so we caught the bus at about 1720. There was plenty of space on the bus, and it was a magical journey through the forested hills overlooking the southern lowlands as the sun sets over the mountains. Keep your eyes peeled for macaques as you drive up!

Give yourself more time than we did if you're using public transport. Alternatively, if you have your own transport, take a torch with you, stay to see the elephants. :)

Enjoy Diyaluma !

review_text:
it's about an easy 30 minute trail path walk from the car park.

directions:

Facing the car park take the road left and follow it bearing right around the corner. After about 5 minutes you will come across and green and white gate (looks like private property drive going downhill). Go through the gate, or if it's locked you can walk around it. a few metres in front is a sign and take the path that leads right. it's a clear footpath the whole way and it leads through a field of long grass, not very steep. follow this trail for about 15/20 minutes and you will hear the waterfall. you will see a hut and follow the path to the right a few hundred metres. you will see the pools and the rest is pretty simple from there! Be careful the big rock you have to walk across is quite steep, some people were sliding down on their bums. 

its totally worth it even just to swim around the upper pools, they are beautiful. some points you can jump off ledges into, they're very deep. the Sri Lankan children are dare devils and very fun to watch. we didn't go down to the actual waterfall because we didn't have time, our taxi driver gave us 2 hours. but could have easily spent half a day here.

review_text:
Natural rock pools and waterfalls. 
We first visited the bottom of the falls by tuk tuk, then he drove us another 30 minutes to reach a property at the top. From here we walked about 20-30 minutes with the help of our tuk tuk driver pointing us in the right direction. People will ask to take you on a Â‘guidedÂ’ tour, our driver said not to do this because itÂ’s unsafe and costs a lot of money. The people offering tours are not guides and not have licenses.
You have to pay 100 rupee parking fee at the place you park your tuk tuk or scooter. After the walk we then reached the first rock pool and waterfall where you can bathe and jump down a big waterfall into a plunge pool. You can then ask some locals to direct you to a path that takes you to the edge of where the waterfall drops down 200 or so metres. 
Moderate fitness level recommended.

review_text: i and my family had a thoroughly enjoyable trip to this 170 m high waterfall . it is about 14 km from the hilly town of Haputale. The view moving out of the this town is captivating as it is situated on a ridge .  the bus trip from Haputale to the Diyaluma falls takes 45 minutes., going towards welawaya. The falls is  situated by the roadside with sprays falling onto the road . we took a walk thru the rubber plantation with many village homes enroute. there is a few paths leading up but one can always ask the village folks.  A young boy of 12 years became our guide and he is really well informed and fun to be with. we walked up  through temperate shrub land for about 45 minutes with many stops along the way to enjoy the views . At  the top it was pristine and gives a top of the world feeling looking down at the massive falls below.  many small falls are scattered around and provided much fun for my teenage childrem.  One can choose to explore further inland following the river but it was too tiring. there are  villagers selling coconuts and food  at the bottom of the falls.

One of the main attractions of the falls is the stunning views it offers, with water cascading down from a height of over 80 feet. Apart from the scenic views and playful monkeys, visitors can also take a refreshing swim in the cool waters of the pool at the base of the falls. The water is crystal clear, and the pool offers a great spot to cool off after a day of exploring the area.

In summary, Ravana Falls in Ella is a picturesque destination that offers breathtaking views, playful monkeys, and the opportunity to take a refreshing swim in the pool at the base of the falls. It's a great spot for nature lovers and adventure seekers alike, and it's definitely worth a visit when exploring the region.

review_text:
As other reviewers have said, these falls are quite impressive, and probably busy with tourists most of the time.

The view is nice and you can get some good photos, either from a distance or on the falls themselves.

Definitely need to be a bit careful when climbing over the rocks and pools.

There are some stalls where you can buy fruit and corn on the cob, and plenty of cheeky monkeys who you can feed !

Its a bit chaotic with traffic and tourist buses stopping all over the place, but then so is much of Sri Lanka ... but I mean that in a nice way, it all adds to the unique charm of this amazing, beautiful country.

We spent just over half an hour here, and to be honest that's probably all you would need.

If staying in Ella I would recommend a visit here would be on your itinerary.

review_text:
This is easily accessible and clearly visible from the main road, so you don't even need to get your toes wet!

We drove to the falls and were a little disappointed to find a parking attendant there asking for a parking fee on the public road!  It was only 50LKR and I noticed all the locals had been issued with the same ticket, so not much, just frustrating.

The falls are impressive and make for some excellent photos, you can even scramble across a small river just by the road to get some close up shots if you desire.

Having driven past on a few occasions during our time in Ella we noticed it always seems busy, so be prepared to have to wait in turn to get the 'perfect' shot!

Yukon Bil

review_text:
Ravana Waterfall is a popular sightseeing attraction in Sri Lanka. It is currently ranks as one of the widest falls in the country. The falls have been named after the legendary king Ravana, which is connected to the famous Indian epic, the Ramayana. According to legend, it is said that Ravana, who was the king of Sri Lanka at the time had kidnapped Queen Sita, and had hidden her in the caves behind this waterfall, now simply known as the Ravana Ella Cave.

The Ravana Waterfall can be viewed from the roadside. People try and climb the rocks for a closer view which is not advisable. As told by my Tuk Tuk driver, there were some death cases of tourist who tried to climb up the waterfall. The water is very cooling and you can take a bath if you want, but no place to change clothing. 

Tuk Tuk Driver Name: Jeewantha Madushan
Tuk Tuk Driver Contact: +94711296224

review_text: This place is certainly worth a stop if you're passing by, but I definitely wouldn't pay a tuk tuk to take me there. Yes it's impressive, yes it's beautiful, but it was packed with people, and there's really no place to just sit and soak in the feel of the place. Five or ten minutes, a few photos, and you're on your way. On the plus side, it's free. Also, I rode there from Ella on a scooter, and the ride itself was beautiful, enjoyable ride even without a waterfall. Beware of the beggers and of the snack sellers. I was charged an absolutely extortionist price on a coconut and some roti. One last note - some people hike in to the top of the falls. Perhaps this would've been a better experience?

Yes of course there are a lot of tourists, it's an incredible piece of nature!!! Go there to see this natural phenomenon and appreciate it for what it is instead of complaining about the tourists. If the tourism is such a huge issue for you then visit in the morning 8am. We arrived before 9 and there was nobody there, other tourists started arriving from 9:30ish. 
This isn't a 'day out' thing, you can't swim in the main part of the waterfall, it's just a passing site which is truly beautiful and well worth a quick detour. Also, the bus from Ella is 25-30 rupee, roughly 20 minutes. (You can get any bus leaving Ella south)

review_text: I had a chance to visit the famous Ravana Falls in Ella during the month of January. I was visiting Ella with my friends, and when we were leaving from Ella towards the Udawalawe sanctuary, we decided to stop by the falls. The falls are beautiful and especially in January when the waters were more free flowing than during the rest of the year. The falls are of mythological significance for me, so I was truly delighted to have been able to come here. It is believed in Hindu mythology that Ravana had abducted and kept Sita in the cave behind the falls. The falls are crowded so do plan your visit, keeping in mind that there are many locals and tourists here. Definitely worth a visit.

The waterfall was 2km away from my hostel and on my way to Ella, so I decided to give it a try and visit the Ravana Falls.
It's free and there are a lot of small food and souvenir dealers in front where you can buy fresh fruits, drinks and rocks/souvenirs.
The waterfall itself is impressive and very powerful. Wouldn't take a bad in there.

review_text: Again a hard place to review. It depends on what you like. I knew that the tree wouldn't be big or look particularly special, but if you expect something extraordinary you'll be dissapointed. What is special about the place is that the tree is taken from the original tree where the Buddha is said to have achieved enlightenment. Just that it is a 2000 year old tree is quite amazing, no matter what it looks like. Also to get to observe the reverence the locals pay the tree is fascinating. I suppose it is sometimes loud, confusing and the offerings litter the place. But as long as you know why you go it might be a good experience.

review_text:
It is the totally relaxed feeling that one enjoys at this sacred place of worship venerated by the Buddhists from all over the world. Early in the morning surroundings were very tranquil and comfortable, before the area got warmer with the days hot sun and before the premise got filled with larger numbers of devotees.  Environment was very calm and conducive for a moment in silent meditation.  Entire precinct has so many Bodhi trees escorting the sacred Bodhi tree which is at the highest terrace. It is known to be the oldest surviving planted tree in the world with a recorded history.  

The granite balustrades are very attractive with beautiful motifs engraved in to them.

Any case if you want to go out after visiting this place, you can try Dhambulla side or Jaffna side or even polonnaruwa side after visiting this place. The divinity here must be experienced by one and all.
A must see in Lankan tour

review_text:
It is impossible to cover all the sites in a single day, as there are so many places to see.
The museum is small but has a good collection of artefacts from the ruins of Anuradhapura. There is a gallery showing the original form of various ruins when they were discovered, and their post-restoration form.
There are so many stupas scattered around a vast area. All the stupas are huge that one must be spellbound thinking how they were built so long ago. 
Then there is Samadhi stupa. The highlight of Anuradhapura is the Mahabodhi tree, which is the offspring of the original Mahabodhi tree from Bodhgaya, under which Goutama achieved Moksha!
A visit to Anuradhapura is a must while visiting Srilanka.

Thousands of devotees visit this place everyday and there is dress code and shoe and hat not allowed. It's believed that Princess Sangamitra, sister of Mahinda who introduced Buddhism in Sri Lanka brought the cutting of Bodhi tree from India to this place. This place is most important religious centre for people of this country. Since this is a spiritual place one should maintain proper decorum and dignity here
A must visit in this ancient city.

review_text:
Seeing the bodi tree and temple complex was really interesting. This was the start of our tour of the cultural triangle and it makes a great place to start. 

Our driver suggested a guide which we took for 2000r and it was well worth it to understand the symbolism and rituals s week as the history which you can get from any guidebook. Understanding the moon and guardstones for example set us up for appreciating all the other temples we saw and was a good starting point for our  kids aged 13 and 10.

The site is super busy with tourists but also regular worshippers and that's what made it so interesting compared with other less busy temples.  Stay and watch the processions and you will learn about local/religious customs.

On a practical note as it's so hot and you need to remove your shoes, kids (and sometimes adults) can wear socks so bring a pair with. You need to cover shoulders and below the knee so having a sarong in your bag is very handy if you don't want to wear trousers. You can't wear hats or caps either.

review_text:
Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi is the most sacred place in Anuradhapura. It is a raised platform in Mahameghawana Gardens which contains a branch of a fig tree (called Maha Bodhi in Buddhism) under which Mahatma Buddha is stated to have attained enlightenment (nirwan) in Buddha Gaya, India. 
This tree (sapling) was planted here in 249 BC and is known as the oldest surviving tree in the world which has a known date of plantation. It was brought here by Sangamitta, daughter of Emperor Ashoka of India with great pomp and show 2500 years ago. Emperor Ashoka was himself present in the celebrations held at the Indian port of Tamalitta in which this sapling was dispatched to Sri Lanka in a ship. Sri Lankan King Devanam Piyatissa himself received the sapling at the Sri Lankan port with great honor and pageantry. While standing under this tree, I thought that it was like a Â‘peepelÂ’ tree. For about two billion people of the world, it is the most sacred tree and is called Â“Roots of Paradise on EarthÂ” by Buddhists.

review_text:
Such a beautiful site, the Bodhi tree also neighbors other attractions seen in Anuradhapura such as Lovamahapaya ( the stone ruin pillars ) and Ruwanwelisseya Dagoba ( the large white building that normally represents the main attraction in Anuradhapura ) 

Our day was simply amazing due to one key factor, our Tuk Tuk driver "Lalith Priyashantha" This kind man is the only reason I have started my trip adviser account so I could blog about his services to us. 

We arrived at 9:05am and only had until 3:30pm ,all other drivers only offered to drive us to each site. He took us around like we were family and explained his culture and the Buddhist religion, history and meanings behind every single detail at each location. He made us feel safe, welcomed and very comfortable. 

As we only had a short time we needed a place to store our bags so he called his shop owner friends and organized everything for us. 

Here comes the crescendo, he wanted to do it all for only $15 AUD which is 1500 rupees . A FULL 6 hours of driving us:  to get food ,storing our bags and even including the prices for the attractions we viewed for well over half the going price of everyone else ( $40aud for a tour guide ) he knew EVERYTHING about each site, down to the year it was made, who made it the history and the stories behind everything, he cared about us learning his culture. We could not have asked for a better 6 hours in this beautiful ancient city. 

By the end of it my girlfriend and I were so happy with his service we gave him $30 AUD because how special he made the day, he WOULDN'T EVEN ACCEPT THE MONEY !! He asked us if we were students, we told him we weren't and that we had full time jobs just so he'd take the offer. 

His contact numbers are :

+94 777 951719
+94 7111 24601
+94 768502504
You can also contact him on Facebook via his name above 

Feel free to contact me for any information about the day :)

The sand covered grounds are a relief for your bare feet.

Definitely a powerful feeling while visiting.

review_text:
The great Sri Maha Bodhi is one of the top places a tourist has to visit in the sacred city of Anuradhapura. Mind the dress code please since this is a temple. There is a car park quite close to location and we walked a short distance to a side entrance where two senior ladies operate a shoe-keeping hut. We gave them 50 LRK for two pairs. Then you walk in and absorb the serene surroundings while watching pilgrims pay their respects. There is no fee to get in.

Once we were done, returned to collect our shoes and walked a path towards the other wonderful place, Ruwanwelisaya Dagoba. Do not feed the monkeys or the stray canines for health reasons.

Not just one of the very important monument of the Sri Lankan early kingdoms and buddhism history! It's a really living sacred place now.
The world's oldest documented tree, under which Buddha meditated and enlightened. One branch of this tree in 288 BC was brought from India by Sangamitta - the daughter of King Asoka. 

Don't forget, hat and shoes forbidden inside the sacred area. You will need sun protection cream, and exchange socks is very practical. The reason not just the dirty floor (these places wasn't really dirty), very often the stone very hot without shoes.
I recommend you, before the visit you must read some historical fact about this place, will be interesting the visit!

review_text: In SriLanka, a Buddhist religious country, people worship this tree as a sacred place. This tree is a sapling from the historical Bodhi tree, where Buddha enlightened. It was planted here in 288 BC and is the oldest living human planted tree in the world. (But the oldest living tree is in California USA, is 5064 years old). The tree is surrounded by thick walls, on top of that golden fence also there. Just for anyone it's an ancient tree surrounded by historical statues, walls etc, but for Buddhists this place is a very holy site. My personal opinion if I visit a place for the ancient value, I have to see the place on my own way, not distracted by other people. Already I traveled all over the world, and visited most of the ancient monuments. But here religious value distracted the real ancient value. I am disappointed.

review_text: Bodhi Tree - the seat of Vajrashan which provided the shelter to Siddharth Gautam to rise as the Lord Buddha. The most defining tree which historically changed and alter the pace of time and crossed horizons and boundaries of class, caste, creed, culture, race and regions. The tree is magnificent, its persona is symbolic to wisdom-hood. Mere looking at it takes you to millennia at a time when it must only have been a tree, just another tree in the forests of Gaya sheltering thousands of sadhus and monks who were searching of knowledge, enlightenment and peace. With Rahul and Sanghmtra sent by Emperor Ashok himself, who planted the tree at the present site of Anuradhapura is frequently visited place in Sri Lanka. It holds immense importance as it provides the unbroken chain with the original tree of Gaya that was burnt during the 7th century A.D. I have found the site very peaceful and will encourage tourists and pilgrims to visit at the right time and it is one of the most revered and holiest of the sites.

Namo Buddhaya, Budu Saranai, Theruwan Saranai.

May all beings be happy and well.

review_text: To experience the immensity, history and beauty of this complex of temples, palaces and museums, one may want to fortify themselves and plan to tour for a good part of a day.  We visited on a Sunday during which multitudes of pilgrims dressed in white were bringing flowers and offerings to the ancient temple Mahavihara, the site of the Sacred Bo Tree.  Here is a good place to sit or pause to absorb the spiritual meaning of this site for the Sri Lankan people.  After visiting here, my guide led me to the following main sites within this complex:  Ruvansalisaya Dogoba, Jetavana Museum, Jetavana Dagoba, LUNCH (outside of the complex), Lankarama Abhayagir Dogoba and the Twin Ponds (aka Kuttam Pokuna).  To cover this large area you will need a car/tuk tuk or marathon stamina to go on foot.  In the end, this visit was a 5 star experience.

"A twig coming from the Bodhi tree (ficus religiosa) under which the Buddha found enlightenment was planted over 2000 years ago. And since then this tree was always cherished." - this is the story or legend oft this tree 
It's amazing to see this tree and imagine that it had been standing here for thousands of years.
And it's definitely very interesting to see that nothing has changed, people are coming in masses, all clothed in white (the traditional colour if you go to the temple) with flowers - mostly lotus flowers or water lilies - to bring as offerings. As this tree is important to every Buddhist worldwide I've also seen a large group of Japanese people bringing there offerings. 
Around the tree there are some buildings actually constructed with Japanese money - you can read the memorial plaques.

review_text: The bodhi tree itself is not that impressive. It is not particularly good looking or graceful. Its branches are very gnarled, its bark is very rough, and it just shows LOTS of signs of aging. Course, what do you expect for a tree that's hundreds of years old? But the sheer historical significance of it is enough to make any visit to the tree absolutely compulsory for anyone visiting Sri Lanka. It is, after all, more or less the heart and soul of the country. This tree was descended from the very tree that Buddha meditated under and as such is absolutely sacred to Sri Lankans, who, in my honest opinion, seem the most conservative and committed Buddhists I have ever encountered. One cannot truly understand Sri Lankan culture until one is truly aware of how important Buddhism is and how hard Sri Lankans have fought to latch onto it. And it is really hard to get that awareness without beholding this most sacred of Sri Lankan treasures.

review_text:
Sacred Sri Maha Bodiya, 2,300 year old site - Visited this National Heritage site as part of a 17-day Bunnik tour.
Note: Shoulders & knees covered + Rupees for the person who looks after your shoes + you might like to have an old pair of socks to wear as the ground does get quite hot + 200 Rupee entry charge.
Fold the leaf of the Bodi tree and it represents many shapes = Stupa, Dagaba, Pagoda, etc. 
An interesting site to visit.

review_text:
Having visited Bodh Gaya it was fascinating to see the "son" or "daughter" of the original tree. This is older than the one now in place in Bihar where the Buddha was enlightened. Yet it is also protected behind railings and propped up with gold struts. In addition there is a guardian force comprised of those descendants of locals who protected the tree during various incursions. 

At the time of our visit there was a pilgrimage by the military comprised solely of officers. It did seem slightly incongruous with the juxtaposition of peace/enlightenment with arms.

review_text: Local people throng hatless and shoeless in the hot sun bearing lotus blooms to perform ancient rituals that seem to have nothing to do with the Buddhism taught to Western consumers. Set among the ruins and other Buddhist sites both ancient and modern, the tree was purported to have been brought over from India as the original the Enllightened One sat under. Worth seeing and free but not so the $25 for a few crumbilng stones and a very ordinary trio of "museums" with artifacts that look more interesting in the gift stalls lining the way to one of the many stupas. Tropical countries and preservation of what looks like sand stone is I would have thought an impossibility. Is there anything to restore - doesn't look like it!!!! The stupas are intact but do not look ancient and no one could tell me what they were for and what was inside. Thank goodness for Google! Tip - get a guide that knows something and watch out - they lay in wait at the station and make promises they don't keep.

review_text:
The area is that much extensive: not to manage without a car. It starts with the Bodhi Tree and all the worshipping people (after having passed a security check!). Then you go out for the ruins an the famous twin pools. Lots of small stores offering (handcrafted) souvenirs, food, drinks...lots of local people, less tourists than in Polonnaruwa. Ruins more destroyed than in Polonnaruwa, and widely spread (under shadowy trees). One needs more imagination to "see" the oldest king's city. There is a small museum: kind of weird - and kind of charming.
The drive from Habarana might take up to 3 hrs (one way). 
You can combine Anurahapura with Mihintale.

review_text:
One of the worldÂ’s oldest recorded trees and certainly the most revered, visited by buddhists from all around the world.  It is said to have grown from a cutting of the original tree under which the Buddha attained Enlightenment in India. The tree has been tended for 23 centuries and cuttings have been taken and planted in temples throughout the island. 

There is no entrance charge as far as we could tell but security here is tighter than at other attractions in Sri Lanka (a result of the bombings in 1998) and there separate lines for men and women. This is a sacred place so, as for all temples, you must dress respectfully (legs and shoulders covered).  You need to remove hats and shoes. You are allowed to keep socks on and I would recommend this as it is a bit of a walk to get to the tree at the centre of the complex.  

The site was very tranquil and it was interesting to visit for the history.  You need to bear in mind that you will not be able to get a close up view of the tree as it is enclosed by a wall and railings.  Only two branches of the original tree remain, and these are supported by props. This is the main reason we personally didn't feel able to score higher than a '3'.  Devotees on a pilgrimage will obviously feel very differently.

review_text:
We visited the Sri Maha Bodhi at the end of our day cycling 30km around Anuradhapura. While its undoubtedly a very holy place, when we came it wasn't particularly busy and the atmosphere that guide books and other reviewers write about seemed to be lacking. But it was still good to appreciate the age and significance of the tree and wider site. Perhaps a visit later in the day would have been more atmospheric as guide books suggest.
When we visited the main entrance was closed so we had to walk round to another entrance (not too far). There was no entrance fee and we were able to leave our shoes for free outside.

review_text:
Visited this with our guide (Sri Lankan guide, not spiritual guide!!).  He reports that it is one of the most holy places in Sri Lanka.  No bare shoulders, and there is upmost respect for the temple and it's statues.  He reports that people wait all day for one of the leaves, from the tree, to drop.  It's meant to bring very good fortune.  
The tree itself was having some work done on it so couldn't see the trunk.  There were masses of people bringing offerings for the tree and to pray. review_text:
As others have said, it's just a tree - but it is a hugely important and sacred one if you are a Buddhist. The amount of care and attention that it has received over the centuries has been remarkable, and all carefully recorded too. It's also worth a visit even if you're not a Buddhist.
However, as others have also said, the extra charge for entry is unnecessary. The Sri Lankan National sport of relieving overseas tourists of their money does get extremely wearing after a while. It's like having someone's fingers perpetually in your wallet. Apparently, there used to be a single payment that got you in to all the ancient sites, but that was discontinued and now each site gets to make it's own charges. Hmmmm. Quite a backward step, I think.

review_text: The branch of bo tree was brought here some 2,300 years ago directly from India by Sanghamitta thero, daughter of Emperor Ashoka.  Although the tree was not very large or bushy in appearance, it has its spiritual value.  As such many worshipers came and made their blessings and offerings and the whole area appeared to be peaceful but lively.  Worshipers could have their lunch in the surrounding area after the pilgrimage visit.

review_text:
Ancient city is amazing,  $25 entry. Can get a tuc tuc anywhere in the new town and do the ancient city in a couple of hours or much cheaper way is to rent a bicycle for the day. It took me almost a whole day to see all the sites in old the city by bicycle ask your hotel for a map. I stayed in Melbourne Hotel, cheap, nice, they have bicycles, see review on Melbourne Hotel. List and brief review of the sights I went to in The Ancient city:
    
Bodhi Tree Temple (The Sri Maha Bodhiya), this was the main thing I wanted to see, bit dissapointing, you can not get close to the tree, big wall around it. it is not possible to drive up to the temple, and one must go through a metal detector before entering the complex. Shoes can be left near the entrance. It is polite to leave a tip.
Ruwanwelisaya: the oldest and most largest stupa at Anuradhapura, has , been fully restored, painted white, and is currently a centre of worship. 
The Archaeolgy Museum, interesting, ask at the entrance for a museum guide, it is free. Showcases many of the artifacts found at the site
The Folk Museum: Showcases the archaeology of Anuradhapura from a more folk perspective.
Jetavana: Large stupa 
The Citadel: This was the secular centre of the city. 
The Moonstone. This moonstone is of particular note, for its size and impressive decoration.
