review_text:
I made an 8-day-trip to Sri Lanka from 8/11/12 to 15/11/12.  On my seventh day in Sri Lanka,  I arrived at the Anuradhapura Railway station at 4.30am.  Earlier, on my sixth day in Sri Lanka,i.e. 13/11/2012, I had boarded a 4.30pm-train from Hatton railway station to Colombo Fort Raiway station.  

Upon reaching Colombo at 10pm, I hopped into the 10.30pm train to the north of Colombo and reached Anuradhapura, one of the ancient capitals of Sri Lanka which is famous for its well-preserved ruins of ancient Sri Lankan civilization, at 4.30am, i.e. after a 12-hours-train-journey from Hatton. Anuradhapura is one of the ancient capitals of Sri Lanka, world famous for its well preserved ruins of the Great Sri Lankan Civilization. The Civilization which was built upon this city was one of the greatest civilizations of Asia and in the world. The city is now a UNESCO heritage site.  Today this ancient city of Sri Lanka, which is sacred to the Buddhist world, and which its surrounding monasteries covers an area of over sixteen square miles ( 40 kmÂ²) and is one of the world's major archaeological sites.

After a morning quick tour of the Ancient Ruins & Holy City of Anuradhapura, including Thuparamaya where the collarbone of Buddha is enshrined, Isurumuniya(a picturesque rock temple) and The Sacred Jaya Siri Maha Bodhi at Mahaviharaya/ Mahameghavana Park which is recorded as the oldest surviving historical tree in the world, I took a bus back to Colombo from Anuradhapura New Town at 1pm. 

The oldest surviving tree in the world, The Sacred Jaya Siri Maha Bodhi at Mahaviharaya/ Mahameghavana Park, Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka, is believed to have been propagated from the original Bodhi tree.  This original Bodhi Tree, also known as Bo (from the Sinhalese Bo), was a large and very old Sacred Fig tree (Ficus religiosa) located in Bodh Gaya (about 100 km (62 mi) from Patna in the Indian state of Bihar), under which Siddhartha Gautama, the spiritual teacher later known as Gautama Buddha, is said to have achieved enlightenment, or Bodhi.  According to Buddhist texts the Buddha, after his Enlightenment, spent a whole week in front of the tree, standing with unblinking eyes, gazing at it with gratitude.  The term "Bodhi Tree" is also widely applied to currently existing trees, including the Bodhi tree in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka, which has a great significance in the history of Buddhism.  

This Bodhi tree in Anuradhapura is widely mentioned in Mahavamsa.  While not considered a canonical religious text, the Mahavamsa is an important text in Theravada Buddhism. It covers the early history of religion in Sri Lanka, beginning with the time of Siddhartha Gautama, the founder of Buddhism.  According to the Mahavamsa, the Sri Maha Bodhi in Sri Lanka was planted in 288 BC, making it the oldest verified specimen of any angiosperm. In this year (the twelfth year of King Asoka's reign) the right branch of the Bodhi tree was brought by Sanghamitt? to Anur?dhapura and placed by Dev?n?mpiyatissa his left foot in the Mah?meghavana. The Buddha, on his death bed, had resolved five things, one being that the branch which should be taken to Ceylon should detach itself. From Gay?, the branch was taken to P?taliputta, thence to T?malitt?, where it was placed in a ship and taken to Jambukola, across the sea; finally it arrived at Anuradhapura, staying on the way at Tivakka. Those who assisted the king at the ceremony of the planting of the Tree were the nobles of K?jarag?ma and of Candanag?ma and of Tivakka.  According to the Mahavamsa, branches from the Bodhi trees of all the Buddhas born during this kalpa were planted in Ceylon (Sri Lanka) on the spot where the sacred Bodhi tree stands today in Anur?dhapura.

Later, after completing my visit to the other attractions of the Ancient Ruins & Holy City of Anuradhapura I took a bus back to Colombo from Anuradhapura New Town at 1pm and reached the Pettah bus station in Colombo at 8pm to put-up a night at a nearby low cost lodge, i.e. Classic Inn in Panchikawatte Road before leaving for the Bandaranaike Airport at 6am of 15/11 to catch the 12.55pm flight back to Malaysia.

review_text:
The surrounding grounds and trees make this an interesting cultural place to visit .. You really need to understand the meaning of religion to Buddhists to appreciate the peace that comes to the followers .. The tree as described is the oldest anywhere, but worth taking a look it ..
The temple itself probably looked much grander in its earlier days but historically has meaning .. Statues around the area are visible for all to see .. I didnt have a guide to pass me any information but still enjoyed wandering around ..
As everywhere else around Sri Lanka monkeys run freely, and might try to grab your bags .. Dont carry any food or they will chase you, otherwise will just leave you alone ..
Its also pretty hot and you will have to walk around barefoot so wear socks to keep your feet protected from the ground ..

review_text:
Let me create a laundry list of pros and cons explaining my poor rating:

Pros:
+ The surrounding park area is nice and relatively peaceful, filled with monkeys and chirping birds.

Cons:
- Touts, touts, touts.  As is endemic throughout Sri Lanka, you find yourself having to stave off wannabe tour guides, and overly aggressive "park attendants".  There was a place left to deposit shoes before entering the holy site, with no sign mentioning a fee.  Within seconds of leaving, I was aggressively hounded for a full 5 minutes by a tout demanding a ridiculous "donation" or "fee" for leaving my shoes outside.  When I politely declined, he left for a moment, then returned to demand a 100 rupee note.  I politely explained that I had paid thousands of rupees to enter the park and grounds (itself an exorbitant 3125 rupees) and that I wasn't in the mood to deposit 100 rupee notes in each and every site I visited, or to every tout who crossed my path - I would have easily been short another 2000 rupees for that day alone.  I ended up, perhaps immaturely, offering a small handful of 2 rupee coins.  He eventually backed off.  This collection of experiences ruined what should have otherwise been a peaceful visit.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
Our guide took us in the evening to see the great buddha tooth - we queued for over 30mins in the heat (no AC inside and lots of people) with people trying to push infront of us! When finally the awful loud procession music stopped, the queue moved forward to see the tooth - except is behind about 2 distance walls of glass and you're not allowed to stop so I had no idea what i was looking at, honestly comical. And locals leave offering to the 'buddha tooth' that the monks love im sure. 
The temple itself is lovely, lots of detail, nice paintings but don't go with the crowds in the evening its not worth it. Enjoy it at a quieter time to take it all in. 
(Note - there is a place to store shoes outside as you have to take them off so pack socks as the floor is dirty) 
Theres also a weird room with a huge stuffed elephant that the president or someone loved. After going to the elephant freedom project sanctuary earlier in the week (highly recommend) it felt cruel he had this as a pet in his garden.

review_text:
If you are not a religious person that understands where to go, when and what's happening there at that moment, you won't enjoy the place much, neither the ceremony that happens at the place when it's open to the public. Not to mention that the place is a maze and it took me and my boyfriend some time to get to the entrance that we needed. Different prices for locals and for tourists are present also here, as everywhere else at Sri Lanka. 
The ceremony is a mass activity where a lot of people pushes themselves to a certain place at the temple, and you push yourself to get there also, since you don't know why are others pushing themselves so much. The fact it, the religious people want to give their offerings to the temple and to Buddha. You will end up in a room where everyone is packed, waiting to get to the room for offerings, where you won't get. Inside the temple was very busy but everyone was friendly and the atmosphere was nice . 
The queue to see the relic was well organised and went down quickly.
 
Altogether a very nice experience .

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
Planning the visit is extremely important- given the ceremonies & limited window when doors are opened. We hired a guide & got there around 5.45pm- just in time for us to enter the central premises & visit other shrines. Guide helped us navigate & explained the different parts of the temple in details. 

Some tips for fellow travellers- 
1. The tooth relic is not for public viewing everyday- only taken our during ceremony. Instead we get to see the golden caskets holding the relic from 6.45pm in the evening. So get there on the right time! 
2. Several shrines are present inside temple premises, like Crystal budhha, Hari Krishna, original manuscripts, museum & royal elephant memorial. Taking a guide is best to navigate & not miss out key sights. 
3. Golden Canopy above the relic is not to be missed- stunning sight in the evening light! 
4. Moonstone entrances, beautiful paintings & carvings- despite the rush, take sometime to admire the place.
5. There are some ground rules for taking photographs- No selfies, no photos showing back to the Buddha statues, etc. So be mindful of them, while enjoying the temple. 

Entry fee for SAARC members is 1500 SLR per person. Ticket counter is next to the temple on side of the lake. Would suggest so spend atleast 1.5hrs to cover the entire temple.

Out guide took us right up to the front of the line to peer into the vault containing the Tooth Relic.  I was told that this was unheard of and that we were so unbelievably fortune to be on front and to have seen the opening of the religious vault.
 The territory is absolutely amazing.
Be prepared to show your Passport upon entry through the security check ooint iutside the temple area.  It is mandatory!

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
Visited on 18 February 2020 at 10.30am

Dress decently. Very important is to wear cloths which cover the body and legs. No shorts or sleeveless tops allowed. For hot days carry cap/scarves. Please note.

On Kandy sightseeing, this was the first stopover of the day. The entry tickets were arranged as part of the package which included a CD and souvenir. The location of this temple is beside a lake and approach road has many colonial buildings.

The temple complex has many attraction within. Museum, floors, different portions dedicated to rituals and related things.

Photos are allowed but not selfies. Respect the rules.
This attraction will have long walks so suggest take a guide along and senior citizens must take rest breaks.

There is a souvenir shop inside the Museum complex selling authentic Sri Lankan craft at appropriate prices. Authenticity is guaranteed.  Do use this opportunity to take few products back to your country. I bought Elephants (SLR 350), key rings (SLR 80) and fridge magnets  (SLR 200).

Beautiful flower shops will amaze you when you exit the temple.

You will feel a calmness and happy after visiting this place.

Go and enjoy .

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
We joined the queues during morning prayer. There are two queues to get in: one for the men and one for the women. Like most things in life, the men's line moved faster. This is mainly due to two things: 1) most women carry bags that need searching (most men don't) 2) the women perhaps face a little more scrutiny over what they can wear and must cover-up. Shoulders and legs need to be covered, so make sure you have a light scarf and sarong. Men too should carry a sarong to put on although some western males it seemed were managing to get through in shorts.

Once inside make sure you follow the tourist crowds to the right and enter the temple through the tourist entry. Here you leave your shoes, you will be expected to tip after collection. 

Inside, at prayer, this place is busy. At times you are moved along with the crowd. The locals are of course queuing to leave gifts and to pray so don't feel too bad if you 'skip' queues and glide past those locals waiting on the stairs.

The relic itself can't be seen. Instead, you can peer into the golden shrine where it is stored, but at this point in the temple, the crowds are at their busiest so you main only manage a cursory glance.

The best part about the temple is exploring the grounds and additional rooms and buildings. The carvings and sculptures of Budha are beautiful, and in most spaces, you can take photos. Just be mindful of people worshipping and not to take pictures with your back to any Budha statue.

The grounds of the temple are beautiful, and there is an elephant on the site too, which is used in ceremonies. Although, it is clearly an old elephant and seeing it so heavily chained doesn't make for the best view.

At night time, around the temple and Lake, there is a cacophony of noise as bats and birds come to roost in their hundreds. It is the most spectacular site in Kandy and a must-see.

The museum of World Buddhism, which is on the site is also worth a visit, and with a tourist ticket to the temple, you have access.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
Always wanted to visit here as a highly regarded religious site. Had to wear a sarong as we tuned up in shorts. Immediately when we went in a male latched on to us to give us a guided tour. Although he gave much detail he was a bit irritating and hard to shake off. To be fair he showed us everything we wanted to see eg the temple of the tooth and other things in other temples including a stuffed elephant we wouldn't have known about. Temple was being cleaned when we visited so you ended up with very wet feet. 
I asked why flowers were such a big thing and was told that the Buddha didn't want material things like money or gold so flowers were preferred. I was slightly bemused when on leaving the temple he asked for money. When I offered money I was told it wasn't enough. We eventually settled on 1000 rupees. The person holding the shoes also wanted money so the lack of materialism inside didn't stretch to the staff.
Glad I went and would recommend if you have an interest in this sort of thing.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This is another UNESCO World Heritage Site with interesting history and background. The site is located in city centre of Kandy right in front of Kandy Lake. Tooth Relic is believed to be sacred for Buddhism and the royal family was responsible for the safekeeping of the tooth relic. It is believed to be brought from Anuradhapura to Kandy Kingdom. Two storeys building was constructed for safekeeping the tooth relic. But the building was destroyed several times. Each time it was restored whenever it was destroyed. There will be ceremony everyday for the blessings by the devotees. We visited around late afternoon and waited for the ceremony around 6pm plus. Interesting cultural sights, but be prepared for uncontrollable crowds and haphazard situation during the ceremony. The tooth relic is said to be kept within a gold plated ornament, hence it cannot be seen by anyone even during the ceremony. The international Buddhism Museum within the compound is worth to check out too for the interesting architecture and interior design. Overall, it is still worth the entrance fee of LKR1,500 per person and appropriate attire is required and tight security check at the entrance.

review_text: When you arrive you are sent to foreign visitors section. They ask for a donation when you go back to get your shoes which i think is unnecessary after your entrance fee.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
We are a couple in early 30s with 9 and 10yr old daughters.
Firstly we hadn't dressed appropriately so had to rent sarongs to cover up. The guy was nice enough but still 400rs down.
It's a bit of a faff to get in, we went through one lot if security then you get your bag checked again before you go in. We had a tip off from the sarong guy that they take away your cigarettes and lighters so I hid them well in the bag.
You have to put your shoes in a shoe storage area. Other reviews are correct about them asking for a donation, I was aware of this and just played deaf when they asked me, I had to assist my child... Oh and don't think you can put your shoes in your bag - that's not allowed! 
The ticket machines don't give change so you do have to have the right amount on you. There was an attendant who said we didn't have to pay for the children which was good and we didn't have the right change but he helped a guy behind us which then gave us the right change. So that was kind.

First off you walk on boiling hot pavement in bear feet. Then I guess the rest is interesting if you like architecture and religious history. As atheists we were a little bemused by all of it. There's nothing to tell you where the tooth is. We assumed we were in the right place by the people praying on the floor... But there's no signs etc and we didn't have a guide.
There's a museum which was a little interesting.
The saddest part is the taxidermied elephant. Poor thing was captured and kept for a good 50years before he died. He's now stuffed in a glass cabinet. There's a photo timeline of his life since capture but it doesn't have any translation so we don't really know the story...

If you like this sort if thing and are in Kandy then maybe pay it a visit... But I definitely wouldn't drive to Kandy for a day trip just for that. In my husbands words "I wouldn't go again even if it was outside my front door".

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: Hard to review. It is a place of devotion and spirituality for the local buddhists and it has an interesting history, the tooth. They don't show the actual tooth to the public anymore, maybe once a decade according to the guidebook. If you go here don't expect to we wow'ed by the tooth. I enjoyed the Buddhism history museum (included in the ticket) and the light during dusk outside. I found it interesting just to observe the local absolute devotion to a relic, real or not, (no offence intended) and the ceremony going on where you can glimpse the inner shrine for a moment. It is also interesting to walk through the museum of the tooth relic and read the signs inside the new shrine. It will cost you 2000 rupees to go inside + some tip to the shoe guy. Remember to cover your knees and shoulders (both men and women). I would say that if you find the local traditions and religion interesting it is a place to visit, otherwise maybe not.

review_text:
This place brings sanctity to Kandy. It is called Dalada Maligawa in the local language. The temple is golden-roofed. Locals and tourists visit the temple for prayers with flowers and incense throughout the day. The temple keeps the tooth relic of the Buddha in its main shrine. The premises also houses several shrines, museums, and temples. Museums include the International Buddhist Museum, Dalada Museum, Raja Tusker Museum, and Royal Palace Archaeological Museum 

The temple is open for tourists from 5: 30 AM to 8:00 PM. Pujas happen at three different timings Â– 5:30 AM to 6:45 AM, 9:30 AM to 11:45 AM, and 6:30 PM to 8:00 PM. It's advised to dress conservatively and wear outfits that cover your shoulders and legs.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The holy of holies for Sri Lankan Buddhists, the visit is a must though perhaps for tourists not at one of the scheduled pujas when you feel the crush of devotees attending to pray and offer food. If you want the atmosphere of a puja, drum beating will announce its start and continue throughout, the actual ceremony performed by the monks behind the closed temple doors with massive elephant tusks in front of it. The highlight is the ever so brief time you have looking at the large gold casket in the distance, devotees handing food and flowers over to the monks. Visit the library with its Buddhist texts on palm leaf and dazzle at some of the jewel-encrusted vases and the like. In another area you can get a history of the tooth relic over 21 panels. As you exit, the grounds are rather pretty. While there are elements of the visit that will leave you dissatisfied, try to soak up the overall atmosphere. You have to go through security.

review_text: Colourful Temple with lots of history attached.  Worth seeing. We were unable to time our visit with the ceremonial Puja, but found the museum really interesting.  Don't miss a visit to the Tusker museum to see the life sized Elephant Raja (now preserved) who carried the sacred tooth for over 50 years.  You have to remove your shoes to enter but socks are allowed.  I would highly recommend you bring a pair of socks to wear as the ground can be a bit stoney and unpleasant for bare feet! We arranged a day visit here through Ceylon Escapes.  Our lovely driver Peter was so helpful and informative and brought us on a most enjoyable day out including a visit to a family run tea factory, lunch in the Olde Empire Cafe, Temple of Tooth and finished with cultural dance. BRilliant day out and thanks to Ceylon Escapes and  our wonderful driver Peter for making it all so enjoyable.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We arrived here at about midday and it was extremely crowded.  Our guide took us round to the various important parts of the temple and we felt very humbled to be sharing this place with hundreds of worshippers who were there for a very serious reason to offer flowers and pray - we appreciated how much this meant to the people who had come far and wide to be here. I felt almost like an intruder and we didn't loiter too long.  We did see the place where the sacred tooth is stored but we didn't get to see the daily ceremony where the door is opened.  Apparently it is inside several caskets and is now never seen.  The building and contents are beautiful and it was lovely to see and briefly be part of this important place.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
Religious site with a Buddha tooth relic with a newer building built over the original relic casket. Been told that at twice a day the casket door will be opened for special prayers. The temple was built circa  4th century AD. 

When we visited there were so many locals sitting on the floor for prayers. They offered white flowers for prayers. 

The tooth relic was brought over by the King and Queen, and she hid the relic in her hair, when the capital was moved to Kandy. 

Every year in August, the Festival of the Tooth is one of the grandest festivals in Sri Lanka and in the Buddhist world. So we went early the next day. It is quite a walk from the main gate and the surroundings are really beautiful. Once we got in, we were surprised at the people inside. They were mainly devotees. We had to inch our way up through a crowded staircase to the main relic. I felt claustrophobic.You are allowed just a second and then you have to move. It was a relief to get out.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
Get your information and timing right if you wish to visit this ancient and holy place. The door to the main relic is opened at specific timings, so check before you plan your trip. While the doors to the main shrine are closed, the crowds start building up, so if crowds scare you this place is an absolute no. Although the crowds are quite well behaved. 
Be sure to cover your shoulders and legs else shell out money to locals for giving you wraps etc. 
You need to buy tickets at the entrance from kiosks which need exact change. You will need to remove and deposit shoes at the counters outside. Once inside it gives you the feel of an ancient place but well preserved and maintained. Lots of devotees with offerings throng the temple every day. 
Do not miss the oil lamps lighted outside by numerous devotees. You are allowed to take pictures but take care not to have your back towards the main shrine - else you will be asked to delete them by the vigilant guards. 
You marvel at the architecture of the temple and palace and leaves you asking fir more. The gardens are huge and well kept. 
I would recommend going there in the evenings, and once the temple visit is done you can enjoy the beauty of the kandy lake and the hills in the background.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
We saw that the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic was on every list when we researched things to do in Kandy.  It is, of course, a beautiful temple.  I especially liked the ceiling murals near the main entrance.  The main temple, however, was so crowded that it was hard to enjoy.  We happened to be there near the new year, when many people were coming with offerings.

You will need to leave your shoes at one of two kiosks before entering the temple.  Therefore, the walk from the shoe kiosk to the temple can be uncomfortably hot on your feet, so plan accordingly and perhaps wear socks.  Also, there are ticket machines where you buy your tickets, and for some reason they require exact change.  Very bizarre.  There is a man sitting near the machines who will give you change, but it was an odd encounter because we didn't really know who he was or what he was doing.  

Overall, I was underwhelmed and went because it is so famous.  However, I feel our visit to Kandy could have been fine without this.

review_text:
As perhaps the most important Buddhist site in Sri Lanka, it is almost always busy, even when we went in the last few hours it was open.

Yet, there is no denying it is a special place, with its ornate design (it was formerly the Kandyian kingÂ’s palace), and beautiful artwork within.

It is a bit of a process to enter, multiple security checkpoints, a shoe drop off and automatic ticket machines that have several other visitors frustration (we agreed to let a gentleman who offered insert our payment and all was fine - these others seemed concerned this was a scam of some sort, it was not...).

Bring your patience and you will be rewarded with a memorable visit.

review_text:

We did not enjoy it, as right after we got passed the security gate some charlatan tried to pursue us to hire him as guide to explain us the surroundings - he insisted 3 times after which he gave up and insulted us.
After that, we found that there are special prices for tourists (even though everyone arrives in the main hall) so we had to leave our shoes in the storage area, where we were asked again, on somewhat aggresive tone for a donation.
We got inside just before the service started and it was way overcrowded with people shoving themselves all the time.
All in all, not a good experience.

Be aware that your legs and shoulders must be covered (no shorts allowed), so local sellers do sell some wraps or baggy loose trousers for a fee. Once in, a short stroll through the garden to the museum itself. If you are not native to Sri Lanka, you must go to the right to deposit your shoes in a locker/storage area before then queuing, searching and enter the temple. You also may want to pick up lotus or incense offerings before you go in too. Follow the crowds, itÂ’s easy to navigate, and try not to take too many photos inside (which may offend) and pay the appropriate respects to those there for religious purposes. There is also a museum on site too towards the rear of the temple thatÂ’s worth a look too.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: The temple shows how Buddhist worshippers from Sr Lanka and around the world show their devotion. We were there in afternoon to look at the different parts of the temple including the history of the relic being enthroned in the temple. At the back is a museum of Buddhist religions in the world (included in your ticket but no photos allowed). Our visit culminated with the afternoon prayers with monks bringing offerings into the chamber of the sacred tooth (off limits to worshippers). Visitors need to be appropriately dressed and leave shoes in holding places. Since the holding place for foreigners' shoes was far from the entrance, we left our shoes (in our shoe bags) in the locals' holding place which is nearer the entrance. Just show your ticket.

review_text: Stayed in kandy for one night and we were getting mixed reviews about this temple so decided to visit and check on our own. While we as tourists manage to pass the queue by paying some 1000 LKR per person, you hardly get some space inside the temple. The so called chamber with the sacred tooth remains open only for a specific time and you hardly get a glimpse of it. Keeping aside the history and faith of locals, there is nothing much for the tourists here.

Also watch out for your valuables as it's very crowded inside.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
We visited this place on a Sunday so it was crowded however it was so serene to see all the devotees in white with their love offerings waiting for the evening prayer time at 6:30 p.m. 

It is a very big complex, neat and well maintained and has security checks at all entry points. Our guide Hiren explained the significance of this holy place.  The statues and artifacts are so beautiful to see.  The motifs and frescoes are a treat to the eye.

The sacred relic is exposed in a procession every 5 years. The altar housing the relic is so beautifully decorated.

They even have a museum included in the cost which has rich culture and heritage explained thru the artifacts well preserved where photography is not permitted.  There's an entrance fee for foreigners at this place.

This place is bang in the city so parking can be a challenge especially in peak hours.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
The sacred temple of tooth relic is located right in d centre of kandy city. There are multiple entrances and we made d mistake of entering from d main entrance. We literally stood for a good half hour to clear security. Its too crowded. After entering inside we realised theres other not so crowded entrances too. 
Entry for foreigners is 1000LKR. Its a huge temple complex. The actual tooth relic is open to public only twice a day. We werent tht lucky to see it. There are also a couple of museums inside d complex,do check them out. Spend some time exploring d whole complex. Click a lot of pics. If ur in kandy then do visit this temple that holds the actual tooth of Lord Buddha. Whole temple had peaceful positive vibes. We especially enjoyed the visit to the Buddhism in the world museum,u will easily miss it in d premises if u dont go looking for it. Do visit it, the entrance ticket includes d entry for d museum. It has some unbelievably amazing exhibits

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: This temple is very interesting and it's good to have a guide explaining all about bhuddism and the story of the tooth and the temple itself. However, be careful of the person who offers himself as a guide. He will be very polite and knowledgeable but will not tell you what he charges. As a tourist paying an entrance ticket,we thought that at the end of his explanation we would give him a tip. However, when he finished, he asked to see our tickets to check how much time he had spent with us. He then asked for 3000 rupees per hour. We decided to give them to him to save arguing, however, we told him that he was a dishonest person and should be ashamed. Sri Lanka is a lovely country but such actions will not help their bid to regain their tourism again.

review_text: The Temple of the Sacred Tooth holds Sri Lanka's most sacred Relic, a tooth of the Buddha. Unfortunately we did not get to see the casket housing the Relic, but were still awed by the beauty of the architecture and the dÃ©cor of the frescoes, moonstones and wooden frames. See the beautiful seated statue of a golden Buddha flanked by two white marble statues, other images and the ivory tusks, and then look to the ornamentation of the ceiling above. The Main Hall showcases man statue of the Buddha in various poses; suspended plaques over each give an explanation of he painted scene above. At ceiling height, above each statue, there is a sculpture of an elephant head and tusks, all coloured gold. Some wonderful features both indoors and to the buildings' exteriors. The complex was crowed with tourists and worshippers, sound muted as if all acknowledge the sanctity of the place.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
This is the place where they house the tooth of the the great Gautam Buddha. 

Points to note:
1. Pl wear at least knee length clothes to respect the area and the concept. 
2. Avoid visiting during peak noon hours as the distance between the shoe stand and the covered temple premise is a long one and you may get discomfort due to the heated stoned pathway.
3. Take a guide and as k him not to hurry.
4. Do not take snaps with the idols in the background. It is considered as a mark of disrespect.

My experience for a guide was not very great. So, will not dwell in this issue much. The entry fees is less for SAARC country members, so pl use the correct machine. The machine is automated well enough to provide you with the tickets. 

The casket - made of gold and the tooth is protects is not open throughout the year. So, check your visit date and EXPECT accordingly. 

There is a museum within this premises and it is heart touching enough to see how well they have created the various blocks of all countries where Buddhism is or was prevalent.

Date of Experience : March 2019.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
Considered as a sacred temple complex containing the sacred tooth relic of Lord Buddha, Shri Dalada Maligawa also known as Palace of sacred tooth.

This temple is a must visit for every Buddhist.

The tooth relic was originally housed in a rock carved temple in Anuradha pura before it was moved to the present palace / temple at Kandy about five hundred years ago.

This centuries old temple is serene and the worshippers pray in silence.

The temple was originally built as a royal residential palace by the royal family of Sri Lanka long time ago.

The remarkable features of this temple is the renowned recital of Kandy drums is a joy to hear.

The musical performance is unique for Sri Lanka.The musical instruments are two drums and a pipe instrument. The performance lasting about half an hour is precisely choreographed.

The puja timings are fixed  lasting about half an hour three times in a day - morning, noon and evening.

The temple premises are very well secured and spotless maintenance is visible everywhere.

You need to be properly dressed to enter the temple. Ensure that your shoulder and knees are covered.

The temple management treats every body equal. No preference seems to be given for any one. There is no shouting at or pushing of the pilgrims in the sanctum sanctorium. Everything is done in dignified silence.

The temple is a must visit while you are in Kandy, Sri Lanka.

Highly recommended.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text: We were staying close to Kandy and knew that this was one of the biggest attractions in the area and our only available day to go was on a Saturday. We left early and got to the temple area around 9:30am. You must leave your shoes with a shoe keeper and buy your ticket in the same area. Make sure you are properly dressed as they will not let you in with any knee or shoulder showing (although you can buy a sarong right there if necessary). Women and men go through separate security lines and for us, the lines were extremely long and quite slow-I believe this was because of our timing. From there, you can make your way into the main temple and line up in a hectic, crowded, and sweaty manner for a VERY quick look at the golden casket which holds the sacred tooth of Buddha. From there, you are free to wander the grounds and look into the different buildings, including a museum with artifacts under glass, a room devoted to the famous temple elephant Raja the Tusker, and also some archeological artifacts. Altogether a very fascinating look into the passionate devotion to Buddha in Sri Lanka.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
We visited this temple as part of an organised tour with Walkers tours and definitely benefited from having our guide, Sumith, giving his insight and sharing his expertise whilst we were there.  I don't think the experience would have been the same without this personal insight and informed commentary.

Firstly, to be clear you do not see the sacred tooth! If you are lucky you may get a quick peek at the casket (with its separate 5 locks) where it is housed.  If you are a tourist you can reach this by one very quick queue where Buddhists who wish to leave an offering may queue for 3 hours to reach the relic.  The feeling of reference and respect is overwhelming and moving, just close your eyes for a moment and take in the sounds of chanting and drumming, the smells of essence and offerings, the emotions shown by people of faith.  I can honestly say I felt completely overcome and still shiver at the memory.

On leaving this area there is plenty more to see which are less crowded and easier to view.  We particularly enjoyed the room with the pictures outlining the history of the sacred tooth around a statue of Buddha with another place for offerings

a must do place in Kandy, particularly if you can have an insight as to why it is so important to the people of Sri Lanka

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
I am not religious. We are here for however long whatever you believe in wants you to be and then that's it. Religion has been the cause for more trouble than almost anything. However going to see sights like this and respect another culture is surely a good way of learning. I might not understand people giving offerings but the passion and belief they have is hard to ignore. Yes its busy, yes we were pushed and shoved as people tried to get to give their offerings and yes you need to cover up. But respecting another way of life is surely what we all need to strive to do. It hasn't changed my mind, I'm not a believer but seeing people that are makes me rather humble.
Go and visit.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
We came to visit on a Saturday at around 7:00am. There were already lots of devotees coming in since it was a day of worship and offering for most of the locals. 

Upon entering the temple grounds, we went to buy our tickets and leave our shoes at the designated counter.

Although I am not a Buddhist, it was still a very special spiritual feeling coming inside. Devotees mostly in white were already lined up to go to the top to give their offerings. While the relic room was not yet open, we went inside the other small rooms. One room housed many books written by Buddha himself.

Wearing modest clothes is a must. Please also be mindful and respectful of the rules. This is their sacred place of worship and we are very lucky to be granted access inside. Read the signs around and be sure to follow them.

You cannot bring in drinks, cigarettes or lighters.

location: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
review_text:
Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic is a Buddhist temple in the city of Kandy, Sri Lanka. It is located in the royal palace complex of the former Kingdom of Kandy.  It is a very important Sri Lankan temple as it houses the relic of the tooth of the Buddha. 

We visited this temple as part of a G Adventures tour in the evening when the doors of the area where the casket that houses the tooth relic is open,  This allows the locals as well as the tourists to see this casket.  

Due to problems with possible terrorists, there are high security measures taken before you can enter the temple.  You must also be appropriately dressed with women wearing clothes that cover their shoulders and knees and men should wear full length pants.  Most of the locals wear complete white outfits to show their respect when visiting the temple.

It is a very busy in this temple and you cannot wear your shoes in it.  I had a guide help me through the temple, which I would not have been able to do if he had not helped me up and down the numerous stairs you need to use to see the entire temple.  

The museum that is attached to the temple was also interesting to see as it held many sacred texts about Buddha's life.

review_text:
From the car park, there is a 10-minute walk upstairs, it is steep but mostly in the shade. The caves are next to each other and the total time you need for this place is about 1 hour.

The cave temples are well preserved and very richly decorated -statues, wall and ceiling paintings with vivid colours and nice details. Absolutely worth visiting. After looking at other drip-ledge caves this brings the whole idea to a new level.

Some caves are lit up by nice yellow lights, which are properly positioned and I assume to give some resemblance to the candles once used in those temples. Others, unfortunately, are blasted in all directions by bright white hospital-like lights.

On our way out we decided to revisit some caves, but the power was down, so if you are unlucky to visit during a power outage you won't be able to fully enjoy this site.

Entrance fee: 1500 LKR
Guide: sign says 750, the one who tried to trick us into guiding us offered his services at 500 before us declining his offers, unfortunately, I couldn't understand him well. 

Some unpleasant things:
- We encountered a very rude staff member at the entrance.
- Scaffolding has been left inside some of the caves, despite no signs of any work going on. Ruins the atmosphere and some photos.
- No information at the site at all, hire a guide or read online.

review_text: This is a really interesting place. It's a small temple complex at the top of a hill off of the main road through Dambulla town. It is quite a long, steep climb from the Golden Buddha statue up the steps to the caves so take your time. No shoes allowed in the temple area (there's a place to store them outside the entrance) so have some socks with you as it is very hot underfoot. Once you're in, there are five main caves accessed by a small temple facade built into the rock face. In each of the caves there are lots of Buddha statues of various sizes ranging from human sized up to massive lying down Buddhas about 15 metres long. Take a note of the ornately painted cave ceilings too. Depending on when you visit, the monks do occasionally shut the caves for prayer, but no problem it's only for about 15 minutes. Tip - if you're driving or being driven, enter by the rear steps on the access road a little further into town, as this way you pass the ticket office. Otherwise you'll climb all the way up to the entrance and then have to descend by about 100 steps down to buy your ticket, then climb back up again to get in.

review_text:
We stopped off here on our way to sigiriya and honestly wished we didn't bother. You have to walk all the way up to the entrance to the temples and walk back down the other side to get a ticket. In the sweltering heat this is not ideal as it's a lot of steps (and we're pretty fit!). There were a lot of older people who made it all the way to the top but then had to give up because the paving is so uneven and there are no hand rails, we felt really bad for them!!
Once your shoes are off you have to walk on boiling hot stones, so I would recommend you bring some socks to prevent blisters/burns. 
Once we were up there the temples were ok but not great... Maybe we're just not that cultured?! 
You get constantly harassed by people asking if you want a guide/ buy a 'magic box'or very sadly if you want to watch a poor snake which has been 'charmed' and shoved in a basket. 
The monkeys on the way up are cute though!

The monument itself is amazing and unique, a temple full of any kind of buddha statue but unfortunately left at is fate without any signs anywhere.

review_text: This site is also known as the Golden Temple of Dambulla, a UNESCO site, and the largest and best-preserved cave temple complex in Sri Lanka. The climb to the caves can be fairly taxing depending on age and fitness levels, but worth the effort to view this great complex. There are five caves containing in excess of 150 statues,  and extensive murals relating to the Gautama Buddha and his life. The caves are formed by a very large overhang in the face of the rock that has been partitioned and now sits behind a structure of white painted arched colonnades and gabled entrances. It is a mystical site. Enjoy wonderful panoramic views outside, the sun shone and the Rock of Sigiriya was visible in the distance. The visit was made more relevant and informative by our excellent tour guide.

There is a flight of stairs before reaching the temple. The route has shade. There are many monkeys so make sure not to feed them and keep your bags closed and belongings in check so the monkeys will cannot snatch them. 

We entered the temple complex on foot. When visiting any of the temples in Sri Lanka, it is a must that the knees and shoulders are always covered. Wear modest clothes during your trip. Bring along a skirt and a shawl inside your bag. It really comes in handy.

As I entered each of the five chambers of the Golden Temple, I felt a sense of serenity that's almost overwhelming. 

When planning your trip to Sri Lanka, don't miss this temple. It is amazing, I guarantee. Take some time to close your eyes and meditate for a few minutes.

Dambulla Royal Cave Temple or the Golden Cave Temple of Dambulla is the most well preserved cave temple in Sri Lanka. The paintings and statues depict the life of Gautama Buddha. The paintings on the walls and the ceilings tell many stories. These paintings are all made from natural dyes mainly from saps of plants.

review_text:
This is a complex of caves/ temples, accessible after a fairly steep climb. The climb might be difficult, especially once the sun is up but this attraction is worth all the effort and trouble. The statues, carvings and paintings on the walls and ceilings are all awe-inspiring, making you wonder how this must have been built centuries back. The people are very friendly and the place spic and span. 
I would suggest wearing loose and comfortable clothes which cover your body (at least the knees), to counter the heat and the climb, as well as to avoid hurting religious and cultural sentiments.

review_text:
It was early evening when we arrived at the temple of five caves of varying size and interior dated 1st BC.

There are more than 80 caves in the area with the 5 caves most worth viewing. The first king turned the caves into a temple complex and many kings added to it later until the 11th century. It is still a functioning temple complex till this day.

The spectacular murals on the ceilings were of sheer magnificence. They depicted BuddhaÂ’s life and sermons. 

The guide pointed out the large statue of the reclining Buddha on his deathbed judging by the way the feet was displayed. Stupas, a hundred small Buddha statues, some gods and goddesses and kings statues were on display. 

One of the five caves was under repair, and we managed to take a quick look of it. The second cave was the largest and most impressive.

They say you must never turn your back to the Buddha when taking a photo. I felt intense spiritual power in these ancient caves and decided against taking any pictures out of respect.

There was a small basin with water dripping down from the ceiling that the guide said would never dry up and have healing powers.

Once out of the temple caves we realised how the temple was cut out of a massive overhanging rock. We went under a huge Bodhi tree and made a wish. It was just too bad we could not find time to see the ancient Bodhi tree at Anuradhapura. 

A very moving spiritual experience indeed.

review_text:
The climb up the steps to the temple offers some wonderful views including a panorama of Lion Rock and Pidurangala Rock.  It is steep in places, so take some water with you; there's nowhere to buy any at the top!

You need to leave your shoes (100 Rps per person) and entry to the temple complex is 1500 Rps each. Remember to dress appropriately for visiting a temple.

There are 5 caves; the newest being the furthest away.  Perhaps worth starting here and working back as the older caves have the better workmanship.  The statues and wall paintings are very impressive. You can get up close; which is maybe not such a good thing given the age of some of the caves.

There is little (or no) information whilst walking around.  If you are touring Sri Lanka with a guide, then not a problem as the guide will relay the important information.  Otherwise read up beforehand as part of what makes it really impressive is the knowledge that some parts are over 2000 years old!

The whole visit only takes an hour or so.  For us it was a really convenient stopping off point on the drive between Kandy and Habarana (where we based ourselves to see Lion Rock, Minneriya and Polonnaruwa)

review_text:
For our final stop in Sri Lanka we came here in the late afternoon on the way from our hotel in the Sigiriya area to the airport in Negombo. 

It was very hot and impossible to avoid dripping in sweat by the time you get to the top (not ideal when heading to the airport). Once at the top, the cave temples are fascinating, though relatively compact. As ever there is the annoyance of having to take your shoes off and navigate the burning hot stone.

Major disappointment though was the absolutely outrageous charge for the toilets once we got to the bottom. R100 is 5-10x the going rate in Sri Lanka. Money grabbing attitude that is going to get a bad review from me every time

review_text:
The Dambulla Cave Temple is reached by climbing a lot of steps. The trick is to make sure you buy your ticket to enter the caves at the bottom of the steps, as it is not obvious this is the process. To enter most Buddhist Temples you need to dress modestly, no exposed shoulders and knees covered - they do rent items to cover you at the temple entrance. You also need to pay to have your shoes minded whilst you are in the temple and the person you pay is very reluctant to give change so make sure you have the exact amount of 25 rupees. The cost to enter the cave is 1500 rupees. 
There are five caves and they are stocked with many Buddhas in all manner of positions - if you are yet to visit Myanmar, Thailand, or other such Buddhist countries you will be amazed, but to be honest the South East Asian countries have many of these caves and do it all a lot better. 
It is though an interesting experience to visit this cave temple.

review_text:
The cave temple complex is around 300 steps from the plains. The ticket price is 1500 Srilankan rupees. Please make sure to cover your legs and shoulders. Incase if you dont cover, they provide some clothes to cover and charge 100 Rs. You have to remove shoes before you enter the temple. There is a shoe stall, you can leave your shoes there, they charge 25 Rs. As soon as you enter, there are tour guides, who will approach you to take the tour with them, they will try to insist on it but decline them politely. Incase if you want to take, fix the price first.
There are no written stories about the 5 cave temples, so i guess the tour guides can be helpful, if you really want to know the stories. Orelse you can google about it and find it on wikipedia Â“Dambulla cave templeÂ” 
There are around 150 Buddha statues with lot of fresh flowers, some Srilankan Kings and Hindu gods. The paintings on the ceilings, walls are amazing.
After you leave the temple, you can take another exit and head down to the Golden Buddha temple where the huge statue of Buddha facing the mountains is astonishing.

After visiting the temple you can head over to the Golden Buddha temple which is on the way down from other side, so take the other way down and its the entrance is free of cost there.

review_text:
You don't need a guide, just a guide book to appreciate the history and beauty of the cave temples.  
You will need to wear clothes that cover your knees and your shoulders.  Don't be one of those disrespectful tourists that hasn't bothered and has to borrow a sarong.  Also, it's worth wearing socks - you are asked to take your shoes off but the rock paving is very hot by the afternoon and hard to walk on in bare feet - socks help!
The temples date back to the 1st century BC and there is evidence of settlement here before that.  The main attractions are 5 caves full of ancient Buddhist frescos and Buddha statues.  Because they have been protected from sunlight the colours are vivid and beautiful.  The whole place is very peaceful and relaxing - enjoy.  Also, there are lots of monkeys outside who provide great entertainment!

It was a bit of a trek, but fine, definitely worth it to see the cave temple. ItÂ’s amazing how tranquil they are considering the crowds. There are 5 caves in all. The first one is tiny so some patience (and queuing) is needed. The second one is huge and the third is pretty big too. When youÂ’ve seen those three youÂ’ve seen the best of it and the other caves are just more of the same. 

Remember to cover your shoulders and knees. Take a pair of socks because you canÂ’t wear shoes inside. They will look after your shoes outside the entrance for 50Sr a pair. Otherwise take a bag and carry them around. Also, most importantly donÂ’t pose for pictures with your back to Budda, itÂ’s a big no no. The path to the left on the way down leads you to the Golden Temple Of Dambulla, with its giant Budda, which is worth seeing just by itself. Overall this was definitely worth the trek and weÂ’re happy we saw this impressive cave temple. 

Iain, London

The caves are fantastic and hard to believe they are man made.  The history is incredible and all the caves are worthy of a visit. Hard to believe the paintings and Buddhas in the caves.

The views are also good from the top.  You can also have a blessing whilst there.

It is worth rembering that shoulders and knees must be covered and no shoes allowed when you go through the entrance.

review_text:
Made a special trip here based on TA reviews and very glad we made the effort. 

Three very different caves the last one of which used to be a store room before being converted. The reclining Buddha which had been carved out of the granite is truly wonderful. The effort required to carve the granite with what we a know as very primitive tools must have been immense. 

Our guide talked us through each cave and the history surrounding it.

One piece of advice, we ate in the cafe by The Foreigners car park, the food was amazing. Two Rotis and a bottle of water 150 rupees, its government funded which is why itÂ’s so cheap.

review_text:
This is a very interesting temple with an amazing history. Get a guide.
There are a number of steps up from the car park but they are level and easy walking. There are five temples to see each with different statues, rock carvings and wall paintings.
The views are stunning, the temple flowers beautiful and the monkeys delightful.
In the car park is a cafe (of sorts) and toilets. Look out for the "Jack fruit" tree with the amazing and very large Jack fruits. Tasty too.

review_text: The hike up to the caves is by a longish flight of steps and takes about 20 minutes. There is an extensive array of Buddha statues and painted images (>150) many of which are interesting. We were unfortunate to arrive at a time when the caves were closed for prayers and so a large number of visitors accumulated outside the caves waiting to be admitted, which meant the caves became extremely crowded and difficult to move around once they reopened - I imagine it would be much less of a problem if you are able to arrive some time after the caves have been reopened (unfortunately I do not know when the prayer times are).

review_text:
Stopped here on our tour of Sri LankaÂ’s cultural triangle. 

Very interesting place and worth a visit (and worth climbing all the steps). 

A few pointers:

ItÂ’s worth having a guide with you. We were on a private tour of the country with a driver/guide and he was able to explain the history of the caves and the significance of the paintings in each one. It would have been quite difficult to have the same appreciation if you just went up and looked around by yourself.  

ItÂ’s a fully functioning religious site, of huge significance to the Sri Lankan people. There are periods of worship throughout the day when visitors need to wait outside. Both ladies and gentlemen need to wear clothes which cover the elbows and their knees. Transgressors were turned away without exception (and left at the mercy of the very enterprising sarong salesman on the steps outside!)

Our guide intervened when a Japanese tourist was about to commit the massively disrespectful offence of photographing his companion with her back to an image of Buddha. There are warnings about this everywhere and in every guide book, so there is really no excuse.

review_text: The Dumbulla Rock Temple is an impressive and interesting place to visit. However, be warned that there are approximately 350+ steps to navigate before you reach the actual caves! I would definitely recommend going during the early part of the morning, before the heat starts to rise. As you enter the complex, you are greeted by a magnificent Buddha statue, and a general information center. Then the ascent begins. I am fairly fit, and it took me and our group about 40 minutes to get to the caves, with a few rest bite stops. Please remember to wear clothes which are longer than knee length as you will not be able to enter. They only seem to charge foreigners (approximately Â£7), to enter the main cave complex, which I don't think is fair,  as either everyone should pay something, or it should be free for all. Either way, the caves are impressive, with several ancient paintings and statues, created over several centuries by devotees to Lord Buddha. As we all religious sites, it is always an interesting visit, and the history of the caves are impressive. As an added bonus, the views from the top are breathtaking and shows the real beauty of Sri Lanka. Definitely worth a visit, but go early to avoid the crowds and the heat.

The most impressive thing is being there and try to imagine how it was built. Out of the 5 caves I found 1 very beautiful. 

I think staff at the entrance is very picky about clothes so you have to borrow a scarf from next door (100 rupees). I was wearing long trousers and very short sleeves t-shirt and they made me go for a scarf. I think it was adequate dressing code but anyway...it seemed to me they have a good business up there because once you are there, it is very unlikely to go down just to bring something to cover your arms. Also, there is a paid place to leave shoes whereas in other temples you could just leave them outside

conservation of the paintings is wonderful. Lighting could be a bit better. Some parts are rather dark.

review_text:
The walk up is scenic and the steps manageable as you can admire the view and take photos if you need a breather.

Go early because itÂ’s cooler and especially at the weekend when the locals will visit to pray.

ItÂ’s the largest conserved cave temple in Sri Lanka. There are four caves containing statues and painted images of budda. The paintings cover the walls and ceilings and you need to allow your eyes to acclimatise to the dim lighting and then take in the detail. It was pretty busy on the Sunday morning that we visited and the caves were humid and full of visitors trying to get the perfect shot which created some bottle necks. Then, in the midst of all the tourist footfall,  there were the local worshippers making their offerings which helped to remind you what this place is really all about. ItÂ’s worth taking some quiet time to soak up the atmosphere and to enjoy the place before heading back down.

Dress modestly, remove your shoes and turn off the flash.

review_text:
This is an ancient Cave temple that dates back to the 1st century. There are five chambers with murals painted all over the walls and Buddha's carved out of stone. 

The golden temple is also part of the UNESCO site.

review_text:
Having been to a large number of buddist temple sites in SE Asia - including other cave temples - I found Dambulla interesting and beautiful but not entirely unique. If you have not been to many other places that are similar it is definitely a must visit. Otherwise, I'd recommend it if you have time and interest in this type of attraction but I would not rearrange my schedule to fit it in.

The caves themselves are not very large and are quite warm inside. The walls and ceilings are painted and beautiful to look at - more so then the Buddhas in my opinion. The lighting is ROUGH for photography unless you have specialized equipment. The caves are dark with spotlights in various areas. This makes the location less of an Instagram-worthy location if that's your thing but most people should enjoy the sights just fine. 

I'd recommend going first thing in the morning to avoid crowds and to avoid the heat. The caves were already hot at 8 am so I can't imagine what it gets like later in the day. Also be prepared to climb stairs to get there. About 365 of them. Its steep and while I thought it was worth the cardio workout - someone who is out of shape or who has impaired mobility may not be able to make it.

Tips:

- don't forget to wear long pants and tops with shoulders covered. Men included. or bring a sarong to wrap around if you have shorts on. 

- This is a Buddhist temple so you need to leave your shoes near the entrance (there is a safe location to do so) and walk around barefoot. You will be walking on stone/concrete. 

- With the climb up and plenty of time spent in each cave we did the whole thing in 1.5 hours. 

- There is plenty of parking and clean bathrooms at the bottom of the stairs for public use.

review_text:
We visited the Dambulla caves on the 18th of December 2018. The caves are at a slight altitude so I would recommend wearing something comfortable for a 20-30 minute hike up some steep steps. Also there were many monkeys near the steps so I would recommend not taking anything edible like fruits etc openly since it could attract the monkeys. Also remember that there is an entrance fee of ~1500 LKR so don't forget to buy these tickets before climbing the steps

Once you climb the steps and reach the top, the view is absolutely beautiful! There is a place to store your footwear near the cave complex just besides the entrance.

The caves themselves are very beautiful and I would recommend that you take your best night/low light photography equipment you have. The paintings on the top of the caves are very colorful and detailed and you would definitely want to take a few shots of these pictures. The statues of the Buddha's in various poses are a real sight to see. The cave complex itself is very well maintained and shouldn't take you more than 50-60 minutes to complete.

TIP: if you plan to visit the Temple complex during the evening I would highly recommend a torch light and some mosquito repellent. It can get very dark once the sun sets and there were many mosquitos on the way down mainly because of the surrounding forests.

This place is definitely worth a visit with family and friends.

Called here in November. I think the guide said there were 450 steps but not arduous, although the steps have been worn in place. Taken carefully well worth the effort. Once at the top you will need to remove you shoes, and there's an area that will cost charge you 25 rupees to look after. You can put socks on and some may need it when really hot as the stone does hold the heat. 
Multiple caves with a huge amount of Buddhas and statues.
Worth having a guide or reading the story beforehand as this helps understanding what each area represents. 
Please bear in mind when what their culture finds rude and offensive especially taking photos (turning your back in the Buddha I've selfies is offensive and unacceptable as well as posing with the Buddhas)

The toilets and facilities at the bottom of the steps is basic.

But would recommend this area.

review_text:
I had the opportunity to visit the cave two weeks ago.  It is an inspiring experience where you feel that you have gone back in time.  The caves are full of incredible carvings of the "Lord Buddha."  The expertise of the artists who created this incredible religious sanctuary is up there with the tomb painters of Egypt.

The view from the temple complex is beautiful and looks over a lush and verdant valley. Look out for the monkeys - they might grab food out of your hands.  The climb is not to bad - nothing like Sigiriya and is a experience that children of all ages will enjoy.  Bring drinking water with and do the climb early or late to avoid the midday heat.

review_text:
There are 5 caves here reached by a staircase which is a little climb. These are temples and you need to remove your shoes and be appropriately dressed before entering the complex. There is a shoe place just by the entrance where you can pay to leave your shoes. 

The caves are of varying ages and interest. There is still a lot of restoration work taking place on the walls and ceilings but the main caves are quite beautiful and glisten with the colours of the various Buddhas; there are over 150 of them. It is the best preserved cave complex in Sri Lanka.

Its also quite dark in the caves so you need to push the camera settings if not using flash.

Its well worth the visit which we did enroute to Kandy from Sigiriya.

We visited this temple as part of a guided tour of parts of Sri Lanka.  I definitely consider our experience was so enhanced by having our tour guide, Sumith, take time to point out to us the history of the 5 caves, the meaning and differences of the various statues and cultural aspects - so much more interesting and of value than "just" walking around. 

If you are not within a guided tour then would highly recommend finding detailed information about this site before you go.

at the time of our visit the only option was to reach the temple caves via about 400 steps, some very steep but there was help at hand along the way, places to stop and good handrails, so dont be put of - well worth the climb

this is a religious site, so light coloured clothing covering legs and arms is required - this was not clear from info provided by tour operators

a stunning temple to visit

review_text:
It's a steep climb up well made steps to reach the caves which are actually rock overhangs which have walls to protect them from the elements. This is is also the site of a monastery and at times of worship ( preceded  by drumming) the caves are closed to the public for a short time.
It's a temple and ladies must have legs and shoulders covered, no shorts or vest tops for men. Shoes are left at the top of the steps ( take socks in hot weather so you don't burn your feet in the courtyard).
The art on the walls and ceilings is magnificent at times looking like beautiful embroidery. The lighting makes the caves very atmospheric with the numerous Buddha statues illuminated.
It's well worth reading up on the caves before you visit as they all date from different periods. The far left cave has had some poor restoration ... it would have been better to leave it as it was.

review_text:
Visited here as part of our tour of Sri Lanka and thought it was very impressive. The climb took me by surprise and after a busy day doing lots of climbing struggled abit but just take it steady.
As with all temples remember to take a pair of old socks to wear as you need to remove your shoes and the ground is uneven and rough under foot.
The caves were amazing and so much better than I expected that this place is definitely worth a visit. 
I read afterwards that you should start with the cave further away and work backwards, we did not do this but would recommend you do.
Outside lots of locals trying to sell you their goods -make sure you barter.

review_text:
Great temple any many statues of budda.

Make sure you buy your ticket at the entrance which is BEFORE the large climb. The ticket booth is a tiny grilled window which is very easy to miss.

The temple is amazing inside considering how much rock there was to carve out.

Make sure you cover shoulders and legs.

Avoid the hustlers at the top by not hanging around. The shoe guardians are also hustlers themselves which is very surpirsing but just roll with it.

The climb is ok but the stairs wear to a slope at one point.

review_text:
Be prepared for a long, steep climb following the Â“KingÂ’s WayÂ”! But worth it and the inevitable stops allow the admire the stunning views over the country side. As in some other places of worship, shoes have to be taken off. May be wearing socks is a good idea. Engaging a guide is highly recommended. Ours was really very good and gave us information broader than only concerning the Temple.
The Temple in the five caves starts from 100 BC - caves 1,2 and 4. The fifth cave is from the beginning of XX century. There are impressive statures of The Buddha as well as other statues all from different materials. The wall frescoes are from later times or have been repainted later. Really interesting and impressive. There is a Stupa which appears broken and repaired. And indeed it had been broken in 1936 and all the treasures, jewellery donated by kings and queens through time, have been stolen. Regrettably, never found and recovered.
Highly recommended and it is a must as it sheds light on Sri Lankan history and relation to Buddhism, stimulating further learning about this nation.

review_text:
The Dambulla Cave Temple, also known as the Golden Temple of Dambulla, is a must-visit attraction when traveling to Sri Lanka. Located just 10 minutes away from Dambulla village, the temple can be easily reached by bus or tuk-tuk. The entrance fee is 2000 LKR (around 5 Euros), which is well worth the cost to experience this unique and sacred place.

Upon arrival, visitors must remove their shoes and dress appropriately out of respect for the temple. The climb to reach the temple takes around 20 minutes, but the views of the surrounding mountains along the way are breathtaking and make the journey even more worthwhile.

The Dambulla Temple is divided into two parts: the temple cave and the golden Buddha. It's important to note that if you want to see the golden Buddha, you should not go back to the main entrance. Instead, continue on to the lower level of the temple, where the golden Buddha is located.

Inside the temple cave, visitors will be amazed by the intricate and well-preserved ancient cave paintings and statues of the Buddha. The peaceful atmosphere of the temple is truly awe-inspiring, and visitors can take their time to explore the cave and take in the stunning surroundings.

Overall, the Dambulla Cave Temple is an unforgettable experience that shouldn't be missed when visiting Sri Lanka. The climb to the temple may be a bit challenging, but the reward of exploring this sacred and historical site, along with the breathtaking views of the mountains, is worth the effort.

review_text:
This almost thousand year old temple was built by a grateful king who was given shelter by Buddhist monks when he was on the run from enemy armies.

The paintings look like they were painted only yesterday but in reality they are many centuries old.

The temple is very well maintained and is a sacred place for Buddhists.

The staff are polite and friendly. They waited patiently for us to see all the caves before closing the temple complex for the day.

The approach to the temple has been very well maintained with chiseled steps, handrails, lights and resting places.

It is suggested that a cable car system could be installed for the pilgrims who are unable to climb all those steps.

The temple is in excellent condition and the rock temple is a beautiful place to visit and meditate.

A must visit while you are in Dambulla, Sri Lanka.

Highly recommended.

review_text:
Visited the cave complex from Habarana for a few hours after a day by the pool. 

Easy to get to by bus (45/48 from Habarana junction in direction of Kandy) but make sure they let you off by the front of the golden Buddha rather than in town (my conductor refused for some reason which meant a bit of a long walk). 

As others have said I can highly recommend getting a tuk tuk round to the ticket office then itÂ’s only a short climb up to the top (15 mins). 

Once you are up there the views are epic, if you go late afternoon (around 4.30pm for me) there are not too many people around so easier to see the caves properly. Suggesting starting from the furthest cave and working your way back towards the entrance as this gives you more of a build up. 

Caves were impressive and had a really peaceful atmosphere, highly recommended. Afterwards just head down main staircase and flag down a bus going back your direction from the road.

review_text: As this is a temple be prepared to dress appropriately, knees and shoulders covered for both men and women.  Note that unlike some temples around the world there is no option outside the temple to hire a sarong type thing to cover up with.  Plan your day accordingly and do what we did, which was to do a quick change in to long pants inside our van prior to heading to the temple, our last activity for the day.  We had a guide which was organised by our driver, he was very good sharing extensive knowledge throughout the various caves.  Be mindful when taking photos as it is disrespectful to face your back to Buddha, so donÂ’t try and take selfies with Buddha in the background.  You need to leave your shoes outside with attendants who charge you a small donation fee, you pay the fee on retrieval of your shoes so have some small change on you.  The caves are amazing and will take approx an hour at the most depending on how much your guide likes to talk to complete the caves.  Another must see while in Sri Lanka.

review_text: We didn't know what to expect and certainly didn't expect the amount of stone steps we had to climb, but it was so worth it when we got to the top.  There are a series of 5 Buddhist temples in the hillside caves.  Start with the oldest, several hundred years old up to the last one which was created in the 1950's. review_text: We made a short visit to this cave temple on way to Sigiriya. It was historic and magnificent and is still used as place of worship. Entrance fee for adult is LKR1,500/- each.  As it was a religious public holiday, we saw many worshippers too and walked up to the temple with one family who showed us the way. I tried to walk barefoot with them but was too much for me. They told me it was okay to wear my shoes up and took it off before entering the temple. We left our shoes at the shoes counter for LKR25/- a pair, no tickets are issued for this but the man with fuzzy hair assured us not to worry as he would remember whose shoes they belong to.  Alternatively, you can leave your shoes in the open at your own risk. review_text:
A short hike up the hill, the Dambulla cave temples are a really great place to be. As it is a working temple, you need to be covered shoulders and below the knees, and take off your shoes when you get there, but this is normal practice around Sri Lanka. 

The 5 temples are cut into the side of the rock - put there by different kings across time, to show their devotion to Buddhism. Do beware of the "guides" that will talk you through the first cave and then offer to take you around the others in return for payment - you can just say no and they will leave you alone.

They are beautiful, the detail and differences between them is amazing. There is also a bag drop in the Buddhist book centre at the bottom of the hill so if you come with travelling backpacks you can leave them there!

To get to the temple you have to take a tuk tuk from Dambulla, expect to pay around 250-300 LKR. Bargain if they ask for more. 
Get your tickets at the office before you start climbing up stairs or you'll have to go back down and you really don't want that. 
The stairs are not too steep but it's being the hottest April in Sri Lanka in 140 years... So if you're planning on going April-May 2019 make sure you take enough water. There's a juice bar near the entrance and after that NOTHING, so again, bring plenty of water and a hat. Socks are recommended cause the floor gets very hot and you have to lose your shoes. 
The caves are nice, totally worth going, specially if you come from another culture where you never get to see budist temples. If you want to see the Buddha of the Golden Temple, go down the stairs right next to the shoe keeper.

review_text: At times, especially on the climb to the top, this site is ramshackle and dilapidated.  Cons and grifters line the route.  Need a ticket? review_text:
It's a bit of a hike - about 200 steps - to get to the top, but it's worth it. The statues are incredibly colorful and well-preserved. The five caves differ in size and in the number of Buddhas, but they all have something special to offer.

Don't miss the Dambulla Cave Temple!

One bit of advice - take an extra pair of socks. As with any temple, you'll have to take your shoes off before entering, but the ground and the walkways between the caves can get VERY HOT, so bring a pair of socks to slip on. Also, go early in the day to avoid the crowds and the heat.

review_text:
The Dambulla Cave Temple, famous for its ancient mural paintings depicting the life and work of Buddha, is a significant site for cultural and history of Sri Lanka.

There are five caves housing statuses of Buddha from different time ranging from 1 century BC to some 200 years ago. It's advisable to get some background of it or hire a guide (in white clothes) from the temple to walk you through. There are so much subtleties on display - for examples, the different postures of Buddha, the material used at different era and the reasons.

There are 2 ways of reaching the temple - one from the Golden Temple from town, and the other one from an open car park. The latter one is shorter but the view is breath taking.

review_text:
Dambulla cave temple also known as the Golden Temple of Dambulla is a World Heritage Site in Sri Lanka. The largest and best-preserved cave temple complex major attractions are spread over five caves, which contain statues and paintings. These paintings and statues are related to Gautama Buddha and his life. There are a total of 153 Buddha statues, three statues of Sri Lankan kings and four statues of gods and goddesses. The latter include Vishnu and the Ganesha. The murals cover an area of 2,100 square metres. Depictions on the walls of the caves include the temptation by the demon Mara, and Buddha's first sermon.

review_text_clean: dambulla cave temple also known as the golden temple of dambulla is a world heritage site in sri lanka. the largest and best-preserved cave temple complex major attractions are spread over five caves, which contain statues and paintings. these paintings and statues are related to gautama buddha and his life. there are a total of 153 buddha statues, three statues of sri lankan kings and four statues of gods and goddesses. the latter include vishnu and the ganesha. the murals cover an area of 2,100 square metres. depictions on the walls of the caves include the temptation by the demon mara, and buddhas first sermon. entrance cost 1500rs shoes deposit 25rs

The whole area around the temples was intriguing and scenic - after all its not every day you see such intricate paintings  set in such an environment. You can take photos but not with flash so phone cameras do quite well here. We decended on the opposite side of the rock which takes you into the Golden Temple that houses the giant budda. We were also able to view Lion rock in the distance and teh nable to do this in reverse the following day at Sirigiya. Worth a short visit as it is unusual.

review_text: I climbed up the 364 steps and found that there is actually another way up slope without having to climb so many steps. Remember to bring a bag to keep your shoes inside your bag or carry it around without having to store with others' shoes.  Many tourists had to use the scarf provided as the guards are pretty strict about covered sholder and over-knee attire. Honestly speaking I find that this place is over-rated after the diffiicult climb.  Been a South-East Asian, I have seen all kinds of temples so there is nothing special for me here except the structure of the building under the rock. Maybe unless one is Buddhist then it may be a must to see Otherwise, I will gladly give it a miss.

review_text:
If you have travelled much around South-east Asia you will have seen all of this before, often better and probably for free. Sure, the setting is a novelty with the temples set inside five decorated caves and there are an incredible number of Buddha statues but, fundamentally, there is little to set the place apart. We had anticipated a series of caverns but the caves are actually 5 individual units. Inside each the lighting is subdued and, as a result, the whole atmosphere is gloomy and uninspiring. We have visited many, many temples in the likes of Thailand, Myanmar and Cambodia, generally without charge, and seen some stunning interiors. Sadly this place didnÂ’t live up to those standards.
On a practical level, the ticket office is located a considerable distance from the road which makes for a significant walk (for those arriving independently) before you even begin the climb up the hill. Enter at the Golden Temple, follow the sign for the Cave Temple and just keep going until, eventually, you get to the ticket office. At 1500 rupees we felt the entry charge was way too much for what is on offer. Also, remember to take a sarong or else you will have to hire one there at additional charge (including men if youÂ’re wearing shorts).
